entry.title: は
entry.meaning: as for ~ (topic)
entry.summary: は marks the topic of a sentence — the thing you are talking about — and the rest of the sentence comments on it. It sets the stage, roughly like "as for ~", and is one of the first particles a learner meets.
pitfalls: Although written with the hiragana は, as a topic particle it is pronounced wa.
は marks the topic (often already known), while が introduces or identifies a subject; 私は学生です presents "me" as the topic, 私が学生です answers "who is the student?"

examples.ja: 私は学生です。
examples.en: I am a student.
examples.f: ｜私[わたし]は｜学生[がくせい]です。

examples.ja: 東京は人が多いです。
examples.en: Tokyo has a lot of people.
examples.f: ｜東京[とうきょう]は｜人[ひと]が｜多[おお]いです。

related.note: が identifies or introduces a subject; は sets up a known topic to comment on.
も replaces は to mean "also / too" instead of marking a plain topic.

entry.title: を
entry.meaning: direct object particle
entry.summary: を marks the direct object — the thing a transitive verb acts on (what you eat, read, buy). It can also mark the place a motion verb moves through or leaves (公園を歩く, 家を出る). Though written を, it is pronounced "o".
pitfalls: を is pronounced the same as お ("o"), but this particle is always written を.
Intransitive verbs take が, not を — say ドアが開く for "the door opens", not ドアを開く.

examples.ja: 毎朝新聞を読みます。
examples.en: I read the newspaper every morning.
examples.f: ｜毎朝[まいあさ]｜新聞[しんぶん]を｜読[よ]みます。

examples.ja: 公園を散歩します。
examples.en: I take a walk through the park.
examples.f: ｜公園[こうえん]を｜散歩[さんぽ]します。

related.note: が marks the subject that acts; を marks the object acted on.
に marks a destination or target; を marks the thing the verb acts on.

entry.title: に
entry.meaning: per; in (X times per a period)
entry.summary: This に marks a period of time as the base for a frequency: 'X times per that period'. The pattern is [time span] に [number + counter]: 一週間に三回 = three times a week, 一日に二回 = twice a day. The time span comes first with に, then the count of how often within it.
pitfalls: Order matters: the period takes に and comes first — 一週間に三回, not 三回に一週間.
This is a frequency-per-period use of に, separate from に marking a point in time (三時に = at three o'clock).

examples.ja: 私は週に二回ジムに行きます。
examples.en: I go to the gym twice a week.
examples.f: ｜私[わたし]は｜週[しゅう]に｜二[に]｜回[かい]ジムに｜行[い]きます。

examples.ja: この電車は一時間に四本来ます。
examples.en: This train comes four times an hour.
examples.f: この｜電車[でんしゃ]は｜一[いち]｜時間[じかん]に｜四[よん]｜本[ほん]｜来[き]ます。

related.note: ごとに means 'every / at each ~'; the frequency に states how many times within one period.
おきに sets the interval between occurrences; this に sets how often per a fixed period.
The base particle に has many roles; this is its 'per (period)' frequency sense.

entry.title: へ
entry.meaning: to; toward
entry.summary: へ marks the direction of movement, pointing the verb toward a place, like "to" or "toward". With motion verbs it is very close to に, but へ stresses the heading or direction rather than the exact arrival point.
pitfalls: As a direction particle, へ is written with the hiragana へ but pronounced e.
For destinations, に and へ are often interchangeable; に leans toward the arrival point, while へ leans toward the direction of travel.

examples.ja: 海へ行きたいです。
examples.en: I want to go to the sea.
examples.f: ｜海[うみ]へ｜行[い]きたいです。

examples.ja: そろそろうちへ帰ります。
examples.en: I'll head home soon.
examples.f: そろそろうちへ｜帰[かえ]ります。

synonyms.note: に marks the destination or arrival point; へ emphasizes the direction you move in.

related.note: へ行く is the common set phrase of this particle with the verb 行く.
まで marks the end point "as far as / up to"; へ just points toward a direction.

entry.title: と
entry.meaning: and (listing nouns)
entry.summary: Joins nouns into a complete list: place と between nouns to connect them, like 'and' in English. It presents the listed items as the full set, implying nothing else is included.
structure: Noun ＋ と ＋ Noun［repeatable with と］
pitfalls: と links nouns only — it cannot join verbs or whole sentences.
と implies a complete list; use や when you want to give just a few examples out of more.

examples.ja: パンと牛乳を買いました。
examples.en: I bought bread and milk.
examples.f: パンと｜牛乳[ぎゅうにゅう]を｜買[か]いました。

examples.ja: 私と妹は学生です。
examples.en: My younger sister and I are students.
examples.f: ｜私[わたし]と｜妹[いもうと]は｜学生[がくせい]です。

related.note: や lists a few representative examples; と lists the items exhaustively.
The same particle と in its other core use, 'together with' someone.
など ('etc.') marks an open-ended list; と marks a closed, complete one.

entry.title: と
entry.meaning: with; together with
entry.summary: Marks the person or thing you do something together with: place と after a noun to show a companion or partner in the action. It answers 'with whom?' and often pairs with 一緒に for emphasis.
structure: Noun ＋ と ＋ 一緒に ＋ Verb
pitfalls: This と marks a co-participant; it is a different use from the と that lists nouns ('A and B').
For a tool or means ('with a pen'), use で, not と.

examples.ja: 友達と映画を見ました。
examples.en: I watched a movie with a friend.
examples.f: ｜友達[ともだち]と｜映画[えいが]を｜見[み]ました。

examples.ja: 家族と一緒に旅行します。
examples.en: I travel together with my family.
examples.f: ｜家族[かぞく]と｜一緒[いっしょ]に｜旅行[りょこう]します。

related.note: 一緒に ('together') often teams up with と to stress doing the action jointly.
The same particle と in its listing use, 'A and B'.

entry.title: や
entry.meaning: and (such as); things like
entry.summary: や links nouns as examples from a larger set, meaning "things like A and B (among others)". Unlike と, which lists everything, や implies the list is not complete. It often finishes with など ("and so on") to make that "among others" sense explicit.
pitfalls: や joins only nouns, and hints there are more items; と joins nouns exhaustively (exactly these).
You can add など after the last item to underline "and such".

examples.ja: 机の上に本やノートがあります。
examples.en: There are books and notebooks (among other things) on the desk.
examples.f: ｜机[つくえ]の｜上[うえ]に｜本[ほん]やノートがあります。

examples.ja: 冷蔵庫に卵や牛乳が入っています。
examples.en: There are things like eggs and milk in the fridge.
examples.f: ｜冷蔵庫[れいぞうこ]に｜卵[たまご]や｜牛乳[ぎゅうにゅう]が｜入[はい]っています。

synonyms.note: と lists nouns exhaustively; や implies the list is only a sample.

related.note: など pairs with や to spell out "and so on".
も adds "also" to a set; や lists example members of a set.

entry.title: も
entry.meaning: too; also; as well
entry.summary: も replaces は, が, or を to mean "too, also", adding one item to something already mentioned. Repeat も on two items to mean "both ~ and ~". It marks the noun as sharing whatever was just said.
pitfalls: も takes the place of は, が, or を; don't stack them — say 私も, not 私はも.
With a negative verb, ...も means "not ~ either": 私も行きません = I'm not going either.

examples.ja: 私も学生です。
examples.en: I am a student too.
examples.f: ｜私[わたし]も｜学生[がくせい]です。

examples.ja: 田中さんも山田さんも日本人です。
examples.en: Both Tanaka and Yamada are Japanese.
examples.f: ｜田中[たなか]さんも｜山田[やまだ]さんも｜日本人[にっぽんじん]です。

related.note: は marks the topic and can contrast; も adds "this one as well".
や lists example items; も adds one more item that shares the statement.
と links nouns into one exhaustive list; も tacks an extra item onto the idea.

entry.title: まで
entry.meaning: until; as far as
entry.summary: まで marks the end point of a span — a time ("until") or a place reached ("as far as, all the way to"). The action or state continues right up to that limit. It frequently pairs with から, which marks where the span begins.
pitfalls: まで means "continuously up until"; to give a deadline ("by a time"), use までに instead.
Pair it with から for a "from ~ to ~" range: 九時から五時まで.

examples.ja: 昨日は夜十時まで働きました。
examples.en: Yesterday I worked until ten at night.
examples.f: ｜昨日[きのう]は｜夜[よる]｜十[じゅう]｜時[じ]まで｜働[はたら]きました。

examples.ja: この電車は横浜まで行きます。
examples.en: This train goes as far as Yokohama.
examples.f: この｜電車[でんしゃ]は｜横浜[よこはま]まで｜行[い]きます。

related.note: から marks the start point, the "from" that pairs with まで.
までに sets a deadline ("by"); まで means continuously until.

entry.title: ね
entry.meaning: isn't it?; right?
entry.summary: A sentence-ending particle that invites the listener to agree or share a feeling, roughly like the English tag "isn't it?" or "right?". You reach for it when you expect the other person already knows or feels the same, so it makes a remark sound friendly and shared rather than blunt.
pitfalls: Don't mix up ね and よ: ね assumes shared knowledge and seeks agreement, while よ pushes new information toward a listener who doesn't have it yet.
It softens speech and sounds warm, but stacking ね on every sentence can come across as needy or overly chatty.

examples.ja: 今日はいい天気ですね。
examples.en: It's nice weather today, isn't it?
examples.f: ｜今日[きょう]はいい｜天気[てんき]ですね。

examples.ja: この店は静かですね。
examples.en: This shop is quiet, isn't it?
examples.f: この｜店[みせ]は｜静[しず]かですね。

related.note: よ tells the listener something new; ね seeks agreement about something shared.
なあ voices your own admiration to yourself; ね turns the feeling toward the listener.
か asks a plain question; ね just checks that the listener agrees.

entry.title: よ
entry.meaning: emphasis / informing particle
entry.summary: よ at the end of a sentence tells the listener something you think they don't already know, or drives your point home — like adding "you know" or "I'm telling you". It presents new information or reassurance from the speaker to the listener.
pitfalls: よ presents information the speaker assumes is new; ね instead seeks the listener's agreement about something shared.
Overusing よ can sound pushy, so save it for when you are genuinely informing or reassuring.

examples.ja: この店のケーキはおいしいですよ。
examples.en: The cake at this shop is delicious, you know.
examples.f: この｜店[みせ]のケーキはおいしいですよ。

examples.ja: 鍵はテーブルの上にありますよ。
examples.en: Your keys are on the table, you know.
examples.f: ｜鍵[かぎ]はテーブルの｜上[うえ]にありますよ。

related.note: ね seeks the listener's agreement; よ informs them of something new.

entry.title: より
entry.meaning: than; compared to
entry.summary: より marks the standard you compare against — the 'than X' in a comparison. It attaches right after the noun used as the yardstick: 去年より暑い = 'hotter than last year'. The thing that comes out higher is usually marked with は or のほうが.
structure: A ＋ は ＋ B ＋ より ＋ adjective
pitfalls: より comes right after the standard being beaten: 電車は車より速い, so 車より sits next to 速い.
To pick the top out of three or more, use 一番, not より (which compares two things).
This より (comparison) is different from the formal より meaning 'from'.

examples.ja: 今日は昨日より涼しいです。
examples.en: Today is cooler than yesterday.
examples.f: ｜今日[きょう]は｜昨日[きのう]より｜涼[すず]しいです。

examples.ja: 電車で行くほうが車より速いです。
examples.en: Going by train is faster than by car.
examples.f: ｜電車[でんしゃ]で｜行[い]くほうが｜車[くるま]より｜速[はや]いです。

related.note: より〜のほうが is the fuller 'B is more ~ than A' frame built on this より.
一番 picks the single best of three or more; より compares just two things.
の中で names the group; pair it with 一番, not より, for the outright top.

entry.title: と～と、どちらが
entry.meaning: between A and B, which one?
entry.summary: This pattern asks someone to compare exactly two things and choose: AとBと、どちらが〜？ = 'Between A and B, which is more ~?' The reply typically comes back with 〜のほうが to name the winner.
structure: Noun［A］＋ と ＋ Noun［B］＋ と、どちらが ＋ い-adjective／な-adjective ＋ か
pitfalls: Use どちら (casual どっち) for a choice between two items; for three or more, ask with どれ or use 一番.
The second と is often dropped: AとB、どちらが〜 is equally natural.

examples.ja: 犬と猫と、どちらが好きですか。
examples.en: Which do you like better, dogs or cats?
examples.f: ｜犬[いぬ]と｜猫[ねこ]と、どちらが｜好[す]きですか。

examples.ja: 電車とバスと、どちらが速いですか。
examples.en: Which is faster, the train or the bus?
examples.f: ｜電車[でんしゃ]とバスと、どちらが｜速[はや]いですか。

related.note: より〜のほうが is the usual shape of the answer that names the chosen one.
For picking the top of three or more, use 〜の中で一番 instead of a two-way どちら.

entry.title: 〜の中で〜が一番
entry.meaning: the most ~ in (a group)
entry.summary: This pattern picks the top member of a defined group: の中で marks the range or category, and が一番 plus an adjective names what stands out the most. It is the everyday way to make a superlative statement about a set of things.
structure: Noun［group］＋ の中で ＋ Noun ＋ が ＋ 一番 ＋ い-adjective／な-adjective
pitfalls: Use の中で to compare within a whole category; when choosing between just two items, use 〜と〜とどちら instead.
一番 here means "number one / the most", turning the adjective into a superlative.

examples.ja: 果物の中でりんごが一番好きです。
examples.en: Of all fruits, I like apples the most.
examples.f: ｜果物[くだもの]の｜中[なか]でりんごが｜一番[いちばん]｜好[す]きです。

examples.ja: クラスの中で田中さんが一番背が高いです。
examples.en: In the class, Tanaka is the tallest.
examples.f: クラスの｜中[なか]で｜田中[たなか]さんが｜一番[いちばん]｜背[せ]が｜高[たか]いです。

related.note: 一番 is the superlative word this pattern is built around.
より〜のほうが compares two items; の中で〜が一番 ranks the top of a whole group.
は〜より…です compares two nouns directly, without singling out a group's best.

entry.title: ます
entry.meaning: polite verb ending
entry.summary: Marks a verb as polite (the ます form), used in everyday conversation with people you are not close to, in public, and at work. It attaches to the verb stem and carries the tense: negative ません, past ました, negative-past ませんでした.
structure: Verb［stem］＋ ません ／ ました ／ ませんでした
pitfalls: ます attaches to the stem, not the dictionary form — 飲む becomes 飲みます, never 飲むます.
The plain (dictionary) form is used with friends and family; switching registers mid-conversation can sound off.

examples.ja: 毎朝コーヒーを飲みます。
examples.en: I drink coffee every morning.
examples.f: ｜毎朝[まいあさ]コーヒーを｜飲[の]みます。

examples.ja: 昨日は学校に行きませんでした。
examples.en: I didn't go to school yesterday.
examples.f: ｜昨日[きのう]は｜学校[がっこう]に｜行[い]きませんでした。

related.note: です is the polite copula for nouns and adjectives; ます does the same job for verbs.
How godan (う) verbs form the stem that ます attaches to.
How ichidan (る) verbs form the stem that ます attaches to.

entry.title: ましょう
entry.meaning: let's ~
entry.summary: Politely suggests doing something together, or offers to do something. Replace the ます of a verb's polite form with ましょう. It invites the listener into an action you assume they will happily agree to, so it sounds confident and upbeat.
pitfalls: ましょう assumes the other person already wants to join; to invite more gently and leave room to decline, ませんか sounds softer.
It is the polite form — among friends the plain volitional (行こう) is used instead.

examples.ja: 一緒に昼ご飯を食べましょう。
examples.en: Let's eat lunch together.
examples.f: ｜一緒[いっしょ]に｜昼[ひる]ご｜飯[はん]を｜食[た]べましょう。

examples.ja: 三時に駅で会いましょう。
examples.en: Let's meet at the station at three.
examples.f: ｜三[さん]｜時[じ]に｜駅[えき]で｜会[あ]いましょう。

synonyms.note: ませんか invites more softly by asking, leaving the listener room to decline.

related.note: ましょうか adds か to propose and check the listener's wishes rather than assume them.
The plain volitional (行こう) is the casual equivalent of ましょう.

entry.title: ましょうか
entry.meaning: shall I ~?; shall we ~?
entry.summary: Adds か to ましょう to turn a suggestion into a question. With one doer it offers help ("shall I ~?"); with a shared doer it proposes a joint action and checks whether the listener agrees ("shall we ~?"). Unlike plain ましょう, it asks rather than assumes.
pitfalls: One subject means offering to do something for someone (手伝いましょうか = shall I help?); a shared subject means proposing to do it together.
It is more tentative than ましょう because it invites a yes-or-no answer.

examples.ja: 荷物を持ちましょうか。
examples.en: Shall I carry your bags?
examples.f: ｜荷物[にもつ]を｜持[も]ちましょうか。

examples.ja: そろそろ帰りましょうか。
examples.en: Shall we head home soon?
examples.f: そろそろ｜帰[かえ]りましょうか。

related.note: ましょう states the suggestion directly; ましょうか asks the listener first.
ませんか is a negative-question invitation; ましょうか proposes and checks agreement.
はどうですか (how about ~?) is another gentle way to float a suggestion.

entry.title: ませんか
entry.meaning: won't you ~?; why don't we ~?
entry.summary: Invites someone to do something by asking a negative question: "won't you ~?" or "why don't we ~?". Because it is phrased negatively, it leaves the listener free to say no, so it feels softer and more considerate than a direct ましょう.
pitfalls: Despite the negative ません, the meaning is a positive invitation, not a literal "don't you?".
ましょう assumes the listener will join in, while ませんか politely offers a choice.

examples.ja: 週末に映画を見ませんか。
examples.en: Why don't we watch a movie this weekend?
examples.f: ｜週末[しゅうまつ]に｜映画[えいが]を｜見[み]ませんか。

examples.ja: お茶を飲みませんか。
examples.en: Would you like to have some tea?
examples.f: お｜茶[ちゃ]を｜飲[の]みませんか。

synonyms.note: ましょう also invites, but assumes agreement instead of asking for it.

related.note: ましょうか proposes and checks; ませんか frames the invitation as a negative question.
はどうですか (how about ~?) suggests something in a similarly soft way.

entry.title: たい
entry.meaning: want to do ~
entry.summary: Expresses the speaker's own desire to do something: attach たい to a verb's stem to say "I want to ~". The result conjugates like an い-adjective (たい → たくない → たかった). Use it for your own wishes, or in a question to ask what the listener wants to do.
pitfalls: たい describes the first person's desire (or asks "you"). To report that a third person wants something, switch to たがる.
The object can take が or を — 水が飲みたい and 水を飲みたい are both fine, with が feeling a touch stronger on the wanting.

examples.ja: 甘いものが食べたいです。
examples.en: I want to eat something sweet.
examples.f: ｜甘[あま]いものが｜食[た]べたいです。

examples.ja: 新しい靴を買いたいです。
examples.en: I want to buy new shoes.
examples.f: ｜新[あたら]しい｜靴[くつ]を｜買[か]いたいです。

synonyms.note: がほしい wants a thing (a noun); たい wants to do an action (a verb).

related.note: たがる reports a third person's desire; たい is for your own.
てほしい wants someone else to do something; たい is wanting to do it yourself.

entry.title: がほしい
entry.meaning: to want (a thing)
entry.summary: ほしい is an い-adjective meaning 'wanted/desired'; 〜がほしい says the speaker wants to have a thing: 新しい靴がほしい = I want new shoes. The desired object is marked with が (sometimes は for contrast). Use たい, not ほしい, when you want to do an action rather than possess a thing.
pitfalls: ほしい describes the speaker's own desire. For what someone else wants, Japanese usually says ほしがっている, not plain ほしい.
Want a thing → 〜がほしい; want to do an action → Verb＋たい (水がほしい vs 水が飲みたい).

examples.ja: 私は新しいかばんがほしいです。
examples.en: I want a new bag.
examples.f: ｜私[わたし]は｜新[あたら]しいかばんがほしいです。

examples.ja: 今、時間がほしいです。
examples.en: Right now I want some time.
examples.f: ｜今[いま]、｜時間[じかん]がほしいです。

related.note: 〜たい wants to DO an action; がほしい wants to HAVE a thing.
〜てほしい wants someone else to do something, not to possess a thing.
The desired object is marked with が, an example of が with an adjective of feeling.

entry.title: をください
entry.meaning: please give me ~
entry.summary: Politely asks for an object by naming it, marking it with を, and adding ください: "please give me ~". Use it to request a thing — in a shop or at a restaurant. To ask someone to do an action instead, use the て form plus ください.
pitfalls: をください requests a thing (a noun); to request an action, attach ください to the て form: 待ってください.
Put a number and counter before ください to ask for a quantity: 切符を二枚ください.

examples.ja: すみません、水をください。
examples.en: Excuse me, water please.
examples.f: すみません、｜水[みず]をください。

examples.ja: この赤いりんごをください。
examples.en: I'll take this red apple, please.
examples.f: この｜赤[あか]いりんごをください。

related.note: てください requests an action; をください requests a thing.
もらう describes receiving; をください is how you politely ask to receive.

entry.title: てください
entry.meaning: please do ~ (polite request)
entry.summary: Makes a polite request or instruction: attach ください to the て form of a verb to ask someone to do something. It is the standard courteous way to tell or ask a person to perform an action, common in classrooms, signs, and everyday service situations.
pitfalls: It is polite but still a request, so to a superior a softer form such as てくださいませんか sounds more respectful.
To ask someone NOT to do something, switch to the ない form: 〜ないでください.

examples.ja: ここに名前を書いてください。
examples.en: Please write your name here.
examples.f: ここに｜名前[なまえ]を｜書[か]いてください。

examples.ja: もう一度言ってください。
examples.en: Please say it one more time.
examples.f: もう｜一度[いちど]｜言[い]ってください。

synonyms.note: Dropping ください leaves just 〜て, a casual version for friends and family.

antonyms.note: 〜ないでください asks someone not to do something; てください asks them to do it.

related.note: なさい is a firmer command used by parents and teachers; てください is a neutral polite request.

entry.title: ないでください
entry.meaning: please don't do ~
entry.summary: Politely asks someone not to do something: attach でください to the ない form of a verb. It is the negative partner of てください, so it is what you use to stop or warn someone gently in everyday polite speech.
structure: Verb［ない form］＋ で ＋ ください
pitfalls: The verb goes into the plain ない form before で — 入らないでください, never 入りませんでください.
Dropping ください leaves plain ないで, which is a casual version fine among friends but too blunt in polite situations.

examples.ja: ここで写真を撮らないでください。
examples.en: Please don't take photos here.
examples.f: ここで｜写真[しゃしん]を｜撮[と]らないでください。

examples.ja: 心配しないでください。
examples.en: Please don't worry.
examples.f: ｜心配[しんぱい]しないでください。

synonyms.note: Plain ないで on its own is the casual version of this same 'please don't' request.

antonyms.note: てください asks someone TO do something; ないでください asks them NOT to.

related.note: The plain ないで connector this polite request is built on.

entry.title: 〜てもいい
entry.meaning: may ~; it's okay to ~
entry.summary: Grants or asks permission: attach もいい to the て form of a verb to say an action is allowed. As a question it politely asks whether something is okay to do; as a statement it gives the go-ahead.
structure: Verb［て form］＋ も ＋ いい／いいです
pitfalls: As a request for permission it usually takes ですか — 入ってもいいですか ('may I come in?').
For nouns and な-adjectives, use でもいい instead of てもいい.

examples.ja: ここに座ってもいいですか。
examples.en: May I sit here?
examples.f: ここに｜座[すわ]ってもいいですか。

examples.ja: 鉛筆で書いてもいいです。
examples.en: You may write in pencil.
examples.f: ｜鉛筆[えんぴつ]で｜書[か]いてもいいです。

synonyms.note: てもかまわない ('I don't mind if') is a more indifferent-sounding permission than てもいい.

antonyms.note: てはいけない forbids the action; てもいい permits it.

related.note: なくてもいい says you don't HAVE to do it; てもいい says you MAY do it.

entry.title: てはいけない
entry.meaning: must not ~; may not ~
entry.summary: States that an action is not allowed: attach はいけない to the て form of a verb to prohibit it. It is the standard way to express rules and forbidden things, and it pairs naturally with the permission form てもいい.
structure: Verb［て form］＋ は ＋ いけない／いけません
pitfalls: In casual speech ては often contracts to ちゃ (食べてはいけない → 食べちゃいけない).
Do not confuse it with なくてはいけない, which means the opposite — that you MUST do something.

examples.ja: ここで写真を撮ってはいけません。
examples.en: You must not take photos here.
examples.f: ここで｜写真[しゃしん]を｜撮[と]ってはいけません。

examples.ja: 授業中に寝てはいけません。
examples.en: You must not sleep during class.
examples.f: ｜授業[じゅぎょう]｜中[ちゅう]に｜寝[ね]てはいけません。

synonyms.note: ちゃいけない is the casual contraction of てはいけない.

antonyms.note: てもいい grants permission ('may'); てはいけない withholds it ('must not').

related.note: The particle な is a blunt 'don't'; てはいけない is the fuller, more explanatory prohibition.

entry.title: なくてもいい
entry.meaning: don't have to do ~
entry.summary: Says an action is not required: change the verb's ない form to なくて and add もいい to mean "it's okay even if you don't do it", i.e. "you don't have to". Reach for it to give permission to skip something or to reassure someone that an action is optional.
structure: Verb［ない → なくて］＋ も ＋ いい
pitfalls: This is the opposite of なくてはいけない — なくてもいい lifts the obligation, なくてはいけない imposes it.
いい can be replaced by 大丈夫 or かまわない with the same 'no need to' meaning.

examples.ja: 明日は来なくてもいいです。
examples.en: You don't have to come tomorrow.
examples.f: ｜明日[あした]は｜来[こ]なくてもいいです。

examples.ja: 全部食べなくてもいい。
examples.en: You don't have to eat all of it.
examples.f: ｜全部[ぜんぶ]｜食[た]べなくてもいい。

antonyms.note: なくてはいけない says you must do it; なくてもいい says you needn't.

related.note: てもいい grants permission to do something; なくてもいい grants permission NOT to.

entry.title: ている
entry.meaning: is doing; is in a state of ~
entry.summary: Attaches いる to a verb's て form to express either an action in progress ("is doing") or a continuing state that resulted from an action ("has done and remains so"). Which reading applies depends on the verb, making this one of the most important — and most versatile — N5 patterns.
pitfalls: With some verbs ている means the resulting state, not an action in progress: 結婚している ("is married"), 知っている ("know"), 住んでいる ("live").
In casual speech the い drops: 食べてる, 見てる.

examples.ja: 今、音楽を聞いています。
examples.en: I'm listening to music right now.
examples.f: ｜今[いま]、｜音楽[おんがく]を｜聞[き]いています。

examples.ja: 田中さんは結婚しています。
examples.en: Tanaka is married.
examples.f: ｜田中[たなか]さんは｜結婚[けっこん]しています。

related.note: てある is a state deliberately left by someone using a transitive verb; ている can be a natural state or ongoing action.
まだ〜ていません says "haven't done yet", the negative counterpart of a ている state.
ている is built on the て form, the same base used to link verbs.

entry.title: てから
entry.meaning: after doing ~; once ~ is done
entry.summary: Chains two actions in strict order: attach から to the て form of a verb to say the second action happens only after the first is finished. It stresses that the first action comes first and is fully done before the next one begins.
pitfalls: てから is about time order, not reason — for 'because', use から attached to a plain sentence instead.
Only the final verb carries the tense; the てから clause stays in the て form no matter when the events happen.

examples.ja: 手を洗ってから昼ご飯を食べます。
examples.en: I eat lunch after washing my hands.
examples.f: ｜手[て]を｜洗[あら]ってから｜昼[ひる]ご｜飯[はん]を｜食[た]べます。

examples.ja: 仕事が終わってから、映画を見に行きました。
examples.en: After work finished, I went to see a movie.
examples.f: ｜仕事[しごと]が｜終[お]わってから、｜映画[えいが]を｜見[み]に｜行[い]きました。

synonyms.note: あとで just means 'afterwards'; てから stresses that the first action must finish before the second.

antonyms.note: まえに puts the main action before the other one; てから puts it after.

related.note: てから is built on the same て form used to connect verbs.

entry.title: 〜たり〜たりする
entry.meaning: do things like A and B
entry.summary: Lists a few representative actions without claiming they are the only ones: take the た form of each verb, add り, and finish with する. It says "I do things like A and B (among others)", which makes it handy for describing what you do on your day off or on a trip.
structure: Verb［た form］＋ り ＋ Verb［た form］＋ り ＋ する
pitfalls: The final する carries the tense and politeness — for the past, only the last verb changes: 〜たり〜たりしました.
Unlike the て form (which lists actions in strict order), 〜たり implies a non-exhaustive sample of activities.

examples.ja: 週末は本を読んだり音楽を聞いたりします。
examples.en: On weekends I do things like read books and listen to music.
examples.f: ｜週末[しゅうまつ]は｜本[ほん]を｜読[よ]んだり｜音楽[おんがく]を｜聞[き]いたりします。

examples.ja: 部屋で泣いたり笑ったりしました。
examples.en: In my room I cried and laughed, among other things.
examples.f: ｜部屋[へや]で｜泣[な]いたり｜笑[わら]ったりしました。

related.note: The て form lists actions in sequence; 〜たり gives a non-ordered sample of activities.
し lists reasons or facts side by side; 〜たり lists example actions.

entry.title: たことがある
entry.meaning: have done ~ before
entry.summary: Talks about past experience: attach ことがある to a verb's た form to say "I have done ~ (at least once) before". Use it to share what you have or haven't tried, or to ask someone whether they have ever done something.
structure: Verb［た form］＋ ことがある
pitfalls: Use the た form for experience. The dictionary form plus ことがある (koto-ga-aru) means "there are times when I do ~", a recurring possibility — not a past experience.
The negative swaps ある for ない／ありません after the same た form: 一度もしたことがありません ("have never ~, not even once").

examples.ja: すしを食べたことがあります。
examples.en: I have eaten sushi before.
examples.f: すしを｜食[た]べたことがあります。

examples.ja: 一度も遅刻したことがありません。
examples.en: I have never been late, not even once.
examples.f: ｜一[いち]｜度[ど]も｜遅刻[ちこく]したことがありません。

related.note: Dictionary form + ことがある means "there are times I do ~"; the た form means "have done before".
ことができる expresses ability ("can do"); たことがある expresses experience.

entry.title: 前に
entry.meaning: before doing ~; in front of
entry.summary: 前に marks what happens before something else. After a dictionary-form verb it means "before doing ~"; after a noun plus の it means "before" that event or, in a spatial sense, "in front of" it.
pitfalls: The verb before 前に stays in the dictionary (non-past) form even when the whole sentence is about the past: 寝る前に, never 寝た前に.
A noun needs の before 前に: 食事の前に, not 食事前に.

examples.ja: 寝る前に歯を磨きます。
examples.en: I brush my teeth before going to bed.
examples.f: ｜寝[ね]る｜前[まえ]に｜歯[は]を｜磨[みが]きます。

examples.ja: 食事の前に手を洗います。
examples.en: I wash my hands before meals.
examples.f: ｜食事[しょくじ]の｜前[まえ]に｜手[て]を｜洗[あら]います。

antonyms.note: 後で means "after"; 前に marks what comes before.

related.note: てから marks doing B after finishing A; 前に marks doing B before A happens.
とき marks "when / at the time of"; 前に pins the moment just before an event.

entry.title: 後で
entry.meaning: after (doing); later
entry.summary: 後で says one thing happens after another. Put the earlier action in the past (た) form before it (食べた後で = after eating), or a noun plus の (食事の後で = after the meal). On its own, 後で simply means 'later': 後で電話します = I'll call later.
pitfalls: Use the past (た) form before 後で even for future plans: 帰った後で, not 帰る後で.
後で just orders the two events in time. If you want to stress 'and only after that', 〜てから carries that 'once ~ is done' feeling more strongly.

examples.ja: 宿題をしたあとで、少しテレビを見ます。
examples.en: After I finish my homework, I'll watch a little TV.
examples.f: ｜宿題[しゅくだい]をしたあとで、｜少[すこ]しテレビを｜見[み]ます。

examples.ja: 昼ご飯のあとで、コーヒーを飲みませんか。
examples.en: Shall we have some coffee after lunch?
examples.f: ｜昼[ひる]ご｜飯[はん]のあとで、コーヒーを｜飲[の]みませんか。

synonyms.note: てから also means 'after doing', but emphasises that the second action waits until the first is finished.

antonyms.note: 前に is the opposite order — doing something before, where 後で is after.

related.note: とき marks 'when' something happens; 後で specifically means after it happens.

entry.title: ながら
entry.meaning: while doing ~ (two actions at once)
entry.summary: 〜ながら joins two actions performed by one person at the same time: 'while doing ~'. Attach ながら to the verb stem; the ながら clause is the background action, and the main clause carries the primary one.
pitfalls: Both actions must share one subject: 歌いながら歩く = one person sings and walks. For two different people acting at once, use 〜間に.
The main point sits in the second clause: 音楽を聞きながら勉強する is about studying.

examples.ja: 音楽を聞きながら勉強します。
examples.en: I study while listening to music.
examples.f: ｜音楽[おんがく]を｜聞[き]きながら｜勉強[べんきょう]します。

examples.ja: お茶を飲みながら話しましょう。
examples.en: Let's talk over some tea.
examples.f: お｜茶[ちゃ]を｜飲[の]みながら｜話[はな]しましょう。

synonyms.note: 〜つつ is the formal, written equivalent of 〜ながら for simultaneous actions.

related.note: 〜間に is 'during the time that', often with two different subjects; 〜ながら is one person doing two things.
〜ながらも adds a concessive twist ('even while / although'), beyond simple 'while'.

entry.title: 〜に行く
entry.meaning: go (somewhere) to do ~
entry.summary: Expresses the purpose of going: put a verb stem (or a する-type noun) before に行く to say you go somewhere in order to do something. It pairs a purpose with a motion verb like 行く, 来る, or 帰る.
structure: Verb［stem］＋ に ＋ 行く／来る／帰る
pitfalls: Use the verb stem, not the dictionary form — 食べに行く, not 食べるに行く.
The place you head to is still marked with に or へ, separate from the purpose に (デパートへ買い物に行く).

examples.ja: 友だちに会いに行きます。
examples.en: I'm going to meet a friend.
examples.f: ｜友[とも]だちに｜会[あ]いに｜行[い]きます。

examples.ja: デパートへ買い物に行きました。
examples.en: I went to the department store to shop.
examples.f: デパートへ｜買い物[かいもの]に｜行[い]きました。

related.note: Built on the に particle, here marking the purpose of the going.
へ marks the destination place, often appearing alongside this 〜に行く purpose pattern.

entry.title: でしょう
entry.meaning: probably ~; ~ right? (polite conjecture)
entry.summary: Expresses a guess or seeks agreement: place でしょう after a noun, adjective, or plain verb to say something is probably the case, or, with rising intonation, to check that the listener agrees. It is the polite counterpart of だろう.
structure: Verb ／ い-adjective［plain form］＋ でしょう
pitfalls: Do not add だ before でしょう — say 学生でしょう, not 学生だでしょう.
Falling intonation makes it a guess ('probably'); rising intonation makes it a confirmation ('right?').

examples.ja: 明日は晴れるでしょう。
examples.en: It will probably be sunny tomorrow.
examples.f: ｜明日[あした]は｜晴[は]れるでしょう。

examples.ja: この店は有名でしょう？
examples.en: This shop is famous, right?
examples.f: この｜店[みせ]は｜有名[ゆうめい]でしょう？

synonyms.note: だろう is the plain, casual form; でしょう is the です-level polite form.

related.note: かもしれない marks a weaker 'maybe'; でしょう sounds more confident about the guess.
と思う states your own opinion; でしょう offers a guess or invites agreement.

entry.title: にする
entry.meaning: to decide on; to choose ~
entry.summary: Expresses a deliberate choice: put a noun before にする to say "I'll go with ~" or "I've decided on ~". It is the everyday phrase for choosing from options, especially ordering food or settling on a plan.
pitfalls: にする is a decision you make; になる is a change that happens on its own — don't swap them (コーヒーにする = I'll have coffee; 秋になる = it becomes autumn).
The choice is marked with に, not を: コーヒーにします, not コーヒーをします.

examples.ja: 私はコーヒーにします。
examples.en: I'll have coffee.
examples.f: ｜私[わたし]はコーヒーにします。

examples.ja: 旅行は来月にしましょう。
examples.en: Let's set the trip for next month.
examples.f: ｜旅行[りょこう]は｜来月[らいげつ]にしましょう。

related.note: 〜になる is a natural change; 〜にする is a deliberate choice you make.
The 'make X into' sense (大きくする) is a separate N4 use of にする/くする.

entry.title: あまり～ない
entry.meaning: not very; not much
entry.summary: あまり teamed with a negative ending softens a 'no' into 'not very' or 'not much'. あまり sets up the expectation and the negative delivers it: あまり高くない = not very expensive, あまり食べない = doesn't eat much. In casual speech あまり often becomes あんまり.
structure: あまり ＋ い-adjective［くない］ ／ な-adjective［ではない］
pitfalls: あまり here must pair with a negative. Without a negative, 〜あまり means an excess ('so much that ~') — a completely different pattern.
It softens the statement to 'not very / not much'. For a flat 'not at all', use ぜんぜん〜ない instead.

examples.ja: この映画はあまり面白くなかったです。
examples.en: This movie wasn't very interesting.
examples.f: この｜映画[えいが]はあまり｜面白[おもしろ]くなかったです。

examples.ja: 最近、あまりテレビを見ません。
examples.en: Lately I don't watch much TV.
examples.f: ｜最近[さいきん]、あまりテレビを｜見[み]ません。

synonyms.note: ほとんど〜ない means 'hardly at all', a stronger denial than あまり〜ない's 'not very'.

antonyms.note: とても is the positive-degree opposite ('very'); あまり〜ない says 'not very'.

entry.title: 全然～ない
entry.meaning: not at all
entry.summary: 全然 in front of a negative predicate denies something completely: 全然読めない = 'can't read it at all'. It is the everyday, conversational way to make a negation total.
structure: 全然 ＋ な-adjective／Noun ＋ ではない
pitfalls: In casual speech 全然大丈夫 ('totally fine') is common, but in tests and careful writing 全然 pairs with a negative.
全然 denies completely; for a milder 'not very', use あまり〜ない.

examples.ja: 漢字が全然読めません。
examples.en: I can't read kanji at all.
examples.f: ｜漢字[かんじ]が｜全然[ぜんぜん]｜読[よ]めません。

examples.ja: このスープは全然熱くないです。
examples.en: This soup isn't hot at all.
examples.f: このスープは｜全然[ぜんぜん]｜熱[あつ]くないです。

synonyms.note: 少しも〜ない is an equally total denial, a touch more formal.
全く〜ない (N3) is the stiffer, more written 'not at all'.

related.note: あまり〜ない is partial ('not much'); 全然〜ない is total.

entry.title: だけ
entry.meaning: only; just
entry.summary: A limiting particle meaning "only" or "just": it marks the noun, verb, or quantity as the sole thing involved, with nothing else. Attach it after the word you want to limit. It is the most straightforward way to say "only ~" at this level.
pitfalls: With を and が, だけ usually replaces them (水だけ飲む, not 水をだけ飲む). With に and で it can attach either way (ここだけに / ここにだけ).
だけ takes a normal verb; しか says the same "only" but always needs a negative verb (水しか飲まない).

examples.ja: 水だけ飲みました。
examples.en: I drank only water.
examples.f: ｜水[みず]だけ｜飲[の]みました。

examples.ja: りんごを一つだけ食べました。
examples.en: I ate only one apple.
examples.f: りんごを｜一[ひと]つだけ｜食[た]べました。

synonyms.note: しか〜ない also means "only" but requires a negative verb; だけ takes a positive one.

related.note: ばかり means "nothing but / only" and often carries a nuance of too much; だけ is a plain limit.
だけで means "just by / with only ~"; だけ alone simply limits the item.

entry.title: くらい・ぐらい
entry.meaning: about, approximately; to the extent that ~
entry.summary: くらい・ぐらい has two jobs: with quantities it means 'about, approximately' (千円くらい = about 1,000 yen), and after a clause it marks a degree by example — 'to the extent that…' (泣きたいくらい = to the point of wanting to cry). くらい and ぐらい are interchangeable.
structure: Verb［plain form］＋ くらい・ぐらい
pitfalls: In the extent sense it gives a vivid example of a degree (立てないくらい疲れた = so tired I couldn't stand), not a precise measure.
くらい and ぐらい mean the same thing; ぐらい just tends to follow certain sounds. Both are fine.

examples.ja: 駅までは、歩いて15分くらいかかります。
examples.en: It takes about fifteen minutes on foot to the station.
examples.f: ｜駅[えき]までは、｜歩[ある]いて15｜分[ふん]くらいかかります。

examples.ja: お腹が痛くて、動けないくらいだった。
examples.en: My stomach hurt so much that I could barely move.
examples.f: お｜腹[なか]が｜痛[いた]くて、｜動[うご]けないくらいだった。

synonyms.note: ほど also marks extent and approximation; it is a bit more formal and common in negative comparisons.

related.note: The standalone N5 くらい covers just the basic 'about' (approximation) sense.

entry.title: くて・で
entry.meaning: ~ and ~ (linking adjectives and nouns)
entry.summary: Links two descriptions in one sentence, meaning "and". Change an い-adjective's ending to くて, and put で after a noun or な-adjective, to connect it smoothly to the next part. It lets you stack qualities without starting a new sentence.
pitfalls: いい (good) is irregular: it becomes よくて, never いくて.
The で here is the connective form of the copula joining nouns and な-adjectives — it is not the で that marks a place or a means.

examples.ja: この部屋は広くて明るいです。
examples.en: This room is spacious and bright.
examples.f: この｜部屋[へや]は｜広[ひろ]くて｜明[あか]るいです。

examples.ja: 兄は先生で、姉は医者です。
examples.en: My older brother is a teacher, and my older sister is a doctor.
examples.f: ｜兄[あに]は｜先生[せんせい]で、｜姉[あね]は｜医者[いしゃ]です。

related.note: そして joins two whole sentences; くて・で links descriptions inside a single sentence.
Same い-adjective conjugation family — くない is the negative, くて the connective form.

entry.title: てあげる
entry.meaning: to do something (as a favor) for someone
entry.summary: Verb［て form］＋ あげる does an action as a kindness for someone else, with the favor flowing away from the doer toward the receiver. It parallels あげる ('give'), but what's handed over is an action rather than an object. Use it when you help someone out.
pitfalls: The favor goes outward, from the doer to someone else; a favor done toward you takes 〜てくれる.
Said straight to a superior it can sound condescending ('I'll kindly do this for you'), so use it humbly or reword.

examples.ja: 友だちに本を貸してあげた。
examples.en: I lent my friend a book (as a favor).
examples.f: ｜友[とも]だちに｜本[ほん]を｜貸[か]してあげた。

examples.ja: 母のかばんを持ってあげた。
examples.en: I carried my mother's bag for her.
examples.f: ｜母[はは]のかばんを｜持[も]ってあげた。

synonyms.note: 〜てやる does a favor for someone below you, a pet, or a plant; 〜てあげる is the neutral-polite version.

antonyms.note: 〜てあげる sends a favor away; 〜てくれる is a favor done toward you.

related.note: 〜てもらう receives a favor; 〜てあげる gives one.
あげる hands over an object; 〜てあげる does an action as the favor.

entry.title: てくれる
entry.meaning: to do (a favor) for me/us
entry.summary: てくれる marks that someone does an action as a favor for the speaker or the speaker's in-group. The doer is the subject (が/は); the beneficiary is you, often left unstated. The direction of the favor points toward the speaker's side.
structure: Noun［giver］＋ が ＋ Verb［て form］＋ くれる
pitfalls: The direction is fixed toward the speaker: 友だちが手伝ってくれる (my friend helps me). If you do the favor for someone else, switch to てあげる.
Contrast てもらう: with てくれる the giver is the subject (友だちが〜くれた); with てもらう the receiver is (私が友だちに〜もらった). Same event, different viewpoint.
The honorific version is てくださる: 先生が教えてくださった.

examples.ja: 友だちが宿題を手伝ってくれました。
examples.en: My friend helped me with my homework.
examples.f: ｜友[とも]だちが｜宿題[しゅくだい]を｜手伝[てつだ]ってくれました。

examples.ja: 母がお弁当を作ってくれた。
examples.en: My mom made me a boxed lunch.
examples.f: ｜母[はは]がお｜弁当[べんとう]を｜作[つく]ってくれた。

related.note: plain くれる gives an object toward the speaker; てくれる gives an action as a favor.
てあげる does a favor moving away from the speaker; てくれる, toward the speaker.
てもらう describes the same favor from the receiver's viewpoint (receiver = subject).

entry.title: てもらう
entry.meaning: to have/get someone to do ~ (for one's benefit)
entry.summary: てもらう describes receiving the favor of someone's action — you get someone to do something for you. The receiver (you or your in-group) is the subject; the doer is marked with に. The viewpoint is the receiver's.
structure: Noun［receiver］＋ が ＋ Noun［doer］＋ に ＋ Verb［て form］＋ もらう
pitfalls: Mark the doer with に: 友だちに手伝ってもらった (I had my friend help me).
Viewpoint flips vs てくれる: てもらう makes the receiver the subject (私が〜もらう); てくれる makes the giver the subject (友だちが〜くれる). Same event.
The humble/polite version is 〜ていただく (先生に教えていただいた).

examples.ja: 友だちに引っこしを手伝ってもらいました。
examples.en: I had my friend help me move.
examples.f: ｜友[とも]だちに｜引[ひ]っこしを｜手伝[てつだ]ってもらいました。

examples.ja: 駅で道を教えてもらった。
examples.en: I got someone to show me the way at the station.
examples.f: ｜駅[えき]で｜道[みち]を｜教[おし]えてもらった。

related.note: plain もらう receives an object; てもらう receives an action as a favor.
てくれる frames the same favor with the doer as subject; てもらう, with the receiver as subject.
てあげる is doing a favor for someone else; てもらう is getting one done for you.

entry.title: ていく
entry.meaning: to go on doing; to do and then go; to continue from now
entry.summary: Verb［て form］＋ いく carries an action or change away from the present into the future — 'keep on ~ing from here.' It can also mean 'do something, then head off.' Its mirror image is 〜てくる, which brings change up to now. Write the auxiliary いく in kana.
pitfalls: 〜ていく moves change away into the future (増えていく); 〜てくる traces it up to the present.
When いく is the 'continue' auxiliary, write it in kana (〜ていく) rather than as the full verb 行く.

examples.ja: これからも日本語を勉強していきます。
examples.en: I'll keep on studying Japanese from now on.
examples.f: これからも｜日本語[にほんご]を｜勉強[べんきょう]していきます。

examples.ja: 朝ご飯を食べていきます。
examples.en: I'll eat breakfast and then head out.
examples.f: ｜朝[あさ]ご｜飯[はん]を｜食[た]べていきます。

antonyms.note: 〜ていく moves change away into the future; 〜てくる brings it up to the present.

related.note: だんだん often pairs with 〜ていく to describe gradual change ahead.
〜ようになる marks reaching a new state; 〜ていく traces the ongoing change toward it.

entry.title: てくる
entry.meaning: to do and come back; to come to ~; to have been ~ing (up to now)
entry.summary: てくる attaches the motion verb 来る and carries several linked senses: (1) do something and come back (買ってくる = go buy and return); (2) a change moving toward the present or the speaker (寒くなってくる = it's getting cold); (3) an action or state continuing up until now (ずっと勉強してきた). It is the mirror of ていく.
structure: Verb［て form］＋ くる／きます
pitfalls: Direction is the key: てくる moves toward the speaker or up to the present, ていく moves away or into the future.
Don't read every てくる as literal 'come'. With change verbs it means 'come to / begin to': 慣れてくる = 'get used to it (gradually)'.

examples.ja: ちょっとパンを買ってきます。
examples.en: I'll go buy some bread and come right back.
examples.f: ちょっとパンを｜買[か]ってきます。

examples.ja: だんだん暖かくなってきましたね。
examples.en: It's gradually gotten warmer, hasn't it?
examples.f: だんだん｜暖[あたた]かくなってきましたね。

related.note: ていく moves away from the speaker or into the future; てくる moves toward the speaker or up to now.
plain 来る is literal coming; てくる uses it as a helper attached to another verb.

entry.title: てしまう・ちゃう
entry.meaning: to do completely; to do (unfortunately, by accident)
entry.summary: てしまう adds one of two nuances: (1) completion — doing something fully, all the way through — or (2) regret — an action that turned out badly or happened by mistake. Context decides which. Casual contractions: 〜てしまう → 〜ちゃう, 〜でしまう → 〜じゃう.
structure: Verb［て form］＋ しまう／しまいます
Verb［て form］＋ ちゃう／じゃう［casual］
pitfalls: The two nuances overlap: 全部食べてしまった can mean 'ate it all up' (completion) or 'ate it, oops' (regret).
Watch the voiced contraction: 〜てしまう → 〜ちゃう (食べちゃう), but 〜でしまう → 〜じゃう (飲んじゃう, 死んじゃう).
The regret sense very often appears in the past: 〜てしまった／〜ちゃった.

examples.ja: 大事な書類をなくしてしまった。
examples.en: I went and lost an important document.
examples.f: ｜大事[だいじ]な｜書類[しょるい]をなくしてしまった。

examples.ja: 宿題はもう全部やってしまいました。
examples.en: I've already finished all my homework.
examples.f: ｜宿題[しゅくだい]はもう｜全部[ぜんぶ]やってしまいました。

related.note: both are て + helper verb; てしまう marks completion or regret, ておく marks doing in advance.

entry.title: ておく
entry.meaning: to do in advance; to do (and leave it that way) on purpose
entry.summary: From 置く (to place), ておく means doing something ahead of time as preparation, or deliberately leaving something in a certain state. In casual speech it contracts: 〜ておく → 〜とく, 〜でおく → 〜どく.
structure: Verb［て form］＋ おく／おきます
pitfalls: Two senses share the form: preparing beforehand (予約しておく) and leaving something as-is on purpose (窓を開けておく).
The casual contraction drops いてお/んでお: 買っておく → 買っとく, 読んでおく → 読んどく.

examples.ja: 明日試験があるので、今夜勉強しておきます。
examples.en: I have an exam tomorrow, so I'll study tonight to be ready.
examples.f: ｜明日[あした]｜試験[しけん]があるので、｜今夜[こんや]｜勉強[べんきょう]しておきます。

examples.ja: 客が来る前に、部屋をそうじしておいた。
examples.en: I cleaned the room before the guests came.
examples.f: ｜客[きゃく]が｜来[く]る｜前[まえ]に、｜部屋[へや]をそうじしておいた。

related.note: both attach a helper verb to the て form; てみる means 'try and see', ておく means 'do in advance'.
another て + helper; てしまう marks completion or regret, ておく marks doing ahead of time.

entry.title: てみる
entry.meaning: to try doing (and see how it goes)
entry.summary: From 見る, てみる means doing something to see how it turns out — 'try ~ing' / 'give it a go'. The focus is on the attempt and finding out the result, not on whether you succeed. It is usually written in kana, since 見る here is a helper, not literal 'look'.
structure: Verb［て form］＋ みる／みます
pitfalls: てみる is 'try and see the outcome'. For 'try hard to / attempt', use 〜ようとする instead.
Write it in kana (〜てみる); the auxiliary 見る has lost its literal 'look' meaning here.

examples.ja: この店のラーメンを食べてみます。
examples.en: I'll try this shop's ramen and see how it is.
examples.f: この｜店[みせ]のラーメンを｜食[た]べてみます。

examples.ja: 新しいくつをはいてみた。
examples.en: I tried on the new shoes.
examples.f: ｜新[あたら]しいくつをはいてみた。

related.note: ようと思う intends or plans to do; てみる just gives it a try to see the result.
both attach a helper verb to the て form; てみる = try and see, ておく = do in advance.

entry.title: てある
entry.meaning: has been done (state)
entry.summary: Describes a state that remains because someone did something on purpose: attach ある to the て form of a transitive verb to say "~ has been done (and is still that way)". It implies deliberate preparation, so you'll meet it when talking about things set up in advance.
pitfalls: てある takes a transitive verb and usually が, implying a person did it on purpose (窓が開けてある = someone opened it and left it).
Compare 〜ている with an intransitive verb for a plain state (ドアが開いている = the door is open) versus てある for a deliberately made state.

examples.ja: テーブルに花が飾ってあります。
examples.en: Flowers have been arranged on the table.
examples.f: テーブルに｜花[はな]が｜飾[かざ]ってあります。

examples.ja: 黒板に名前が書いてあります。
examples.en: The names are written on the blackboard.
examples.f: ｜黒板[こくばん]に｜名前[なまえ]が｜書[か]いてあります。

related.note: ている covers ongoing actions and natural states; てある is a state left on purpose by someone.
ておく is doing something in advance; てある is the resulting state after it's done.

entry.title: とき
entry.meaning: when; at the time of ~
entry.summary: Marks the time or occasion when something happens: place とき after a verb, adjective, or noun phrase to mean 'when ~'. The form and tense of the word before とき shows whether the action is before, during, or after the main event.
pitfalls: The tense before とき matters: 食べるとき is 'when about to eat', 食べたとき is 'when I had eaten'.
It is often written in kana (とき) in this grammatical 'when' use, rather than as the plain noun 時.

examples.ja: 子供のとき、田舎に住んでいました。
examples.en: When I was a child, I lived in the countryside.
examples.f: ｜子供[こども]のとき、｜田舎[いなか]に｜住[す]んでいました。

examples.ja: 暇なとき、本を読みます。
examples.en: When I'm free, I read books.
examples.f: ｜暇[ひま]なとき、｜本[ほん]を｜読[よ]みます。

related.note: まえに pins the action to just before an event; とき marks the general time it happens.
あとで marks 'after'; とき marks the moment 'when' something is the case.
あいだ covers a whole span 'while'; とき points to a particular time or occasion.

entry.title: らしい
entry.meaning: apparently; it seems; I hear that
entry.summary: らしい reports a conclusion the speaker draws from information that came from outside — something heard, read, or otherwise gathered. It is less about the speaker's own eyes and more 'from what I gather'. It attaches to plain forms; with nouns and な-adjectives it joins bare, with no の or な.
pitfalls: Nouns and な-adjectives attach bare — 学生らしい, 元気らしい — with no の or な, unlike ようだ (学生のようだ).
らしい leans on secondhand or gathered information; for a guess from what you directly see, ようだ fits better.
This hearsay らしい is a separate point from the らしい meaning 'typical of' (男らしい 'manly').

examples.ja: 天気予報によると、明日は雪が降るらしいです。
examples.en: According to the forecast, it's apparently going to snow tomorrow.
examples.f: ｜天気[てんき]｜予報[よほう]によると、｜明日[あした]は｜雪[ゆき]が｜降[ふ]るらしいです。

examples.ja: あの店のラーメンはとてもおいしいらしい。
examples.en: Apparently the ramen at that shop is really good.
examples.f: あの｜店[みせ]のラーメンはとてもおいしいらしい。

synonyms.note: そうだ (hearsay) passes on information more directly from its source; らしい filters it as 'from what I gather'.

related.note: ようだ reasons from the speaker's own observation; らしい from outside information.
Same shape, but 'typical of / befitting' rather than hearsay.
みたい is the casual 'it seems' from what you sense; らしい tilts toward secondhand info.

entry.title: ようだ
entry.meaning: it seems that; it appears (from evidence)
entry.summary: ようだ expresses a conjecture the speaker draws from what they can see, hear, or otherwise sense. It is a fairly objective 'it seems / it appears', grounded in evidence rather than a wild guess. It attaches to plain forms; nouns take の and な-adjectives take な before よう.
pitfalls: Nouns need の, not だ: 学生のようだ, not 学生だようだ.
ようだ rests on the speaker's own observation. For something you only heard from someone else, use そうだ (hearsay) or らしい.
In casual speech みたい replaces ようだ with the same meaning: 雨が降ったみたい.

examples.ja: 電気が消えているので、誰もいないようです。
examples.en: The lights are off, so it seems no one is here.
examples.f: ｜電気[でんき]が｜消[き]えているので、｜誰[だれ]もいないようです。

examples.ja: 彼はこの町のことをよく知っているようだ。
examples.en: He seems to know this town well.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]はこの｜町[まち]のことをよく｜知[し]っているようだ。

synonyms.note: みたい carries the same 'it seems' sense but is casual and spoken; ようだ is more neutral.

related.note: そうだ reads an impression straight off appearances; ようだ reasons from evidence.
らしい leans on outside or secondhand information; ようだ on the speaker's own observation.
The same よう builds ように・ような for 'like / similar to'.

entry.title: すぎる
entry.meaning: too ~; excessively ~
entry.summary: すぎる attaches to a verb or adjective stem to say something is done or is "too much", beyond a good limit. It usually carries a negative feeling — the amount or degree has gone past what's desirable.
structure: い-adjective［〜い → 〜すぎる］／ な-adjective ＋ すぎる
pitfalls: い-adjectives drop the final い before すぎる: 高い → 高すぎる. な-adjectives attach directly, with no だ: 静か → 静かすぎる.
いい (good) is irregular: it becomes よすぎる.
すぎる itself conjugates like a る-verb: すぎます, すぎた, すぎて.

examples.ja: 昨日は食べすぎました。
examples.en: I ate too much yesterday.
examples.f: ｜昨日[きのう]は｜食[た]べすぎました。

examples.ja: このコートは私には大きすぎます。
examples.en: This coat is too big for me.
examples.f: このコートは｜私[わたし]には｜大[おお]きすぎます。

related.note: とても is a neutral "very"; すぎる adds the negative sense of "too much".

entry.title: 〜方
entry.meaning: way of doing; how to ~
entry.summary: Attaching 方 (かた) to a verb's ます-stem makes a noun meaning 'the way of doing ~' or 'how to ~': 使う→使い方 (how to use), 作る→作り方 (how to make). Because the result is a noun, it takes particles like any other noun (使い方が分かる).
pitfalls: Attach 方 to the ます-stem, not the dictionary form: 読み方 (how to read), not 読む方.
The verb's object is usually linked with の: 漢字の読み方 (the way of reading kanji), rather than 漢字を読み方.

examples.ja: この機械の使い方を教えてください。
examples.en: Please teach me how to use this machine.
examples.f: この｜機械[きかい]の｜使い方[つかいかた]を｜教[おし]えてください。

examples.ja: 漢字の書き方が分かりません。
examples.en: I don't know how to write this kanji.
examples.f: ｜漢字[かんじ]の｜書き方[かきかた]が｜分[わ]かりません。

related.note: 〜方 attaches to the same ます-stem that the polite ます ending uses.

entry.title: 中
entry.meaning: during; throughout; within (by the end of)
entry.summary: 中 after a noun means "during / throughout," but the reading shifts the sense. ちゅう marks an ongoing action or a deadline (電話中 = mid-call, 今日中に = by the end of today); じゅう marks a whole span of time or space (一日中 = all day long, 世界中 = all over the world).
structure: Time／period ＋ 中に（ちゅうに）、＋ Sentence
pitfalls: The reading carries meaning: ちゅう = in the middle of / by the end of; じゅう = all through. The split isn't fully regular (今日中 = きょうじゅう, but 午前中 = ごぜんちゅう), so learn set words.
ちゅう〜に often sets a deadline ('by the end of'); for a continuous 'the whole time,' it's じゅう.

examples.ja: 午前中に宿題を終わらせます。
examples.en: I will finish my homework during the morning.
examples.f: ｜午前[ごぜん]｜中[ちゅう]に｜宿題[しゅくだい]を｜終[お]わらせます。

examples.ja: 弟は一日じゅうゲームをしている。
examples.en: My little brother plays games all day long.
examples.f: ｜弟[おとうと]は｜一[いち]｜日[にち]じゅうゲームをしている。

related.note: 間 marks a continuous span 'while / during'; 中 (じゅう) stresses 'the whole extent of' that span.
うちに means 'while / before it ends'; 中(ちゅう)に sets a plain deadline 'by the end of.'
までに gives a specific cutoff time; 中(ちゅう)に gives a looser 'within this period.'

entry.title: つもりだ
entry.meaning: intend to; plan to ~
entry.summary: States a firm intention you have already decided on: attach つもりだ to a verb's dictionary form for "I intend to ~", or to the ない form for "I intend not to ~". It conveys a settled personal plan rather than a vague wish.
structure: Verb［ない form］＋ つもりだ
pitfalls: つもりだ is stronger and more decided than 〜ようと思う ("I'm thinking of doing").
It describes your own intention, not a fixed schedule; for scheduled events use 予定だ.

examples.ja: 夏休みに国へ帰るつもりです。
examples.en: I intend to go back to my home country during summer vacation.
examples.f: ｜夏休[なつやす]みに｜国[くに]へ｜帰[かえ]るつもりです。

examples.ja: 今日は何も買わないつもりです。
examples.en: I don't plan to buy anything today.
examples.f: ｜今日[きょう]は｜何[なに]も｜買[か]わないつもりです。

synonyms.note: 〜ようと思う is a softer "I'm thinking of doing"; つもりだ is a firmer, settled intention.

related.note: 予定だ states a fixed schedule or arrangement; つもりだ states your personal intention.
たい expresses desire ("want to"); つもりだ expresses a decided plan ("intend to").

entry.title: ことにする
entry.meaning: to decide to (do)
entry.summary: Verb［dictionary or ない form］＋ことにする marks a decision you make yourself. 走ることにする = I've decided to run; 飲まないことにする = I've decided not to drink. The past ことにした reports a decision already reached, and ことにしている describes a rule or habit you keep to on purpose.
structure: Verb［dictionary form］／［ない form］＋ ことにする
pitfalls: ことにする is your own choice; ことになる is a decision made by circumstances or others.
ことにしている (ongoing) describes a habit you've resolved to keep, not a single fresh decision.

examples.ja: 来月から毎朝走ることにします。
examples.en: I've decided to run every morning from next month.
examples.f: ｜来月[らいげつ]から｜毎朝[まいあさ]｜走[はし]ることにします。

examples.ja: 今日はお酒を飲まないことにした。
examples.en: I decided not to drink today.
examples.f: ｜今日[きょう]はお｜酒[さけ]を｜飲[の]まないことにした。

related.note: ことになる is when things get decided for you; ことにする is deciding yourself.
〜ようにする is making an ongoing effort toward a state; ことにする is a one-time decision.

entry.title: ことになる
entry.meaning: it has been decided that; it turns out that
entry.summary: Verb［dictionary or ない form］＋ことになる says a decision or arrangement has come about, usually through circumstances or a group rather than your own will. 転勤することになった = it's been arranged that I'll transfer. Even when you were involved, it sounds more modest than ことにする. The form ことになっている describes a standing rule or fixed arrangement.
structure: Verb［dictionary form］／［ない form］＋ ことになる
pitfalls: ことになる presents the decision as coming from circumstances or others; ことにする presents it as your own choice.
ことになっている (ongoing) states a standing rule or arrangement, not a new outcome.

examples.ja: 来月、大阪へ転勤することになりました。
examples.en: It's been decided that I'll transfer to Osaka next month.
examples.f: ｜来月[らいげつ]、｜大阪[おおさか]へ｜転勤[てんきん]することになりました。

examples.ja: 会議は来週に延期することになった。
examples.en: It's been decided to postpone the meeting to next week.
examples.f: ｜会議[かいぎ]は｜来週[らいしゅう]に｜延期[えんき]することになった。

related.note: ことにする is a decision you make; ことになる is one that comes about around you.
ことになっている is the settled-rule form of this pattern.
〜ようになる is a gradual change reaching a state; ことになる is a decision being set.

entry.title: ことができる
entry.meaning: can; to be able to
entry.summary: Verb［dictionary form］＋ことができる expresses ability or possibility — 'can do'. 弾くことができる = can play. It means the same as the potential verb form (弾ける) but sounds a touch more formal and is common in writing and announcements. The verb before ことができる stays in plain dictionary form.
structure: Verb［dictionary form］＋ ことができる
pitfalls: Keep the verb in dictionary form: 弾くことができる, not the potential 弾けることができる.
It's a little more formal than the plain potential form (弾ける), which is preferred in casual speech.

examples.ja: 田中さんはピアノを弾くことができます。
examples.en: Ms. Tanaka can play the piano.
examples.f: ｜田中[たなか]さんはピアノを｜弾[ひ]くことができます。

examples.ja: ここで写真を撮ることができますか。
examples.en: Can I take photos here?
examples.f: ここで｜写真[しゃしん]を｜撮[と]ることができますか。

synonyms.note: The potential verb form says the same 'can do' more casually; ことができる is a bit more formal.

related.note: This is the こと nominalizer plus ができる ('be possible').

entry.title: ようと思う
entry.meaning: I think I'll ~; I'm thinking of ~ing
entry.summary: Volitional verb ＋ と思う states a personal intention the speaker has more or less just formed. It is softer than declaring a fixed plan — it presents the decision as your current thinking. Use ようと思っている for an intention you have been holding for a while.
structure: 食べようと思う ／ 行こうと思う
pitfalls: Attach it to the volitional (行こう), not the dictionary form: 行こうと思う, not 行くと思う (which just means 'I think he'll go').
ようと思う reports the speaker's own intention; you cannot use it to state someone else's will directly.
と思っている suggests a longer-held intention; plain と思う, a decision made at the moment of speaking.

examples.ja: 週末は家でゆっくりしようと思います。
examples.en: I think I'll relax at home over the weekend.
examples.f: ｜週末[しゅうまつ]は｜家[いえ]でゆっくりしようと｜思[おも]います。

examples.ja: 来年、日本語の試験を受けようと思っています。
examples.en: I'm thinking of taking the Japanese exam next year.
examples.f: ｜来年[らいねん]、｜日本語[にほんご]の｜試験[しけん]を｜受[う]けようと｜思[おも]っています。

synonyms.note: つもりだ states a firmer, more settled intention; ようと思う is more 'I've just decided'.

related.note: 予定だ is an arranged, on-the-schedule plan; ようと思う is looser personal thinking.
つもりだ is a firmer intention already held; ようと思う leans toward a fresh decision.

entry.title: なさい
entry.meaning: do ~ (firm, caring command)
entry.summary: なさい makes a firm command that is still gentler than the blunt imperative. Attach it to the verb stem (ます form minus ます): 食べます → 食べなさい. It is the tone a parent, teacher, or older person uses toward a child or student — instructive and caring, but clearly a command, not a request between equals.
pitfalls: Use the stem, not the dictionary form: 起きなさい, not 起きるなさい.
It talks down to the listener, so it is not for a boss, customer, or anyone above you — use てください there instead.
There is no negative なさい. To say 'don't do it' to a child, use the negative request 〜ないで.

examples.ja: もう遅いから、早く寝なさい。
examples.en: It's late already, so go to bed early.
examples.f: もう｜遅[おそ]いから、｜早[はや]く｜寝[ね]なさい。

examples.ja: 静かにして、先生の話をよく聞きなさい。
examples.en: Be quiet and listen carefully to the teacher.
examples.f: ｜静[しず]かにして、｜先生[せんせい]の｜話[はなし]をよく｜聞[き]きなさい。

antonyms.note: な after a dictionary verb is the blunt 'don't do it'; なさい is the positive 'do it' command.

related.note: The plain imperative (行け) is harsher; なさい softens a command into something instructive.
てください is a polite request among equals; なさい is a command directed downward.
なさい comes from the imperative of the honorific verb なさる.

entry.title: ば
entry.meaning: if ~ (then); provided that ~
entry.summary: The ば conditional sets up a general 'if A, then B' link: when the condition holds, the result naturally follows. It suits natural consequences, general truths, and advice. Build it by changing a verb's final -u to -eba (押す → 押せば), an い-adjective's い to ければ (安い → 安ければ), and a noun or な-adjective with なら（ば）; the negative uses なければ.
structure: い-adjective［ー い → ければ］
pitfalls: ば leans toward general or hypothetical conditions. When the main clause is a request or command tied to a one-time action, 〜たら is more natural: 駅に着いたら電話して, not 着けば電話して.
The negative condition is 〜なければ: 行かなければ (if you don't go).

examples.ja: 春になれば、桜が咲きます。
examples.en: When spring comes, the cherry blossoms bloom.
examples.f: ｜春[はる]になれば、｜桜[さくら]が｜咲[さ]きます。

examples.ja: ボタンを押せば、電気がつきます。
examples.en: If you press the button, the light comes on.
examples.f: ボタンを｜押[お]せば、｜電気[でんき]がつきます。

related.note: たら fits one-time 'once A happens, B' sequences; ば states a more general condition-result rule.
と is for automatic, inevitable results; ば allows advice and commands more freely.
なら responds to a topic just raised ('if that's the case'); ば states a plain condition.

entry.title: たら
entry.meaning: if; when; after
entry.summary: 〜たら is the everyday conditional: take the plain past (た form) and add ら. Depending on context it means 'if ~,' 'when ~,' or 'after ~.' Its big strength is that the main clause can be a request, command, or wish, which many other conditionals block.
pitfalls: 〜たら covers both 'if' (hypothetical) and 'when/after' (sure to happen); context decides which.
Unlike 〜と, the main clause may be a request or command: 家に着いたら、電話してください.
Past ＋ 〜たら ＋ past can report a discovery: 窓を開けたら、雨が降っていた ('when I opened the window, it was raining').

examples.ja: 家に着いたら、電話します。
examples.en: When I get home, I'll call you.
examples.f: ｜家[いえ]に｜着[つ]いたら、｜電話[でんわ]します。

examples.ja: 安かったら、買います。
examples.en: If it's cheap, I'll buy it.
examples.f: ｜安[やす]かったら、｜買[か]います。

synonyms.note: 〜ば is a more formal 'if'; 〜たら is the everyday conditional and also means 'when/after.'
〜と is for automatic, always-true results; 〜たら allows requests and one-off cases.
〜なら responds to a supposition someone raised; 〜たら sets up your own condition.

related.note: 〜たらどう suggests 'why don't you,' built on the 〜たら conditional.

entry.title: なら
entry.meaning: if; if it's the case that ~
entry.summary: なら sets up a condition by picking up something just mentioned or assumed: 'if (we're talking about) ~, then ...'. It attaches straight to a noun or to the plain form of a verb or adjective. Its special job is responding to a topic the other person raised — 'if that's what you mean, then here's my point'.
pitfalls: After a noun, use bare なら, not だなら: 日本語なら, not 日本語だなら.
Unlike たら or と, the なら clause need not happen before the main clause; it just frames 'given that ~'. 'If you're going to Kyoto (now/later), take the train' works either way.

examples.ja: 京都に行くなら、電車が便利ですよ。
examples.en: If you're going to Kyoto, the train is convenient.
examples.f: ｜京都[きょうと]に｜行[い]くなら、｜電車[でんしゃ]が｜便利[べんり]ですよ。

examples.ja: 「辞書はどこ？」「辞書なら、机の上にあるよ。」
examples.en: "Where's the dictionary?" "The dictionary? It's on the desk."
examples.f: 「｜辞書[じしょ]はどこ？」「｜辞書[じしょ]なら、｜机[つくえ]の｜上[うえ]にあるよ。」

related.note: たら is a general 'if/when' about what happens next; なら takes up a topic and reacts to it.
と states an automatic result; なら frames a supposition raised in the conversation.
ば gives a hypothetical condition; なら responds to a premise you accept for the sake of argument.

entry.title: のに
entry.meaning: although; even though; despite
entry.summary: This のに links two clauses that clash, adding a feeling of surprise, dissatisfaction, or complaint: 'even though A, B (unexpectedly)'. It follows the plain form; after nouns and な-adjectives, insert な (な-adjective な のに, Noun な のに). Unlike neutral けど, のに carries an emotional 'and yet' that things didn't go as they should have.
pitfalls: Don't confuse it with the purpose のに ('in order to'); that one follows a dictionary verb and pairs with words like 使う/かかる/必要, with no sense of contrast.
Nouns and な-adjectives need な before のに: 学生なのに, 静かなのに — not 学生のに.

examples.ja: たくさん勉強したのに、テストの点が悪かった。
examples.en: Even though I studied a lot, my test score was bad.
examples.f: たくさん｜勉強[べんきょう]したのに、テストの｜点[てん]が｜悪[わる]かった。

examples.ja: 冬なのに、今日はとても暖かいです。
examples.en: Even though it's winter, today is very warm.
examples.f: ｜冬[ふゆ]なのに、｜今日[きょう]はとても｜暖[あたた]かいです。

related.note: Same shape のに but 'in order to'; it follows a dictionary verb and shows no contrast.
けど is a neutral 'but'; のに adds surprise or dissatisfaction that the result went against expectation.
ても is 'even if' about a supposed case; のに is 'even though' about something that actually happened.

entry.title: ので
entry.meaning: because; since
entry.summary: ので connects a reason to its result, joining the cause clause to the main clause. Compared with から it feels softer and more matter-of-fact, so it is common in polite explanations, excuses, and requests.
pitfalls: After a な-adjective or a noun, add な before ので: 静かなので, 学生なので.
ので presents the reason as objective and gentle, so it sounds more polite than から when you make an excuse or ask a favor.

examples.ja: 電車が遅れたので、遅刻しました。
examples.en: I was late because the train was delayed.
examples.f: ｜電車[でんしゃ]が｜遅[おく]れたので、｜遅刻[ちこく]しました。

examples.ja: 今日は寒いので、コートを着ます。
examples.en: Since it's cold today, I'll wear a coat.
examples.f: ｜今日[きょう]は｜寒[さむ]いので、コートを｜着[き]ます。

synonyms.note: から states a reason more directly and personally; ので sounds softer and more polite.

entry.title: し
entry.meaning: and; what's more (listing reasons)
entry.summary: し links clauses that each give a reason or supporting point, with the feeling that the list could go on: 安いし、おいしいし = 'it's cheap, it's tasty (and more besides)'. Attach it to the plain form; nouns and な-adjectives take だし.
pitfalls: し hints that the listed reasons are not the only ones; for a neutral, complete 'and' between clauses, the て form is enough.
Don't forget だ after nouns and な-adjectives: 雨だし, not 雨し.

examples.ja: この店は安いし、おいしいし、よく来ます。
examples.en: This place is cheap, and it's tasty, so I come here a lot.
examples.f: この｜店[みせ]は｜安[やす]いし、おいしいし、よく｜来[き]ます。

examples.ja: 今日は雨だし、家で映画を見ましょう。
examples.en: It's raining today, and all — let's watch a movie at home.
examples.f: ｜今日[きょう]は｜雨[あめ]だし、｜家[いえ]で｜映画[えいが]を｜見[み]ましょう。

related.note: から gives one explicit reason; し piles up several and implies there are more.
それに adds a further point as a separate sentence; し chains reasons inside one.
The て form lists actions neutrally, without the 'reasons, and more' flavor of し.

entry.title: ために
entry.meaning: because of; as a result of (cause)
entry.summary: In this use ために gives the reason or cause for what follows — "because of; as a result of." It often introduces a circumstance that led to a notable or unwanted outcome. It attaches to a plain-form clause, or to a noun with の.
pitfalls: This 'because of' ために tends to explain a notable or negative result and is more formal than から／ので.
The same shape ために also means 'in order to' (purpose); tell them apart by whether the second clause is a goal or an outcome.

examples.ja: 大雨のために、川の水が増えた。
examples.en: Because of the heavy rain, the river's water rose.
examples.f: ｜大雨[おおあめ]のために、｜川[かわ]の｜水[みず]が｜増[ふ]えた。

examples.ja: 事故があったために、道路が渋滞している。
examples.en: Because there was an accident, the road is jammed.
examples.f: ｜事故[じこ]があったために、｜道路[どうろ]が｜渋滞[じゅうたい]している。

synonyms.note: ので states a cause neutrally in everyday speech; ために sounds more formal and often flags a significant result.
から gives the speaker's reasoning; ために more often reports an objective cause and effect.

related.note: Same shape, other sense: ため(に) as 'in order to' states a goal; this ために states a cause.
そのため(に) packages a whole prior sentence as 'that reason'; ために attaches directly to the cause clause.

entry.title: ようにする
entry.meaning: to make sure to; to make an effort to
entry.summary: ようにする says you deliberately arrange your behavior so a certain thing happens (or does not). It expresses making an effort or keeping a conscious habit: 毎日運動するようにする = 'make a point of exercising daily'. With ている (ようにしている) it stresses an ongoing habit you keep up.
structure: Verb［ない form］＋ ようにする
pitfalls: ようにする is a conscious effort you make; ようになる is a change that happens on its own. 早起きするようにする (I make myself get up early) vs 早起きするようになった (I've come to get up early).
For a firm one-time decision, ことにする fits better; ようにする leans toward ongoing effort or habit.
The ている form ようにしている marks a habit you are keeping up, not a single act.

examples.ja: 健康のために、甘い物を食べすぎないようにしています。
examples.en: For my health, I try not to eat too many sweets.
examples.f: ｜健康[けんこう]のために、｜甘[あま]い｜物[もの]を｜食[た]べすぎないようにしています。

examples.ja: 約束の時間には遅れないようにします。
examples.en: I'll make sure not to be late for our appointment.
examples.f: ｜約束[やくそく]の｜時間[じかん]には｜遅[おく]れないようにします。

related.note: ようになる is the change coming about on its own; ようにする is the effort you make.
ことにする is a firm decision to do something; ようにする is ongoing effort or habit.
The same purpose ように, here completed by する into a personal effort.

entry.title: ようになる
entry.meaning: to come to ~; to reach the point where
entry.summary: ようになる describes a change over time — you reach a state or ability you did not have before. It pairs naturally with potential verbs (話せるようになる = 'become able to speak') and marks arriving at a new normal. The negative なくなる shows losing a habit or ability.
structure: Verb［ない form → なくなる, negative］
pitfalls: For 'stopped doing / can no longer', use なくなる, not ないようになる: 食べなくなった rather than 食べないようになった.
ようになる is a change that unfolds; ようにする is a conscious effort. 泳げるようになった (came to be able to swim) vs 泳ぐようにする (make a point of swimming).
ようになる highlights a gradual shift, so it pairs especially well with potential verbs.

examples.ja: 練習して、自転車に乗れるようになりました。
examples.en: After practicing, I became able to ride a bicycle.
examples.f: ｜練習[れんしゅう]して、｜自転車[じてんしゃ]に｜乗[の]れるようになりました。

examples.ja: 最近、からい料理も食べられるようになった。
examples.en: Lately I've become able to eat spicy food too.
examples.f: ｜最近[さいきん]、からい｜料理[りょうり]も｜食[た]べられるようになった。

related.note: ようにする is deliberate effort; ようになる is the change itself coming about.
ことになる is a decision or arrangement being settled; ようになる is a gradual change in ability or habit.
Potential verbs pair with ようになる to say you've become able to do something.

entry.title: てほしい
entry.meaning: to want someone (else) to do ~
entry.summary: てほしい expresses wanting another person to do something. The person you want to act is marked with に, and ほしい inflects like an い-adjective. The negative 'want you NOT to' is 〜ないでほしい.
structure: Noun［person］＋ に ＋ Verb［て form］＋ ほしい
Verb［ない form］＋ でほしい［negative］
pitfalls: The subject differs from 〜たい: 〜たい = I want to do it myself; てほしい = I want another person to do it.
Mark the person you want to act with に: 君に来てほしい.
'Want you not to' is 〜ないでほしい (来ないでほしい = I want you not to come).

examples.ja: 明日は早く来てほしいです。
examples.en: I want you to come early tomorrow.
examples.f: ｜明日[あした]は｜早[はや]く｜来[き]てほしいです。

examples.ja: 私のことを忘れないでほしい。
examples.en: I don't want you to forget me.
examples.f: ｜私[わたし]のことを｜忘[わす]れないでほしい。

related.note: がほしい wants an object; てほしい wants an action from someone.
〜たい is wanting to do something yourself; てほしい is wanting someone else to do it.
ように〜てほしい softens the request, often for outcomes not fully in the person's control.

entry.title: たがる
entry.meaning: to want to (of a third person, shown outwardly)
entry.summary: たがる reports that someone else looks like they want to do something, judged from outside signs. It's built from the 〜たい stem plus がる, and conjugates like an u-verb. Use it for other people's desires; for your own, plain 〜たい is correct.
pitfalls: Use たがる for others' wants observed from outside; for your own desire say 〜たい (食べたい), not 食べたがる.
For a want happening right now, the ongoing 〜たがっている is usually more natural than plain 〜たがる.
たがる tends to take を for its object (お菓子を食べたがる), where 〜たい can also use が.

examples.ja: 弟はいつも外で遊びたがる。
examples.en: My little brother always wants to play outside.
examples.f: ｜弟[おとうと]はいつも｜外[そと]で｜遊[あそ]びたがる。

examples.ja: 子どもはお菓子を食べたがっている。
examples.en: The child wants to eat some sweets.
examples.f: ｜子[こ]どもはお｜菓子[かし]を｜食[た]べたがっている。

synonyms.note: 〜がる makes an adjective of feeling into a third-person 'shows signs of'; たがる does the same for 〜たい.

related.note: 〜たい states your own desire; たがる reports someone else's, seen from outside.
〜が欲しい wants a thing; 〜たがる wants to do an action.

entry.title: かもしれない
entry.meaning: might; may; perhaps
entry.summary: かもしれない marks something as a real possibility — 'might' or 'perhaps'. It attaches to the plain form of verbs and い-adjectives, and to nouns and な-adjectives with no だ. The polite version is かもしれません. It signals genuine uncertainty, weaker than a confident guess.
structure: Verb／い-adjective［plain form］＋ かもしれない
pitfalls: After a noun or な-adjective, drop だ: 病気かもしれない, not 病気だかもしれない.
かもしれない stays genuinely unsure. でしょう and だろう lean toward what you expect is likely, so they sound more confident.

examples.ja: 午後から雨が降るかもしれません。
examples.en: It might rain from the afternoon.
examples.f: ｜午後[ごご]から｜雨[あめ]が｜降[ふ]るかもしれません。

examples.ja: 彼はもう家に帰ったかもしれない。
examples.en: He may have already gone home.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]はもう｜家[いえ]に｜帰[かえ]ったかもしれない。

related.note: だろう is a fairly confident guess; かもしれない admits it could easily be otherwise.
はずだ says you expect it on solid grounds; かもしれない is only a loose possibility.
かな just wonders out loud; かもしれない actually puts a possibility on the table.

entry.title: だろう
entry.meaning: probably; ~right?
entry.summary: Expresses a guess or conjecture in plain speech: だろう means "probably" or, with rising intonation, "~right?" when seeking agreement. Attach it to a plain-form verb, an い-adjective, or a noun. でしょう is its polite twin.
pitfalls: だろう is plain; use でしょう in polite speech for the same meaning.
Don't stack だ before it — after a noun say 学生だろう, not 学生だだろう.

examples.ja: 明日は晴れるだろう。
examples.en: It will probably be sunny tomorrow.
examples.f: ｜明日[あした]は｜晴[は]れるだろう。

examples.ja: 彼はもう帰っただろう。
examples.en: He has probably gone home already.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]はもう｜帰[かえ]っただろう。

synonyms.note: でしょう is the polite version of the same conjecture; だろう is plain.

related.note: かもしれない ("maybe") is less certain than だろう ("probably").
はずだ expects something based on reasoning; だろう is a looser guess.

entry.title: はずだ
entry.meaning: should be; ought to be; supposed to be
entry.summary: はずだ states a conclusion the speaker expects to be true based on reason or evidence — 'it should be the case that ~'. It reflects what logically follows from what you know, not a personal wish. It attaches to plain forms, with な-adjective＋な and noun＋の.
structure: Verb ／ い-adjective［plain form］＋ はずだ
pitfalls: はずだ means 'I expect this from what I know', not 'you should do it'. For advice or obligation use 〜べきだ or 〜たほうがいい.
It expresses expectation, not duty — don't read it as the 'must/have to' of obligation grammar.

examples.ja: この時間なら、店はもう閉まっているはずです。
examples.en: At this hour, the shop should already be closed.
examples.f: この｜時間[じかん]なら、｜店[みせ]はもう｜閉[し]まっているはずです。

examples.ja: 彼は毎日勉強しているから、試験に合格するはずだ。
examples.en: He studies every day, so he should pass the exam.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜毎日[まいにち]｜勉強[べんきょう]しているから、｜試験[しけん]に｜合格[ごうかく]するはずだ。

antonyms.note: はずがない denies the expectation ('no way'); はずだ affirms it ('should be').

related.note: だろう is a looser 'probably'; はずだ rests on concrete grounds for the expectation.
ようだ reports how something seems from direct evidence; はずだ reasons out what ought to be true.

entry.title: はずがない
entry.meaning: there's no way ~; cannot possibly be
entry.summary: はずがない voices the speaker's strong confidence that something is not so — 'there's no way that ~'. You reason from what you know and conclude the situation is impossible or highly unlikely. It attaches to plain forms, with な-adjective＋な and noun＋の; はずはない is a slightly softer variant.
structure: Verb ／ い-adjective［plain form］＋ はずがない
な-adjective ＋ な ＋ はずがない
Noun ＋ の ＋ はずがない
pitfalls: This is confident logical deduction, not a sensory guess; for 'it doesn't look like it' use 〜そうにない or みたい.
It is the flat denial of an expectation — the negative counterpart of はずだ.

examples.ja: 彼がそんなうそをつくはずがない。
examples.en: There's no way he would tell such a lie.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]がそんなうそをつくはずがない。

examples.ja: あの店が今日休みのはずがない。
examples.en: There's no way that shop is closed today.
examples.f: あの｜店[みせ]が｜今日[きょう]｜休[やす]みのはずがない。

synonyms.note: わけがない is a very close 'there's no way'; はずがない frames it as a defied expectation.

antonyms.note: はずだ expects something to be true; はずがない insists it cannot be.

entry.title: かどうか
entry.meaning: whether or not
entry.summary: かどうか packs a yes/no question inside a bigger sentence, meaning 'whether (or not)'. You attach it to the plain form of a verb or い-adjective, and directly to a noun or な-adjective with no だ. The main clause then reacts to that embedded question — you don't know it, you'll check it, you'll decide it.
pitfalls: After a noun or な-adjective, drop だ: 本当かどうか, not 本当だかどうか.
かどうか is for yes/no questions. To embed a question with a question word (どこ・だれ・何), use 疑問詞＋か instead: どこにあるか分からない.

examples.ja: その話が本当かどうか、まだ分かりません。
examples.en: I don't know yet whether that story is true.
examples.f: その｜話[はなし]が｜本当[ほんとう]かどうか、まだ｜分[わ]かりません。

examples.ja: 彼がパーティーに来るかどうか、聞いてみます。
examples.en: I'll ask whether or not he's coming to the party.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]がパーティーに｜来[く]るかどうか、｜聞[き]いてみます。

related.note: 疑問詞＋か embeds a which/where/who question; かどうか embeds a plain yes/no one.
か alone marks a direct question; かどうか buries that question inside a larger sentence.

entry.title: と思う
entry.meaning: I think that ~
entry.summary: 〜と思う states your opinion, guess, or judgment: 'I think that ~'. The idea before と stays in plain form, and 思う holds your personal view. Add the volitional to get 〜ようと思う ('I intend to').
pitfalls: Keep the clause before と in plain form even when polite: 高いと思います, not 高いですと思います.
と思う is your own current opinion. To report what someone else thinks, use 〜と思っている.

examples.ja: この映画は面白いと思います。
examples.en: I think this movie is interesting.
examples.f: この｜映画[えいが]は｜面白[おもしろ]いと｜思[おも]います。

examples.ja: 彼女はもう帰ったと思います。
examples.en: I think she has already gone home.
