examples.f: ｜彼女[かのじょ]はもう｜帰[かえ]ったと｜思[おも]います。

related.note: と思う is the quotative と plus 思う.
だろう states a guess directly; と思う frames it explicitly as your opinion.
〜ようと思う uses 思う with the volitional to say you intend to do something.

entry.title: ばかり
entry.meaning: only; nothing but
entry.summary: ばかり singles out one thing and says it's the only one — 'nothing but ~'. After a noun it means 'only that thing'; after a verb's て form (〜てばかり) it means someone does nothing but that action. It often carries a nuance of excess or complaint that neutral だけ lacks.
pitfalls: Unlike neutral だけ, ばかり often adds a critical 'always just / too much' feeling: 遊んでばかり implies too much playing.
This is the 'nothing but' ばかり — different from the 'just did' ばかり (〜たばかり) and the 'about/approximately' ばかり.

examples.ja: 弟はゲームばかりしています。
examples.en: My little brother does nothing but play games.
examples.f: ｜弟[おとうと]はゲームばかりしています。

examples.ja: 甘いものばかり食べないでください。
examples.en: Please don't eat only sweet things.
examples.f: ｜甘[あま]いものばかり｜食[た]べないでください。

related.note: だけ is a neutral 'only' with no complaint; ばかり tends to imply excess.
しか〜ない means 'only' with a negative verb and a 'nothing more' feel; ばかり keeps a positive verb.
のみ is a formal, written 'only'; ばかり is conversational and often critical.

entry.title: たばかり
entry.meaning: just did; only just happened
entry.summary: Verb［た form］＋ ばかり says an action happened only a short while ago. The 'short while' is how the speaker feels — it can be minutes or, loosely, even longer, as long as it seems recent. Use it to explain that you're still new to or fresh from something.
structure: Verb［た form］＋ ばかり（だ／です）
pitfalls: 〜たばかり is subjective 'not long ago,' while 〜たところ marks the exact moment right after finishing.
Don't confuse it with 〜てばかり, which means 'do nothing but ~.'

examples.ja: この会社に入ったばかりで、まだ分からないことが多い。
examples.en: I just joined this company, so there's still a lot I don't know.
examples.f: この｜会社[かいしゃ]に｜入[はい]ったばかりで、まだ｜分[わ]からないことが｜多[おお]い。

examples.ja: 赤ちゃんは生まれたばかりだ。
examples.en: The baby was only just born.
examples.f: ｜赤[あか]ちゃんは｜生[う]まれたばかりだ。

synonyms.note: 〜たところ marks the exact moment of finishing; 〜たばかり feels 'not long ago,' even loosely.

related.note: ばかり on its own means 'only / nothing but'; 〜たばかり means 'just did.'

entry.title: 〜出す
entry.meaning: to suddenly start doing; to burst into (an action)
entry.summary: 〜出す attaches to the ます-stem and marks the sudden, often unexpected start of an action — 泣き出す = burst into tears, 走り出す = break into a run. The nuance is that the action kicks off abruptly, not that you gently ease into it. The compound conjugates like a normal う-verb.
pitfalls: 〜出す stresses a sudden or spontaneous start; for a plain neutral 'begin to' with no abruptness, use 〜始める.
Attach it to the stem: 笑い出す, not 笑う出す.

examples.ja: 赤ちゃんが急に泣き出しました。
examples.en: The baby suddenly burst into tears.
examples.f: ｜赤[あか]ちゃんが｜急[きゅう]に｜泣[な]き｜出[だ]しました。

examples.ja: 私の話を聞いて、みんなが笑い出した。
examples.en: When they heard my story, everyone burst out laughing.
examples.f: ｜私[わたし]の｜話[はなし]を｜聞[き]いて、みんなが｜笑[わら]い｜出[だ]した。

related.note: 〜始める is the neutral 'begin to'; 〜出す adds the sense of a sudden, abrupt onset.
〜出す marks an action starting; 〜終わる marks one finishing.

entry.title: ほど〜ない
entry.meaning: not as ~ as; not to the extent of ~
entry.summary: In 〜ほど〜ない, the noun before ほど is a standard you fall short of: A は B ほど〜ない = 'A is not as ... as B.' B is the higher one, and A doesn't reach it. It always ends in a negative.
pitfalls: The item after ほど is the higher standard: A は B ほど〜ない means A falls short of B, so B is the greater one.
It requires a negative ending; drop the negative and ほど no longer means 'not as... as'.

examples.ja: 今年の夏は去年ほど暑くない。
examples.en: This summer isn't as hot as last year.
examples.f: ｜今年[ことし]の｜夏[なつ]は｜去年[きょねん]ほど｜暑[あつ]くない。

examples.ja: 数学は思っていたほど難しくなかった。
examples.en: Math wasn't as hard as I'd thought.
examples.f: ｜数学[すうがく]は｜思[おも]っていたほど｜難[むずか]しくなかった。

related.note: より states which side is more ('A is more... than B'); ほど〜ない says A falls short of B.
Plain ほど marks a degree or extent; the negative pattern ほど〜ない turns it into a comparison.

entry.title: なかなか～ない
entry.meaning: not easily ~; hardly ~; won't ~ despite trying
entry.summary: With a negative verb, なかなか〜ない means something doesn't happen easily or as hoped — 'not readily', 'won't ~ no matter what'. It carries a hint of frustration that the expected result is slow to arrive.
structure: なかなか ＋ Verb［ない form］
pitfalls: This meaning needs a negative predicate: なかなか来ない = won't come. With a positive verb, なかなか instead means 'quite / considerably'.
The point is the gap between what you expect and what happens — it implies you're waiting or trying.

examples.ja: バスがなかなか来ません。
examples.en: The bus just won't come.
examples.f: バスがなかなか｜来[き]ません。

examples.ja: この問題はなかなか解けない。
examples.en: This problem is really hard to solve.
examples.f: この｜問題[もんだい]はなかなか｜解[と]けない。

synonyms.note: あまり〜ない means 'not much'; なかなか〜ない means 'not easily', with a sense of trying.

related.note: Positive なかなか means 'quite / fairly'; paired with 〜ない it flips to 'not easily'.
めったに〜ない means 'rarely'; なかなか〜ない is 'won't happen (though expected)'.

entry.title: ずつ
entry.meaning: each; apiece; at a time; in steady increments
entry.summary: ずつ follows a quantity to mean "that much each" or "that much at a time" — 一つずつ = one apiece, 少しずつ = little by little, 三個ずつ = three each. It spreads an amount evenly across people or occasions, or marks steady, equal increments.
pitfalls: ずつ needs a quantity word in front of it (一つ, 少し, 千円); it doesn't attach straight onto a plain noun.

examples.ja: 子どもたちにお菓子を二つずつ配った。
examples.en: I handed out two sweets to each of the children.
examples.f: ｜子[こ]どもたちにお｜菓子[かし]を｜二[ふた]つずつ｜配[くば]った。

examples.ja: 毎日少しずつ漢字を覚えています。
examples.en: I learn a few kanji at a time every day.
examples.f: ｜毎日[まいにち]｜少[すこ]しずつ｜漢字[かんじ]を｜覚[おぼ]えています。

related.note: 〜ごとに marks "every unit" (一日ごとに = every day); ずつ marks "this much each / at a time."

entry.title: までに
entry.meaning: by; by the time (deadline)
entry.summary: までに marks a deadline — the point by which an action must be finished. Unlike まで ('until', for continuous actions), までに is for one-time actions completed at or before a limit: 5時までに帰る (be home by 5). It attaches to a time noun or a verb in dictionary form.
pitfalls: までに (deadline, one-time action) vs まで (continuous action up to a point): 5時まで待つ (wait until 5), but 5時までに来る (come by 5).
Don't use までに with a continuing action like 'wait' or 'stay'; those take まで.

examples.ja: 金曜日までにレポートを出してください。
examples.en: Please hand in the report by Friday.
examples.f: ｜金曜日[きんようび]までにレポートを｜出[だ]してください。

examples.ja: 暗くなるまでに帰りましょう。
examples.en: Let's get home before it gets dark.
examples.f: ｜暗[くら]くなるまでに｜帰[かえ]りましょう。

related.note: まで marks a continuous action lasting up to a point; までに marks a deadline for a one-time action.

entry.title: ことがある
entry.meaning: there are times when; sometimes
entry.summary: With a verb in dictionary form, 〜ことがある says an action happens now and then — 'there are times when...'. 遅れることがある = the train is sometimes late. It describes occasional occurrence, and it's often paired with たまに or ときどき. Watch the tense: the past 〜たことがある means something completely different (past experience).
pitfalls: Dictionary form 〜ことがある = 'sometimes happens'; past 〜たことがある = 'have done before'. 食べることがある is 'I sometimes eat it', while 食べたことがある is 'I have eaten it'.
It states occasional events, so pairing it with たまに or ときどき reads naturally.

examples.ja: 朝、時間がなくて朝ご飯を食べないことがあります。
examples.en: In the morning there are times I skip breakfast because I'm out of time.
examples.f: ｜朝[あさ]、｜時間[じかん]がなくて｜朝[あさ]ご｜飯[はん]を｜食[た]べないことがあります。

examples.ja: この道はたまにとても混むことがある。
examples.en: This road sometimes gets very crowded.
examples.f: この｜道[みち]はたまにとても｜混[こ]むことがある。

related.note: 〜たことがある is the past-experience sibling ('have done'); this one is 'sometimes do'.
This pattern is the こと nominalizer plus がある ('there are occasions of').

entry.title: させてください
entry.meaning: please let me (do)
entry.summary: させてください combines the causative with てください to ask permission politely: 使わせてください = 'please let me use it'. The speaker is the one who wants to act — you are asking the listener to allow it, not to do anything themselves.
structure: Verb［causative form: せる・させる → せて・させて］＋ ください
pitfalls: 〜てください asks the listener to act; 〜させてください asks the listener to let YOU act. 説明してください = 'please explain'; 説明させてください = 'please let me explain'.
In casual speech ください drops off: ちょっと休ませて.

examples.ja: すみません、この電話を使わせてください。
examples.en: Excuse me, please let me use this phone.
examples.f: すみません、この｜電話[でんわ]を｜使[つか]わせてください。

examples.ja: 今日は少し早く帰らせてください。
examples.en: Please let me go home a little early today.
examples.f: ｜今日[きょう]は｜少[すこ]し｜早[はや]く｜帰[かえ]らせてください。

synonyms.note: させてもらう also frames your action as permitted by someone; させてください is the direct request for that permission.

related.note: The causative せる・させる is the engine inside させてください.
〜てください requests the listener's action; 〜させてください requests permission for your own.

entry.title: お～になる
entry.meaning: to do ~ (honorific)
entry.summary: お＋verb stem＋になる is the general honorific (sonkeigo) pattern for a respected person's action. お帰りになる = (they) go home; お書きになる = (they) write. It raises the subject, so you use it about a customer, boss or teacher — not about yourself.
structure: ご ＋ Noun［する-verb］ ＋ になる
pitfalls: It is honorific: it describes someone else's action. For your own action use the humble お～する.
Some verbs use a special honorific word instead of this pattern: 見る → ご覧になる, not お見になる.

examples.ja: 社長はもうお帰りになりました。
examples.en: The president has already left for home.
examples.f: ｜社長[しゃちょう]はもうお｜帰[かえ]りになりました。

examples.ja: 先生はこの本をお読みになりましたか。
examples.en: Did you read this book, sensei?
examples.f: ｜先生[せんせい]はこの｜本[ほん]をお｜読[よ]みになりましたか。

antonyms.note: お～する humbly lowers your own action; お～になる honorifically raises someone else's.

related.note: いらっしゃる is a ready-made honorific verb; お～になる turns ordinary verbs honorific.
お～ください requests an action; お～になる simply describes a respected person doing it.

entry.title: お～する
entry.meaning: to (humbly) do ~ for someone
entry.summary: お＋verb stem＋する is the humble (kenjougo) pattern for your own action when it touches someone you respect. お持ちします = I'll carry it (for you); お送りします = I'll see you off. It lowers you to raise the other person. する-verbs of Chinese origin take ご instead: ご案内する.
pitfalls: It is humble, so the doer is you or your group — never use it for the listener's action (that would be お～になる).
Use the verb stem, not the dictionary form: お持ちします, not お持つします.

examples.ja: お荷物をお持ちします。
examples.en: I'll carry your luggage.
examples.f: お｜荷物[にもつ]をお｜持[も]ちします。

examples.ja: 駅まで車でお送りします。
examples.en: I'll drive you to the station.
examples.f: ｜駅[えき]まで｜車[くるま]でお｜送[おく]りします。

synonyms.note: お～いたす swaps する for the humble いたす — the same pattern, one step more formal.

antonyms.note: お～になる raises the other person's action; お～する humbly lowers your own.

related.note: お～ください asks the listener to act; お～する is you acting humbly for them.

entry.title: でございます
entry.meaning: to be (very polite copula)
entry.summary: でございます is the most formal form of です ('to be'). It belongs to polite/humble keigo and is used in service settings, announcements, and business — typically by staff toward customers. It is built on ございます, the very polite form of ある.
pitfalls: The register is very high: shop staff, receptionists, formal announcements. In everyday conversation でございます sounds stiff and over-formal — use です.
It replaces です as a unit; it attaches to nouns and な-adjective stems, not to plain だ.

examples.ja: こちらが会議室でございます。
examples.en: This is the meeting room.
examples.f: こちらが｜会議[かいぎ]｜室[しつ]でございます。

examples.ja: お手洗いは二階でございます。
examples.en: The restroom is on the second floor.
examples.f: お｜手洗[てあら]いは｜二[に]｜階[かい]でございます。

synonyms.note: ございます is the polite existence verb; でございます is the polite copula built on it.

related.note: お〜になる is respectful (sonkeigo) verb keigo; でございます is the matching polite copula, often used together.

entry.title: ても構わない
entry.meaning: it's fine even if ~; I don't mind if ~
entry.summary: 〜てもかまわない says that even if X happens, it doesn't bother the speaker — so it grants permission or shows willingness. 高くてもかまわない = I don't mind if it's expensive. 構わない literally means 'don't mind', giving it a softer feel than the blunter てもいい.
structure: Verb［て form］＋ もかまわない
pitfalls: 構わない means 'don't mind', so it reads as gentle permission; てもいい is a more direct 'may / it's okay to'.
The negative なくてもかまわない means 'it's fine even if you don't'.

examples.ja: 少し高くてもかまわないので、質のいいものが欲しい。
examples.en: I don't mind if it's a little pricey; I want something of good quality.
examples.f: ｜少[すこ]し｜高[たか]くてもかまわないので、｜質[しつ]のいいものが｜欲[ほ]しい。

examples.ja: ここで写真を撮ってもかまいませんか。
examples.en: Is it all right if I take photos here?
examples.f: ここで｜写真[しゃしん]を｜撮[と]ってもかまいませんか。

synonyms.note: てもいい is a plainer 'may / it's okay to'; てもかまわない softens it to 'I don't mind if'.

antonyms.note: てはいけない forbids the action; てもかまわない allows it.

related.note: ても is the bare 'even if'; てもかまわない adds the judgment that the case is acceptable.

entry.title: ばよかった
entry.meaning: should have ~; I wish I had ~
entry.summary: 〜ばよかった looks back on something and expresses regret — 'I should have ~ / I wish I had ~'. Built from the ば conditional plus よかった ('would have been good'), it says that meeting the condition would have led to a better outcome. To regret having done something, negate the condition with 〜なければよかった.
structure: Verb［え-stem］＋ ば ＋ よかった
Verb［ない → なければ］＋ よかった
pitfalls: Plain 〜ばよかった regrets NOT doing; to regret having done something, negate the condition: 言わなければよかった (I wish I hadn't said it).
It is hindsight about the past, so it pairs with outcomes already known, not future plans.

examples.ja: もっと早く家を出ればよかった。
examples.en: I should have left home earlier.
examples.f: もっと｜早[はや]く｜家[いえ]を｜出[で]ればよかった。

examples.ja: あんなことを言わなければよかった。
examples.en: I wish I hadn't said something like that.
examples.f: あんなことを｜言[い]わなければよかった。

related.note: ば is the underlying conditional; ばよかった adds よかった to turn it into hindsight regret.
〜たらよかった expresses the same regret with the たら conditional instead of ば.

entry.title: たらどう
entry.meaning: why don't you ~?; how about ~ing?
entry.summary: 〜たらどう offers a suggestion to the listener: 'why don't you ~?' The どう is short for どうですか ('how would it be?'), attached to the 〜たら conditional. Use it to gently recommend that the other person try something.
structure: Verb［た form］＋ ら ＋ どう（ですか）
pitfalls: It advises the other person, not yourself; you can't use it about your own actions.
Said bluntly it can sound pushy or critical, so soften it with どうですか or a caring tone.

examples.ja: 疲れているなら、少し休んだらどうですか。
examples.en: If you're tired, why don't you rest a little?
examples.f: ｜疲[つか]れているなら、｜少[すこ]し｜休[やす]んだらどうですか。

examples.ja: 一度、医者に相談してみたらどう。
examples.en: How about consulting a doctor once?
examples.f: ｜一度[いちど]、｜医者[いしゃ]に｜相談[そうだん]してみたらどう。

synonyms.note: 〜ほうがいい recommends one choice over another; 〜たらどう floats a suggestion more gently.

related.note: 〜たらどう offers advice; 〜たらいいですか asks for it.
The conditional 〜たら is the base of this suggestion pattern.

entry.title: ほうがいい
entry.meaning: had better; should ~
entry.summary: Recommends an action: attach ほうがいい to the た form of a verb to say "you had better do ~" or "it would be better to do ~". It compares the recommended choice against not doing it, so it sounds like sensible advice rather than an order.
structure: Verb［た form］＋ ほうがいい
pitfalls: The recommendation normally uses the た form even though it talks about the future — 早く寝たほうがいい, not 早く寝るほうがいい (the dictionary form is possible but sounds like a general comparison, not advice).
For advising against something, switch to the ない form: 行かないほうがいい.

examples.ja: 疲れているから、早く寝たほうがいいですよ。
examples.en: You're tired, so you should go to bed early.
examples.f: ｜疲[つか]れているから、｜早[はや]く｜寝[ね]たほうがいいですよ。

examples.ja: テストがあるから、今日は勉強したほうがいいですよ。
examples.en: You have a test, so you should study today.
examples.f: テストがあるから、｜今日[きょう]は｜勉強[べんきょう]したほうがいいですよ。

antonyms.note: ないほうがいい advises against doing something; ほうがいい recommends it.

entry.title: とか～とか
entry.meaning: such as A and B; among other things
entry.summary: とか〜とか lists a couple of examples out of many: 'things like A and B'. It's a casual, non-exhaustive list — you name a few and imply there's more you're not listing.
structure: Noun ＋ とか ＋ Noun ＋ とか
Verb／adjective［plain form］＋ とか ＋ Verb／adjective［plain form］＋ とか
pitfalls: Casual in tone; in formal writing prefer や or など.
Non-exhaustive — it means 'among others'. Plain と, by contrast, lists a complete, exact set.

examples.ja: 週末は掃除とか買い物とかをします。
examples.en: On weekends I do things like cleaning and shopping.
examples.f: ｜週末[しゅうまつ]は｜掃除[そうじ]とか｜買い物[かいもの]とかをします。

examples.ja: 果物ならりんごとかみかんとかが好きです。
examples.en: As for fruit, I like things like apples and oranges.
examples.f: ｜果物[くだもの]ならりんごとかみかんとかが｜好[す]きです。

synonyms.note: や also lists examples but is more neutral; とか is more casual and can list actions.
など rounds off an example list ('and so on') more formally than とか.

related.note: 〜たり〜たり lists example actions with verbs; とか〜とか can list nouns or actions casually.

entry.title: など
entry.meaning: such as; and so on; etc.
entry.summary: など comes after a noun (or a short list of nouns) to mean 'and so on' or 'things like ~'. It signals that the item named is only an example and the list is not exhaustive. It often follows nouns already linked with や: ペンやノートなど = pens, notebooks, and the like.
pitfalls: など marks the list as open-ended ('and others'). If you truly mean a complete list, drop it.
In casual speech なんか and なんて cover similar ground, but they can add a dismissive nuance that plain など does not.

examples.ja: 週末は買い物や掃除などをします。
examples.en: On weekends I do things like shopping and cleaning.
examples.f: ｜週末[しゅうまつ]は｜買い物[かいもの]や｜掃除[そうじ]などをします。

examples.ja: かばんの中にペンやノートなどが入っています。
examples.en: There are pens, notebooks, and so on in the bag.
examples.f: かばんの｜中[なか]にペンやノートなどが｜入[はい]っています。

related.note: や links nouns as a partial list; など caps that list with 'and so on'.
とか〜とか lists casual examples; など tacks 'etc.' onto a noun or や-list.
なんか・なんて are the colloquial cousins that can add a belittling tone.

entry.title: おきに
entry.meaning: at intervals of; every other
entry.summary: おきに follows a number-plus-counter to say something repeats with that gap left in between. 10分おきに = every ten minutes; 1日おきに = every other day. The idea is the space you leave between one occurrence and the next.
pitfalls: おきに names the gap left between times, so 1日おきに means every OTHER day (skipping a day), not every day. For 'every single day' use 1日ごとに.
It needs a counted interval in front of it; to say 'each (item)' generally, use ごとに or the prefix 各.

examples.ja: この電車は10分おきに来ます。
examples.en: This train comes every ten minutes.
examples.f: この｜電車[でんしゃ]は10｜分[ふん]おきに｜来[き]ます。

examples.ja: 花に1日おきに水をやっています。
examples.en: I water the flowers every other day.
examples.f: ｜花[はな]に1｜日[にち]おきに｜水[みず]をやっています。

related.note: ごとに counts every unit (毎回); おきに counts the gaps between, giving 'every other'.
各 is a prefix meaning 'each ~' on a noun; おきに measures a repeating interval.

entry.title: がする
entry.meaning: to give off / to sense (a smell, sound, taste)
entry.summary: がする reports a sensation you pick up — a smell, sound, taste or feeling. The sensation noun takes が: においがする = there's a smell, 音がする = there's a sound, 味がする = it tastes (of something). Here する does not mean 'to do'; it means the sensation is present.
structure: Noun［におい／音／味／声 …］ ＋ が ＋ する
pitfalls: Mark the sensation with が, not を: においがする, not においをする.
This する is not the ordinary 'to do'. It is a fixed way of saying a sense-impression occurs, used with a limited set of nouns (smell, sound, taste, chill, feeling).

examples.ja: 台所から、いいにおいがします。
examples.en: A nice smell is drifting in from the kitchen.
examples.f: ｜台所[だいどころ]から、いいにおいがします。

examples.ja: さっき、外で大きな音がしました。
examples.en: A moment ago there was a loud noise outside.
examples.f: さっき、｜外[そと]で｜大[おお]きな｜音[おと]がしました。

related.note: する normally means 'to do'; in においがする it instead reports a sensation being present.

entry.title: わけだ
entry.meaning: that's why ~; so that means ~; no wonder ~ (a natural conclusion)
entry.summary: 〜わけだ presents something as a logical consequence you've pieced together from what's known — どうりで寒いわけだ = no wonder it's cold. It can also restate or interpret ('so you're saying...'). It signals a conclusion that follows naturally from the facts.
structure: な-adjective ＋ な／Noun ＋ という ＋ わけだ
pitfalls: It draws a conclusion that follows from the situation, unlike から／ので, which simply supply a reason.
Keep it apart from わけではない (partial denial) and わけにはいかない (can't afford to).

examples.ja: 彼は十年もパリに住んでいた。どうりでフランス語が上手なわけだ。
examples.en: He lived in Paris for ten years. No wonder his French is so good.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜十[じゅう]｜年[ねん]もパリに｜住[す]んでいた。どうりでフランス｜語[ご]が｜上手[じょうず]なわけだ。

examples.ja: 三時間も歩いたのか。それは疲れるわけだ。
examples.en: You walked for three hours? No wonder you're tired.
examples.f: ｜三[さん]｜時間[じかん]も｜歩[ある]いたのか。それは｜疲[つか]れるわけだ。

related.note: わけではない softly denies a conclusion; わけだ affirms one as the natural upshot.
ことになる is 'it works out / it's been decided that'; わけだ presents a conclusion drawn from reasoning.
ので simply states a reason; わけだ points to the conclusion that reason leads to.

entry.title: わけではない
entry.meaning: it doesn't (necessarily) mean that ~; it's not the case that ~ (partial denial)
entry.summary: 〜わけではない gently denies a conclusion someone might jump to — 'that doesn't mean...', 'it's not that...'. 嫌いなわけではない = it's not that I dislike it. It denies part, not all, and often heads off a likely misunderstanding. Casual: わけじゃない.
structure: Verb／い-adjective［plain form］＋ わけではない
な-adjective ＋ な／Noun ＋ という ＋ わけではない
pitfalls: It's a soft, partial denial ('not necessarily so'), far weaker than わけがない ('no way that's true') or a flat 〜ない.
It typically corrects an assumption the listener might otherwise make.

examples.ja: 野菜が嫌いなわけではないが、あまり食べない。
examples.en: It's not that I dislike vegetables, but I don't eat many.
examples.f: ｜野菜[やさい]が｜嫌[きら]いなわけではないが、あまり｜食[た]べない。

examples.ja: 高いからといって、必ずおいしいわけではない。
examples.en: Just because it's expensive doesn't necessarily mean it's tasty.
examples.f: ｜高[たか]いからといって、｜必[かなら]ずおいしいわけではない。

synonyms.note: 必ずしも〜ない is 'not always/necessarily'; it often teams up with わけではない for the same partial-denial nuance.
というものではない denies that a general claim always holds; わけではない denies a specific inferred conclusion.

related.note: わけがない is a total 'impossible'; わけではない only chips away at part of a conclusion.
わけだ affirms a natural conclusion; わけではない denies one.

entry.title: わけがない
entry.meaning: there's no way that ~; it's impossible that ~ (logical impossibility)
entry.summary: 〜わけがない strongly denies that something could be true, on the basis of reasoning — そんなことあるわけがない = there's no way that's true. It is more emphatic and logic-driven than はずがない. The casual form is わけない.
structure: Verb／い-adjective［plain form］＋ わけがない
な-adjective ＋ な／Noun ＋ の ＋ わけがない
pitfalls: It denies that something can be true (a logical conclusion); 'no means to do it' is ようがない.
It is a stronger, more confident version of はずがない.

examples.ja: あんなに勉強した彼が、試験に落ちるわけがない。
examples.en: There's no way he'd fail the exam after studying that hard.
examples.f: あんなに｜勉強[べんきょう]した｜彼[かれ]が、｜試験[しけん]に｜落[お]ちるわけがない。

examples.ja: 子供にこんな難しい問題が解けるわけがない。
examples.en: There's no way a child could solve a problem this difficult.
examples.f: ｜子供[こども]にこんな｜難[むずか]しい｜問題[もんだい]が｜解[と]けるわけがない。

synonyms.note: はずがない is a softer 'shouldn't / can't be'; わけがない is a more forceful, reasoned 'no way'.

related.note: わけではない is a partial 'it's not that ~'; わけがない is a full-on 'that's impossible'.
ようがない denies any means to do something; わけがない denies that something is true.

entry.title: わけにはいかない
entry.meaning: can't (bring myself to) ~; can't afford to ~ (for social or moral reasons)
entry.summary: 〜わけにはいかない says you can't do something — not because it's physically impossible, but because duty, circumstances, or social pressure won't allow it. 休むわけにはいかない = I can't just take the day off. With a negative verb, 〜ないわけにはいかない flips to 'have no choice but to'.
structure: Verb［dictionary form］＋ わけにはいかない
Verb［ない form］＋ わけにはいかない（＝ must do）
pitfalls: The impossibility is social or psychological, not physical; for 'no means to do it' use ようがない.
The double negative 〜ないわけにはいかない means 'must do', so watch the form carefully.

examples.ja: 大事な会議があるので、今日は休むわけにはいかない。
examples.en: I have an important meeting, so I can't take the day off today.
examples.f: ｜大事[だいじ]な｜会議[かいぎ]があるので、｜今日[きょう]は｜休[やす]むわけにはいかない。

examples.ja: お世話になった先生の頼みだから、断るわけにはいかない。
examples.en: It's a request from a teacher I owe a lot to, so I can't turn it down.
examples.f: お｜世話[せわ]になった｜先生[せんせい]の｜頼[たの]みだから、｜断[ことわ]るわけにはいかない。

related.note: なければならない is a plain 'must'; 〜ないわけにはいかない is 'must' pushed by duty or obligation.
〜しかない is 'have no choice but to' from lack of options; わけにはいかない blocks an option on social grounds.
ようがない is physical/means-based impossibility; わけにはいかない is being unable for social or moral reasons.

entry.title: ものだ
entry.meaning: that's just how it is; one naturally does ~ (general truth or strong feeling)
entry.summary: ものだ attaches to plain form to present something as a general, essential truth or the way things naturally are — 時間が経つのは早いものだ = time really does fly. It can also voice a heartfelt exclamation. It frames the idea as widely shared, not a one-off fact.
pitfalls: It states a general/essential truth or deep feeling, not one specific event; for a single concrete fact use plain だ.
Past 〜たものだ ('used to do') and 〜ものだから ('because') are separate patterns.

examples.ja: 年を取ると、昔のことが懐かしく思えるものだ。
examples.en: As you get older, you naturally come to feel nostalgic about the past.
examples.f: ｜年[とし]を｜取[と]ると、｜昔[むかし]のことが｜懐[なつ]かしく｜思[おも]えるものだ。

examples.ja: 子供は元気に遊ぶものだ。
examples.en: Children are meant to play with lots of energy — that's just how kids are.
examples.f: ｜子供[こども]は｜元気[げんき]に｜遊[あそ]ぶものだ。

related.note: 〜たものだ recalls a past habit ('used to'); ものだ states a timeless general truth.
〜ものではない says something is 'not to be done'; ものだ states how things naturally are.
〜ことだ gives direct advice ('you should'); ものだ describes a general truth or tendency.

entry.title: ものではない
entry.meaning: shouldn't ~; it's not something one does (social norm)
entry.summary: 〜ものではない states that an action goes against common sense or good manners — 'one shouldn't do that / it's not a thing people do'. It appeals to a general social norm rather than a specific rule, and is often used to admonish. Its affirmative 〜ものだ says 'that's how one ought to'.
structure: Verb［dictionary form］＋ ものではない
Verb［dictionary form］＋ もんじゃない（casual）
pitfalls: It scolds based on general decency ('people just don't do that'), not a specific prohibition like てはいけない.
Contrast it with 〜ものだ ('one ought to / that's how it is'); ものではない is its normative negative.

examples.ja: 食べ物を粗末にするものではない。
examples.en: You shouldn't treat food carelessly.
examples.f: ｜食べ物[たべもの]を｜粗末[そまつ]にするものではない。

examples.ja: 人の悪口を、そう簡単に口にするものではない。
examples.en: One shouldn't speak ill of others so lightly.
examples.f: ｜人[ひと]の｜悪口[わるぐち]を、そう｜簡単[かんたん]に｜口[くち]にするものではない。

synonyms.note: べきではない says something is wrong to do by principle; ものではない appeals to common decency and social sense.

related.note: ものだ (affirmative) says 'one ought to / that's how it is'; ものではない is its normative 'one shouldn't'.

entry.title: もの・もん
entry.meaning: because ~ (a reason given emotionally, often as an excuse)
entry.summary: Sentence-final もの (casual もん) gives a reason with feeling — justifying, excusing, or grumbling. It often answers a 'why?' and pairs with だって at the start of the reply. The tone is casual and can sound childish or defensive.
pitfalls: This is emotive, casual reason-giving; it's out of place in polite or formal speech.
It frequently follows a だって opener: 「だって〜だもん」.

examples.ja: 「どうして食べないの？」「だって、おなかがいっぱいだもん。」
examples.en: "Why aren't you eating?" "Because I'm full, that's why."
examples.f: 「どうして｜食[た]べないの？」「だって、おなかがいっぱいだもん。」

examples.ja: もう子供じゃないもの、ひとりで行けるよ。
examples.en: I'm not a child anymore, so I can go by myself.
examples.f: もう｜子供[こども]じゃないもの、ひとりで｜行[い]けるよ。

synonyms.note: ものだから also gives a heartfelt reason but connects mid-sentence; もの／もん closes the sentence.
もので is a softer, more polite excuse-giving connective; もん is blunter and more casual.

related.note: から is a neutral 'because'; もの／もん adds an emotional, self-justifying color.

entry.title: ことだ
entry.meaning: should; the thing to do is to ~ (direct advice)
entry.summary: Attached to a verb, ことだ delivers direct advice or a recommendation — 'the best thing is to do X.' It sounds firm and a little instructive, as if handing down the sensible course of action. Use the dictionary form for what to do, the ない-form for what to avoid.
structure: Verb［dictionary form］／［ない form］＋ ことだ
pitfalls: This advice sense attaches to a verb; when ことだ follows a feeling word (うれしいことだ) it is instead an exclamation, a different use.
It can sound top-down, like giving a lesson; for gentler suggestions use ほうがいい or 〜といい.

examples.ja: 上手になりたいなら、毎日練習することだ。
examples.en: If you want to get good, the thing to do is practice every day.
examples.f: ｜上手[じょうず]になりたいなら、｜毎日[まいにち]｜練習[れんしゅう]することだ。

examples.ja: 風邪のときは、無理をせずにゆっくり休むことだ。
examples.en: When you have a cold, you should take it easy and rest well.
examples.f: ｜風邪[かぜ]のときは、｜無理[むり]をせずにゆっくり｜休[やす]むことだ。

synonyms.note: ほうがいい gently suggests one option is better; ことだ states more forcefully what one really ought to do.

antonyms.note: ことはない says there is no need to do something; ことだ says doing it is exactly what one should do.

related.note: べきだ frames a should as a matter of principle or duty; ことだ gives practical, situational advice.

entry.title: ことはない
entry.meaning: there is no need to ~; no reason to ~
entry.summary: Verb-dictionary + ことはない reassures someone that a certain action isn't necessary — 'you don't need to (do that).' It is gentle, encouraging advice, often used to talk someone out of worrying or overreacting.
pitfalls: Verb-dictionary + ことはない means 'no need to do'; do not mix it up with たことがない, which means 'have never done' (past experience).
It reassures or reduces a burden, so it pairs with actions the listener need not take on.

examples.ja: そんなに心配することはないよ。きっと大丈夫だから。
examples.en: There's no need to worry so much — it'll surely be fine.
examples.f: そんなに｜心配[しんぱい]することはないよ。きっと｜大丈夫[だいじょうぶ]だから。

examples.ja: 一度の失敗で諦めることはない。
examples.en: There's no reason to give up over a single failure.
examples.f: ｜一[いち]｜度[ど]の｜失敗[しっぱい]で｜諦[あきら]めることはない。

antonyms.note: ことだ says doing something is exactly what you should do; ことはない says there's no need to do it.

related.note: ほうがいい recommends doing something; ことはない reassures that you don't have to.
べきだ frames a duty to act; ことはない removes any such obligation.

entry.title: ことになっている
entry.meaning: it is a rule / arrangement / custom that ~; is supposed to ~
entry.summary: ことになっている describes a rule, arrangement, or custom that is already in place and expected to hold — a school regulation, a schedule, a standing plan. It presents the situation as an established norm rather than a fresh decision.
structure: Verb［dictionary form］／［ない form］＋ ことになっている
pitfalls: ことになっている is a standing rule or arrangement in place; ことになる is a decision or outcome coming about at some point.
Do not confuse it with ことにしている, which is a personal habit you keep by choice, not an external rule.

examples.ja: この学校では、教室で物を食べてはいけないことになっている。
examples.en: At this school, the rule is that you may not eat in the classroom.
examples.f: この｜学校[がっこう]では、｜教室[きょうしつ]で｜物[もの]を｜食[た]べてはいけないことになっている。

examples.ja: 来週、社長と会うことになっている。
examples.en: I'm scheduled to meet with the company president next week.
examples.f: ｜来週[らいしゅう]、｜社長[しゃちょう]と｜会[あ]うことになっている。

related.note: ことになる is the moment a decision or result comes about; ことになっている is the rule or arrangement that then stands.
ことにする is deciding to do something yourself; ことになっている is a norm set from outside.

entry.title: ようとする
entry.meaning: to try to ~; to be about to ~ (on the verge of)
entry.summary: The volitional plus とする means either making an effort to do something (立ち上がろうとする = try to stand up) or being right on the point of something happening (日が暮れようとする = the sun is about to set). Context decides which reading applies.
pitfalls: Built on the volitional (帰ろう, 出よう), not the dictionary form.
Different from 〜と思う (stating an intention) and 〜つもり (a settled plan): ようとする is the attempt or the imminent moment itself.

examples.ja: 赤ちゃんが立ち上がろうとしている。
examples.en: The baby is trying to stand up.
examples.f: ｜赤[あか]ちゃんが｜立ち上[たちあ]がろうとしている。

examples.ja: 家を出ようとしたとき、電話が鳴った。
examples.en: Just as I was about to leave the house, the phone rang.
examples.f: ｜家[いえ]を｜出[で]ようとしたとき、｜電話[でんわ]が｜鳴[な]った。

antonyms.note: ようとしない is the negative — refusing to make the attempt that ようとする describes.

related.note: 〜ようと思う states an intention you've formed; ようとする is actually attempting or being on the verge.
〜るところだ is 'about to do' as a scheduled next step; ようとする can also mean caught in the very moment of starting.

entry.title: 一方だ
entry.meaning: to keep ~ing more and more (a one-way, ongoing change)
entry.summary: Verb［dictionary form］＋一方だ says a situation keeps moving in a single direction — it only ~s more and more. 値段は上がる一方だ = prices just keep rising, 実力は落ちる一方だ = one's ability only declines. The change is one-way and continuous, and it often describes an unwanted trend.
pitfalls: It follows the dictionary form and describes a one-directional change; it does not mean 'on the other hand' — that is 一方で.
It usually paints a steadily worsening or intensifying trend, not a two-sided comparison.

examples.ja: 最近、物の値段は上がる一方です。
examples.en: Lately, prices just keep going up and up.
examples.f: ｜最近[さいきん]、｜物[もの]の｜値段[ねだん]は｜上[あ]がる｜一方[いっぽう]です。

examples.ja: 毎日練習しないと、実力は落ちる一方だ。
examples.en: If you don't practice every day, your skills will only keep declining.
examples.f: ｜毎日[まいにち]｜練習[れんしゅう]しないと、｜実力[じつりょく]は｜落[お]ちる｜一方[いっぽう]だ。

related.note: 〜つつある marks a change that is currently in progress; 一方だ stresses that the change keeps going one way, more and more.
一方で uses the same 一方 but means 'on the other hand'; 一方だ means a situation only keeps ~ing.

entry.title: 一方で
entry.meaning: on one hand ~, on the other hand ~; while
entry.summary: 〜一方（で） contrasts two sides of a situation that hold at the same time — 'on one hand…, while on the other…'. 明るい一方で = cheerful, while (on the other hand)…. It links two coexisting facts that pull in different directions, often about the same person or thing.
pitfalls: 一方で sets up a contrast between two coexisting sides; don't mix it up with 一方だ ('keeps ~ing more and more').
The two sides usually pull in opposite directions, so it is not just neutral addition.

examples.ja: 兄は明るい一方で、弟はとても静かです。
examples.en: My older brother is cheerful, while my younger brother is very quiet.
examples.f: ｜兄[あに]は｜明[あか]るい｜一方[いっぽう]で、｜弟[おとうと]はとても｜静[しず]かです。

examples.ja: この仕事は大変な一方で、やりがいもあります。
examples.en: This job is hard, but on the other hand it's rewarding.
examples.f: この｜仕事[しごと]は｜大変[たいへん]な｜一方[いっぽう]で、やりがいもあります。

synonyms.note: 〜反面 also contrasts two sides of the same thing; 一方で can present two separate subjects side by side as well.

related.note: 逆に flips to the opposite ('conversely'); 一方で holds up two coexisting sides at once.
一方だ uses the same 一方 but means a situation only keeps ~ing; 一方で marks a two-sided contrast.

entry.title: に対して
entry.meaning: toward (a target); in contrast to ~
entry.summary: に対して has two jobs. It aims an action or feeling at a target — お客様に対して丁寧に話す ('speak politely toward customers'). It also sets two things in contrast — 兄が明るいのに対して弟は静かだ ('in contrast to the cheerful older brother, the younger one is quiet'). Before a noun, use に対する.
pitfalls: Two jobs: aiming an action or feeling at someone ('toward'), and setting two things against each other ('in contrast to').
に対して directs something at a target; keep it apart from に関して／について, which mean 'on the topic of'.

examples.ja: お客様に対して、丁寧な言葉を使いましょう。
examples.en: Let's use polite language toward customers.
examples.f: お｜客様[きゃくさま]に｜対[たい]して、｜丁寧[ていねい]な｜言葉[ことば]を｜使[つか]いましょう。

examples.ja: 兄が明るいのに対して、弟は静かだ。
examples.en: In contrast to the cheerful older brother, the younger one is quiet.
examples.f: ｜兄[あに]が｜明[あか]るいのに｜対[たい]して、｜弟[おとうと]は｜静[しず]かだ。

related.note: に比べて weighs one thing against a baseline; に対して sets two things side by side in contrast.
に反して means 'contrary to (what was expected)'; に対して's contrast sense is a neutral 'whereas'.
に向かって is aiming at a physical direction; に対して aims an action or attitude at a target.

entry.title: について
entry.meaning: about; concerning; regarding ~
entry.summary: について marks the topic you speak, write, or think about — 'about / concerning ~'. この町の歴史について調べる ('research about this town's history'). Before a noun, add の — その問題についての意見 ('an opinion about that problem'). It is the everyday way to name a subject.
pitfalls: Add の to modify a noun: 事故についての説明, not 事故について説明.
について marks the topic you speak or think about; に対して aims an action at a target — don't swap them.

examples.ja: この町の歴史について、調べています。
examples.en: I'm researching the history of this town.
examples.f: この｜町[まち]の｜歴史[れきし]について、｜調[しら]べています。

examples.ja: その問題についての意見を聞かせてください。
examples.en: Please let me hear your opinion about that problem.
examples.f: その｜問題[もんだい]についての｜意見[いけん]を｜聞[き]かせてください。

synonyms.note: に関して is the more formal 'regarding'; について is the everyday equivalent.

related.note: に対して aims an action or feeling at a target ('toward'); について names the topic.
において marks a place, time, or field; について marks the topic under discussion.

entry.title: ばかりでなく
entry.meaning: not only ~ but also ~
entry.summary: 〜ばかりでなく means 'not only X but also Y', adding a second, often broader point on top of the first — 彼は英語ばかりでなく、中国語も話せる = he can speak not only English but also Chinese. The second part usually carries も ('also'). It is a slightly more formal way to say 〜だけでなく.
structure: Noun ＋ ばかりでなく ＋ … も
Verb［plain form］／い-adjective ＋ ばかりでなく
な-adjective ＋ な ＋ ばかりでなく
pitfalls: The added part often takes も ('also'): 子供ばかりでなく、大人も楽しめる.
〜だけでなく is the everyday equivalent; 〜ばかりでなく sounds a little more formal or written.

examples.ja: この公園は子供ばかりでなく、大人も楽しめます。
examples.en: This park can be enjoyed not only by children but also by adults.
examples.f: この｜公園[こうえん]は｜子供[こども]ばかりでなく、｜大人[おとな]も｜楽[たの]しめます。

examples.ja: 彼女は歌が上手なばかりでなく、ダンスもできる。
examples.en: She's not only good at singing but can also dance.
examples.f: ｜彼女[かのじょ]は｜歌[うた]が｜上手[じょうず]なばかりでなく、ダンスもできる。

synonyms.note: 〜だけでなく is the more everyday 'not only… but also…'; 〜ばかりでなく is a bit more formal.

related.note: 〜のみならず (N1) is the formal, written version of the same 'not only… but also…'.
〜ばかりで complains that there is only one thing; 〜ばかりでなく adds a second thing on top.

entry.title: だけでなく
entry.meaning: not only ~ (but also)
entry.summary: だけでなく says that the point isn't limited to the first item — a second one applies as well. The second item usually gets も ('also'). It joins both halves inside one sentence and sounds neutral, fitting both writing and everyday speech.
structure: Noun ＋ だけでなく ＋ Noun ＋ も
Verb／い-adjective［plain form］＋ だけでなく
pitfalls: The second item usually carries も: A だけでなく B も.
It's more neutral than the emphatic 〜ばかりでなく and more explicit than joining items with just 〜も.

examples.ja: 彼女は英語だけでなく、中国語も話せる。
examples.en: She can speak not only English but also Chinese.
examples.f: ｜彼女[かのじょ]は｜英語[えいご]だけでなく、｜中国[ちゅうごく]｜語[ご]も｜話[はな]せる。

examples.ja: この店はケーキだけでなく、パンも人気だ。
examples.en: At this shop, not only the cakes but also the bread is popular.
examples.f: この｜店[みせ]はケーキだけでなく、パンも｜人気[にんき]だ。

synonyms.note: 〜ばかりでなく carries the same 'not only'; だけでなく is the more neutral, common choice.

related.note: だけで is 'just by'; だけでなく is 'not only.'
それに adds a point in a new sentence; だけでなく joins both inside one.

entry.title: も〜ば〜も
entry.meaning: both ~ and ~; (with negatives) neither ~ nor ~
entry.summary: も〜ば〜も lists two parallel facts about one topic, using the ば conditional on the first predicate — 歌も歌えばギターも弾く = both sings and plays guitar. With negatives it becomes 'neither...nor'. It piles up matching items rather than stating a real condition.
structure: Noun ＋ も ＋ Verb／い-adjective［ば form］、Noun ＋ も 〜
pitfalls: The middle predicate takes ば form (多ければ, なければ); it is a listing device, not a genuine 'if'.
In a negative frame it reads as 'neither ~ nor ~': お金もなければ時間もない = have neither money nor time.

examples.ja: この店は品数も多ければ、値段も安い。
examples.en: This shop has a wide selection and low prices too.
examples.f: この｜店[みせ]は｜品数[しなかず]も｜多[おお]ければ、｜値段[ねだん]も｜安[やす]い。

examples.ja: 今はお金もなければ時間もない。
examples.en: Right now I have neither money nor time.
examples.f: ｜今[いま]はお｜金[かね]もなければ｜時間[じかん]もない。

related.note: だけでなく adds a second point onto a first; も〜ば〜も sets two items side by side as a balanced pair.
ばかりでなく is 'not only...but also'; も〜ば〜も simply lists two coexisting facts.

entry.title: っぽい
entry.meaning: -ish; -like; has the quality of; tends to
entry.summary: っぽい tacks onto a noun, adjective stem, or verb stem to say something has the quality or tendency of that word — 子供っぽい = childish, 忘れっぽい = forgetful, 安っぽい = cheap-looking. The whole compound behaves like an い-adjective. It's colloquial and often carries a mildly critical tone.
pitfalls: With a verb stem it means 'tends to / easily does' (怒りっぽい = quick to anger), not 'looks like.'
It's casual and can sound negative: 安っぽい means 'cheap-looking,' not simply 'inexpensive.'

examples.ja: 彼は忘れっぽくて、よく約束を忘れる。
examples.en: He's forgetful and often forgets his promises.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜忘[わす]れっぽくて、よく｜約束[やくそく]を｜忘[わす]れる。

examples.ja: その色は少し子供っぽいと思う。
examples.en: I think that color is a little childish.
examples.f: その｜色[いろ]は｜少[すこ]し｜子供[こども]っぽいと｜思[おも]う。

synonyms.note: みたいだ says something resembles or looks like another thing; っぽい says it has that quality or tendency, more casually.

related.note: がち is about how often an event tends to happen; っぽい 'tends to' describes a lasting quality or trait.
らしい means 'befitting / typical of'; っぽい often means the opposite — merely -ish, or not quite befitting.

entry.title: 的
entry.meaning: -al; -ic; relating to; turns a noun into a な-adjective or adverb
entry.summary: 的 attaches to a noun to make an adjective-like word meaning 'relating to / -al / -ic' — 一般的 = general, 科学的 = scientific, 積極的 = proactive. Add な before a noun (的な考え) and に to use it adverbially (的に説明する). It's extremely common in both writing and speech.
pitfalls: Use 的な before a noun and 的に as an adverb: 具体的な例, 具体的に説明する.
It attaches mainly to kanji compound nouns (社会的, 経済的), not usually to everyday native words.

examples.ja: もっと具体的に説明してください。
examples.en: Please explain it more concretely.
examples.f: もっと｜具体[ぐたい]｜的[てき]に｜説明[せつめい]してください。

examples.ja: 彼は積極的な性格で、すぐ友達を作る。
examples.en: He has a proactive personality and makes friends quickly.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜積極[せっきょく]｜的[てき]な｜性格[せいかく]で、すぐ｜友達[ともだち]を｜作[つく]る。

related.note: っぽい is a casual '-ish' added to everyday words; 的 forms categorical '-al/-ic' adjectives from kanji compounds.

entry.title: に違いない
entry.meaning: must be; surely; no doubt that ~
entry.summary: に違いない states a firm guess based on evidence — 'it must be ~ / surely ~'. 電気が消えているから、もう寝たに違いない ('the lights are off, so he must have gone to bed'). It is stronger than かもしれない but is still an inference, not a confirmed fact. It follows a noun, adjective, or plain verb.
structure: Noun／な-adjective／い-adjective／Verb［plain form］＋ に違いない
pitfalls: に違いない voices a confident guess from evidence — stronger than かもしれない, but still a guess, not a known fact.

examples.ja: 電気が消えているから、彼はもう寝たに違いない。
examples.en: The lights are off, so he must have already gone to bed.
examples.f: ｜電気[でんき]が｜消[き]えているから、｜彼[かれ]はもう｜寝[ね]たに｜違[ちが]いない。

examples.ja: この宝石は本物に違いない。
examples.en: This jewel must be genuine.
examples.f: この｜宝石[ほうせき]は｜本物[ほんもの]に｜違[ちが]いない。

synonyms.note: はずだ is a logical expectation from known facts; に違いない is a strong personal conviction.
に決まっている is an even more emphatic, casual 'bound to be'; に違いない is confident but a bit more measured.

related.note: かもしれない is a weak 'might be'; に違いない is a strong 'must be'.

entry.title: に決まっている
entry.meaning: surely; of course; it's bound to be
entry.summary: に決まっている voices the speaker's firm personal conviction that something is obviously the case — 'of course it is; it's bound to be'. そんな話うそに決まっている ('that story is obviously a lie'). It is subjective, emphatic, and rather casual, attaching straight to the plain form.
structure: Verb／い-adjective［plain form］＋ に決まっている
Noun／な-adjective ＋ に決まっている
pitfalls: It states the speaker's personal conviction ('obviously!'), so it is emphatic and casual — weaker in objective or formal writing than に違いない or に相違ない.
Attach directly to the plain form; with nouns and な-adjectives no だ appears: 便利に決まっている, not 便利だに決まっている.

examples.ja: あんなに練習したのだから、彼が勝つに決まっています。
examples.en: He practiced that much, so of course he'll win.
examples.f: あんなに｜練習[れんしゅう]したのだから、｜彼[かれ]が｜勝[か]つに｜決[き]まっています。

examples.ja: こんな時間に電話しても、みんな寝ているに決まっている。
examples.en: Calling at an hour like this — everyone's obviously asleep.
examples.f: こんな｜時間[じかん]に｜電話[でんわ]しても、みんな｜寝[ね]ているに｜決[き]まっている。

synonyms.note: に違いない is a more measured 'must be' based on reasoning; に決まっている is a blunter, more emotional 'obviously'.
に相違ない is the formal, written 'without a doubt'; に決まっている is its casual, conversational cousin.

related.note: はずだ is a reasoned expectation that can be revised; に決まっている is a stubborn conviction that brooks no doubt.

entry.title: ずに
entry.meaning: without doing ~
entry.summary: ずに attaches to a verb's negative base to mean "without doing ~" — 朝ご飯を食べずに家を出た = went out without eating breakfast. It's the more formal, written equivalent of ないで. The one irregular form is する → せずに.
pitfalls: する becomes せずに, not しずに.
ずに is more formal and written; ないで is the everyday spoken choice.

examples.ja: 傘を持たずに家を出て、雨に降られてしまった。
examples.en: I left home without taking an umbrella and got caught in the rain.
examples.f: ｜傘[かさ]を｜持[も]たずに｜家[いえ]を｜出[で]て、｜雨[あめ]に｜降[ふ]られてしまった。

examples.ja: よく考えずに返事をして、あとで困った。
examples.en: I answered without thinking it through, and had trouble later.
examples.f: よく｜考[かんが]えずに｜返事[へんじ]をして、あとで｜困[こま]った。

synonyms.note: ないで is the everyday spoken "without doing ~"; ずに is the same meaning in a formal, written register.

related.note: 〜ことなく is a formal "without ever ~ing"; ずに is the plainer "without doing (this time)."
〜ずに済む builds on ずに to mean "get by without having to ~."

entry.title: まま
entry.meaning: as it is; leaving/staying unchanged
entry.summary: まま describes a state left unchanged while something else happens — 'as it is / still in that condition'. Something stays the way it was instead of being set right: 窓を開けたまま出かけた (went out with the window left open). It attaches to た form, ない form, な-adjective＋な, or noun＋の.
pitfalls: The state carries over into the next action: 靴をはいたまま入る (enter with shoes still on).
Different from ながら: ながら is two actions happening at once; まま is one unchanged state persisting during another action.

examples.ja: 窓を開けたまま出かけてしまった。
examples.en: I went out leaving the window open.
examples.f: ｜窓[まど]を｜開[あ]けたまま｜出[で]かけてしまった。

examples.ja: 立ったままで食べないでください。
examples.en: Please don't eat while standing.
examples.f: ｜立[た]ったままで｜食[た]べないでください。

related.note: ながら is doing two actions simultaneously; まま is keeping one state unchanged during another action.

entry.title: うちに
entry.meaning: while (still) ~; before ~ changes
entry.summary: 〜うちに picks out a window of time and says to act within it. After a plain state it means 'while ~ still holds' (熱いうちに = while it's still hot); after a ない-form it means 'before ~ happens' (忘れないうちに = before I forget). The nuance is that the window will close, so do it now.
pitfalls: 〜ないうちに means 'before ~ happens' (暗くならないうちに = before it gets dark); plain 〜うちに means 'while the state still lasts'.
It carries the sense that the window will end, so act during it — it is not a neutral 'while'.

examples.ja: 熱いうちに、どうぞ召し上がってください。
examples.en: Please eat it while it's still hot.
examples.f: ｜熱[あつ]いうちに、どうぞ｜召し上[めしあ]がってください。

examples.ja: 忘れないうちに、メモしておきます。
examples.en: I'll jot it down before I forget.
examples.f: ｜忘[わす]れないうちに、メモしておきます。

related.note: 〜間に marks a defined span and something happening within it; 〜うちに adds the sense that the state may change, so act now.
〜ないうちに is the negative pattern of this point — 'before ~ happens'; plain 〜うちに is 'while ~ still lasts'.
〜前に just says 'before' a point in time; 〜ないうちに adds 'while it hasn't yet happened, take the chance'.

entry.title: ば〜ほど
entry.meaning: the more ~, the more ~
entry.summary: ば〜ほど links two changes that rise together — 練習すればするほど上手になる = the more you practice, the better you get. You repeat the same word, first in ば-form and then in dictionary/plain form, before ほど. As the first grows, so does the second. It is the standard 'the more…, the more…' pattern.
structure: Verb［ば form］＋ Verb［dictionary form］＋ ほど
い-adjective ＋ ければ ＋ い-adjective ＋ ほど
な-adjective ＋ なら ＋ な-adjective ＋ なほど
pitfalls: Repeat the same word: 見れば見るほど, 高ければ高いほど — the ば-form, then the plain form before ほど.
For な-adjectives, the frame is 〜なら〜なほど (静かなら静かなほど); do not force them into the verb pattern.

examples.ja: この本は、読めば読むほど面白くなる。
examples.en: The more you read this book, the more interesting it gets.
examples.f: この｜本[ほん]は、｜読[よ]めば｜読[よ]むほど｜面白[おもしろ]くなる。

examples.ja: 部屋は、広ければ広いほどいいです。
examples.en: As for rooms, the bigger the better.
examples.f: ｜部屋[へや]は、｜広[ひろ]ければ｜広[ひろ]いほどいいです。

related.note: ほど by itself marks a degree or extent; ば〜ほど pairs two rising degrees into 'the more…, the more…'.

entry.title: ほど
entry.meaning: to the extent that; so ~ that; about (an amount)
entry.summary: ほど marks a degree or extent — it sets a vivid yardstick for how far a state goes: 立てないほど疲れた = 'so tired I couldn't stand.' The clause before ほど paints how extreme the situation is. After a number, ほど means 'about' (三十分ほど), much like くらい.
pitfalls: ほど often sets a striking measure for a degree (死ぬほど疲れた = 'dead tired'); the part before ほど shows how extreme the state is.
After a number, ほど means 'about/approximately' (三十分ほど), overlapping with くらい.

examples.ja: 立てないほど足が疲れてしまった。
examples.en: My legs got so tired that I couldn't stand.
examples.f: ｜立[た]てないほど｜足[あし]が｜疲[つか]れてしまった。

examples.ja: 泣きたいほど嬉しかった。
examples.en: I was so happy I could have cried.
examples.f: ｜泣[な]きたいほど｜嬉[うれ]しかった。

synonyms.note: くらい／ぐらい also marks extent and approximate amount and often swaps in for ほど; ほど is favored for a striking upper-limit yardstick.

related.note: ば〜ほど is 'the more... the more'; plain ほど here marks a single degree or extent.
ほど〜ない uses the same word in a comparison to mean 'not as... as'.

entry.title: さえ
entry.meaning: even; so much as; not even
entry.summary: さえ singles out an extreme or surprising example to imply the rest follows — 子どもでさえ知っている (even a child knows), 時間さえない (I don't even have time). The idea is 'if even this, then surely everything else.' It is emphatic and often a touch more formal than も.
pitfalls: さえ picks an extreme case to make its point; it is more emphatic and often more written-sounding than も.
Do not confuse plain さえ ('even') with the conditional さえ〜ば ('if only').

examples.ja: そんなことは子どもでさえ知っている。
examples.en: Even a child knows something like that.
examples.f: そんなことは｜子[こ]どもでさえ｜知[し]っている。

examples.ja: 忙しくて、食事をする時間さえない。
examples.en: I'm so busy I don't even have time to eat.
examples.f: ｜忙[いそが]しくて、｜食事[しょくじ]をする｜時間[じかん]さえない。

synonyms.note: すら is a more formal, literary 'even'; さえ is the everyday emphatic 'even.'

related.note: まで stresses reaching an unexpected extreme ('to the point of even'); さえ picks a minimal example to imply the rest.
さえ〜ば uses さえ to mark the one sufficient condition; plain さえ just highlights an extreme example.

entry.title: さえ〜ば
entry.meaning: if only ~; as long as (just) ~
entry.summary: さえ〜ば names the one and only condition needed for a result — 'just do X, and that's all it takes.' A noun takes さえ plus a ば-clause (お金さえあれば), while a verb becomes stem + さえすれば (押しさえすれば). It says nothing else is required.
pitfalls: It marks the sole sufficient condition — 'just this, nothing more' — unlike plain さえ, which only means 'even.'
With verbs, use stem + さえすれば (見さえすれば), not the dictionary form.

examples.ja: お金さえあれば、何でも買えるというわけではない。
examples.en: It's not as if you can buy anything just as long as you have money.
examples.f: お｜金[かね]さえあれば、｜何[なに]でも｜買[か]えるというわけではない。

examples.ja: このボタンを押しさえすれば、機械が動きます。
examples.en: As long as you just press this button, the machine will run.
examples.f: このボタンを｜押[お]しさえすれば、｜機械[きかい]が｜動[うご]きます。

related.note: ば states a general condition; さえ〜ば narrows it to the single sufficient one.
だけで means 'just with / just by' doing something; さえ〜ば frames that one thing as the only condition needed.
Plain さえ highlights an extreme example ('even'); さえ〜ば turns さえ into a sole-condition pattern.

entry.title: こそ
entry.meaning: precisely; for sure; this very one (emphasis)
entry.summary: こそ spotlights the word right before it, singling it out as 'this one, precisely, and not another.' Attached to a noun or phrase it says 'this is the one that really counts' — 今度こそ (this time for sure), こちらこそ (no, thank YOU). It highlights rather than contrasts.
pitfalls: こそ spotlights one item as 'precisely this'; unlike は it does not set up a topic-and-contrast, it simply emphasizes.
In reply exchanges こちらこそ means 'the feeling is mine, precisely' — the emphasis lands on こちら, not on thanking again.

examples.ja: 今年こそ日本語能力試験に合格したい。
examples.en: This year for sure, I want to pass the Japanese Language Proficiency Test.
examples.f: ｜今年[ことし]こそ｜日本語[にほんご]｜能力[のうりょく]｜試験[しけん]に｜合格[ごうかく]したい。

examples.ja: 「手伝ってくれてありがとう。」「いいえ、こちらこそ。」
examples.en: "Thanks for helping me." "No, thank YOU."
examples.f: 「｜手伝[てつだ]ってくれてありがとう。」「いいえ、こちらこそ。」

related.note: からこそ means 'precisely because'; here こそ is fused with the reason から, while plain こそ can spotlight any noun.
さえ emphasizes by giving an extreme example ('even this'); こそ emphasizes by singling one thing out as the very one.
だけ limits to 'only this'; こそ spotlights 'this, precisely,' without excluding others.

entry.title: として
entry.meaning: as; in the role of; in the capacity of
entry.summary: Noun ＋ として names the role, position, or capacity in which someone or something acts — 医者として働く = work as a doctor; お礼として渡す = give it as a token of thanks. It labels the standpoint from which the action is done, so the noun before it is a role, status, or purpose rather than a person's viewpoint.
pitfalls: として marks the role something serves in (代表として = as a representative); にとって marks whose viewpoint you judge from (私にとって = for me) — don't swap them.
For 'as a rule / in principle' senses, として combines into set phrases like 原則として; the core idea is still 'in the capacity of'.

examples.ja: 彼女は通訳として、その会議に参加した。
examples.en: She took part in that meeting as an interpreter.
examples.f: ｜彼女[かのじょ]は｜通訳[つうやく]として、その｜会議[かいぎ]に｜参加[さんか]した。

examples.ja: この部屋は、今は物置として使っています。
examples.en: We're using this room as a storage space for now.
examples.f: この｜部屋[へや]は、｜今[いま]は｜物置[ものおき]として｜使[つか]っています。

related.note: にとって gives the standpoint from which you evaluate ('for ~'); として gives the role in which one acts ('as ~').

entry.title: にとって
entry.meaning: to; for; from the standpoint of ~
entry.summary: にとって attaches to a noun — usually a person, group, or organization — and weighs something from that party's standpoint: how it looks, matters, or feels to them. 私にとって = for me / as far as I'm concerned. It is almost always followed by an evaluation (大切だ, 難しい, 幸せだ). Use it to say who something is significant, hard, or valuable for.
pitfalls: にとって marks whose viewpoint you are judging from; it is not the 'for whose benefit' に of あげる/くれる. For 'I bought it for my mother', use のために, not にとって.
Follow it with an evaluation or judgment (大切, 必要, つらい…), not an ordinary action — にとって does not mark the doer of a plain verb.

examples.ja: 私にとって、家族が一番大切です。
examples.en: For me, family is the most important thing.
examples.f: ｜私[わたし]にとって、｜家族[かぞく]が｜一番[いちばん]｜大切[たいせつ]です。

examples.ja: この問題は子供にとって難しすぎます。
examples.en: This problem is too difficult for children.
examples.f: この｜問題[もんだい]は｜子供[こども]にとって｜難[むずか]しすぎます。

related.note: として states the role or capacity someone acts in; にとって states whose viewpoint something is weighed from.
に対して directs an action or attitude toward a target; にとって gives the standpoint from which something is judged.

entry.title: にしては
entry.meaning: for; considering it's ~ (the result is unexpected)
entry.summary: にしては judges a result against a clear yardstick and notes it doesn't fit — 'for ~ / considering it's ~'. 初心者にしては上手 ('good for a beginner'), 冬にしては暖かい ('warm for winter'). The outcome is usually a mild surprise given the standard you'd expect.
pitfalls: にしては measures a result against a definite reference point (a beginner, winter …) and finds it doesn't match; the outcome tends to be surprising.
わりに(は) is close, but its standard can be looser; にしては needs a clear reference point.

examples.ja: 彼は初心者にしては、上手にピアノを弾く。
examples.en: For a beginner, he plays the piano well.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜初心者[しょしんしゃ]にしては、｜上手[じょうず]にピアノを｜弾[ひ]く。

examples.ja: 今日は冬にしては暖かいね。
examples.en: It's warm for winter today, isn't it?
examples.f: ｜今日[きょう]は｜冬[ふゆ]にしては｜暖[あたた]かいね。

synonyms.note: わりに means 'considering / for', with a looser standard; にしては needs a definite reference point.

related.note: くせに adds blame or criticism to the contrast; にしては simply notes an unexpected result.
にしても means 'even if / even supposing'; にしては judges a result against a standard.

entry.title: にしても
entry.meaning: even if; even though; even supposing ~
entry.summary: にしても grants a point and then pushes back against it — 'even if ~ / even supposing ~'. 行くにしても準備に時間がかかる ('even if we go, prep takes time'), 冗談にしてもひどい ('even as a joke, that's awful'). You accept the situation for the sake of argument, then state something that still holds.
pitfalls: にしても grants a point ('even supposing X') and then counters it; don't mix it up with にしては ('for / considering', which judges a result against a standard).

examples.ja: 行くにしても、準備には時間がかかる。
examples.en: Even if we go, the preparations will take time.
examples.f: ｜行[い]くにしても、｜準備[じゅんび]には｜時間[じかん]がかかる。

examples.ja: 冗談にしても、その言い方はひどいよ。
examples.en: Even as a joke, that way of putting it is awful.
examples.f: ｜冗談[じょうだん]にしても、その｜言い方[いいかた]はひどいよ。

related.note: にしろ〜にしろ pairs two cases 'whether A or B'; にしても concedes a single point.
いずれにしても means 'in any case, whichever it is'; にしても concedes one specific supposition.
にしては judges a result against a standard ('for ~'); にしても concedes 'even if ~'.

entry.title: に比べて
entry.meaning: compared to; in comparison with ~
entry.summary: に比べて sets a baseline you measure something against — 'compared to ~'. 去年に比べて雨が多い ('there's more rain compared to last year'), 都会に比べて田舎は安い ('the countryside is cheaper compared to the city'). The noun before に比べて is the reference point; the new information comes in the main clause. に比べ is the same, a touch more formal.
pitfalls: The thing after に比べて is the baseline you measure against; the point you want to make comes in the main clause.

examples.ja: 去年に比べて、今年は雨が多い。
examples.en: Compared to last year, there's a lot of rain this year.
examples.f: ｜去年[きょねん]に｜比[くら]べて、｜今年[ことし]は｜雨[あめ]が｜多[おお]い。

examples.ja: 都会に比べて、田舎は物価が安い。
examples.en: Compared to the city, prices are cheaper in the countryside.
examples.f: ｜都会[とかい]に｜比[くら]べて、｜田舎[いなか]は｜物価[ぶっか]が｜安[やす]い。

synonyms.note: より marks the standard in a plain comparison ('than'); に比べて frames a broader 'compared with'.

related.note: に対して sets two things in direct contrast; に比べて weighs one against a baseline.
わりに means 'considering / for (what you'd expect)'; に比べて is a straight comparison.

entry.title: に代わって・に代わり
entry.kana: にかわって・にかわり
entry.meaning: instead of; in place of; on behalf of ~
entry.summary: に代わって marks doing something in place of, or on behalf of, a specific person or thing — 社長に代わって挨拶する ('give the greeting on behalf of the president'), 現金に代わって電子マネーを使う ('use electronic money instead of cash'). に代わり is the same in a slightly more formal style.
structure: Noun ＋ に代わって／に代わり
pitfalls: に代わって replaces a specific person or thing ('in place of A'); 代わりに can do that too but also means 'in exchange / to make up for'.

examples.ja: 社長に代わって、私がご挨拶いたします。
examples.en: In place of the company president, I will give the greeting.
examples.f: ｜社長[しゃちょう]に｜代[か]わって、｜私[わたし]がご｜挨拶[あいさつ]いたします。

examples.ja: 最近は現金に代わって、電子マネーを使う人が増えた。
examples.en: Recently the number of people using electronic money instead of cash has grown.
examples.f: ｜最近[さいきん]は｜現金[げんきん]に｜代[か]わって、｜電子[でんし]マネーを｜使[つか]う｜人[ひと]が｜増[ふ]えた。

synonyms.note: 代わりに also means 'instead of', but it can additionally mean 'in exchange / to make up for'.

entry.title: 代わりに
entry.meaning: instead of; in place of; in exchange for
entry.summary: 〜代わりに carries two linked senses: 'instead of / in place of' (substitution) and 'in exchange for / to make up for' (compensation) — バターの代わりにオイルを使う = use oil instead of butter; 手伝う代わりに昼ごはんをおごる = treat someone to lunch in return for help. Context tells you which.
pitfalls: After a noun it takes の: 私の代わりに, not 私代わりに.
The same form covers both 'instead of' and 'in exchange for'; read the context to tell substitution from compensation.

examples.ja: 今日は父の代わりに、私が会議に出た。
examples.en: Today I attended the meeting in place of my father.
examples.f: ｜今日[きょう]は｜父[ちち]の｜代[か]わりに、｜私[わたし]が｜会議[かいぎ]に｜出[で]た。

examples.ja: 手伝ってくれる代わりに、晩ごはんをごちそうするよ。
examples.en: In exchange for helping me, I'll treat you to dinner.
examples.f: ｜手伝[てつだ]ってくれる｜代[か]わりに、｜晩[ばん]ごはんをごちそうするよ。

entry.title: にしたがって
entry.meaning: as (one thing changes, another does); in accordance with ~
entry.summary: にしたがって has two related senses. As a proportional link it means 'as one thing changes, another changes with it' — 山を登るにしたがって空気が薄くなる ('as you climb, the air thins'). As 'in accordance with' it means following rules or instructions — 指示にしたがって動く ('act according to the instructions'). Context tells the two apart.
structure: Verb［dictionary form］／Noun ＋ にしたがって
pitfalls: One form, two senses: 'as one thing changes, another follows' (proportional) and 'obeying / following (rules, instructions)'; context decides which.

examples.ja: 山を登るにしたがって、空気が薄くなってきた。
examples.en: As we climbed the mountain, the air gradually grew thinner.
examples.f: ｜山[やま]を｜登[のぼ]るにしたがって、｜空気[くうき]が｜薄[うす]くなってきた。

examples.ja: 係員の指示にしたがって、避難してください。
examples.en: Please evacuate in accordance with the staff's instructions.
examples.f: ｜係員[かかりいん]の｜指示[しじ]にしたがって、｜避難[ひなん]してください。

synonyms.note: につれて covers only the proportional 'as ~ changes' sense; にしたがって also means 'following (rules)'.

related.note: に伴って marks a change that accompanies another; にしたがって stresses the two moving together in step.
したがって at the head of a sentence means 'therefore'; にしたがって attaches to a noun or verb.

entry.title: につれて
entry.meaning: as (one thing changes, another follows); in proportion as ~
entry.summary: につれて links two gradual changes: as one thing progresses, another shifts along with it — 時間がたつにつれて痛みが消える ('as time passes, the pain fades'), 年をとるにつれて体力が落ちる ('as you age, your stamina drops'). Both sides must move gradually and together.
pitfalls: につれて needs a gradual, linked change on both sides; it doesn't fit a one-time or sudden event.

examples.ja: 時間がたつにつれて、痛みは少しずつ消えていった。
examples.en: As time passed, the pain gradually faded away.
examples.f: ｜時間[じかん]がたつにつれて、｜痛[いた]みは｜少[すこ]しずつ｜消[き]えていった。

examples.ja: 年をとるにつれて、体力が落ちてきた。
examples.en: As I've grown older, my stamina has declined.
examples.f: ｜年[とし]をとるにつれて、｜体力[たいりょく]が｜落[お]ちてきた。

synonyms.note: にしたがって covers this same proportional 'as ~ changes', and also 'following (rules)'.
に伴って marks a change accompanying another; につれて stresses the two moving together step by step.

related.note: 〜ば〜ほど means 'the more ~, the more ~'; につれて tracks two changes progressing together over time.

entry.title: と共に
entry.meaning: together with; along with; at the same time as
entry.summary: と共に has two related uses. With a noun it means 'together with' — 家族と共に新年を迎えた = I welcomed the new year together with my family. With a verb of change it means 'as ~ happens, so does ...' — 年を取ると共に体力が落ちる = as you age, your stamina declines. It is a formal, written-flavoured equivalent of 〜と一緒に and 〜につれて.
pitfalls: It is stiff and written; in casual speech 〜と一緒に is more natural for 'together with'.
The 'as ~ changes' use needs a verb of change or development (増える, 進む), where two things shift in parallel.

examples.ja: 卒業生たちは、家族と共に喜びを分かち合った。
examples.en: The graduates shared their joy together with their families.
examples.f: ｜卒業生[そつぎょうせい]たちは、｜家族[かぞく]と｜共[とも]に｜喜[よろこ]びを｜分[わ]かち｜合[あ]った。

examples.ja: 技術が進むと共に、私たちの生活も変わってきた。
examples.en: As technology has advanced, our lives have changed along with it.
examples.f: ｜技術[ぎじゅつ]が｜進[すす]むと｜共[とも]に、｜私[わたし]たちの｜生活[せいかつ]も｜変[か]わってきた。

related.note: と同時に pins two things to the same instant; と共に can be broader 'together with' or a gradual parallel change.
につれて is 'as A gradually changes, B changes too'; と共に covers that plus plain 'together with'.
にしたがって also means 'as ~ proceeds'; と共に adds the separate sense of accompaniment ('together with').

entry.title: たびに
entry.meaning: every time; whenever
entry.summary: たびに says that each time one thing happens, another regularly follows — "every time; whenever." It attaches to a dictionary-form verb or to a noun with の, and points to something that repeats on each occasion.
pitfalls: Use the dictionary form, not the past: 会うたびに, not 会ったたびに.
たびに is about repeated occasions; for one sudden moment ('as soon as'), use とたん.

examples.ja: 彼女は会うたびに、新しい話を聞かせてくれる。
examples.en: Every time I see her, she tells me a new story.
examples.f: ｜彼女[かのじょ]は｜会[あ]うたびに、｜新[あたら]しい｜話[はなし]を｜聞[き]かせてくれる。

examples.ja: 旅行のたびに、その土地の名物を買って帰る。
examples.en: Every time I travel, I buy the local specialty to bring home.
examples.f: ｜旅行[りょこう]のたびに、その｜土地[とち]の｜名物[めいぶつ]を｜買[か]って｜帰[かえ]る。

synonyms.note: 毎〜のように means 'nearly every time'; たびに means literally each and every time, without exception.

related.note: とたん marks one sudden instant; たびに marks a recurring pattern across many occasions.

entry.title: ごとに
entry.meaning: each; every; at intervals of
entry.summary: ごとに means 'every' or 'each', attaching to a counter, a noun, or a dictionary-form verb. With a counter it marks a regular interval — 四年ごとに = every four years. With a verb it means 'each time...': 会うごとに = every time we meet. It picks out a repeating unit and says something holds for each one.
pitfalls: 三日ごとに means 'every three days' (a regular interval). Don't confuse it with 三日おきに, which leaves three-day gaps (every fourth day).
ごとに attaches freely to counters and verbs; まい (毎〜) instead prefixes set time-words like 毎日, 毎週.

examples.ja: オリンピックは四年ごとに開かれます。
examples.en: The Olympics are held every four years.
examples.f: オリンピックは｜四[よん]｜年[ねん]ごとに｜開[ひら]かれます。

examples.ja: 彼は会うごとに元気になっていく。
examples.en: Every time we meet, he seems more energetic.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜会[あ]うごとに｜元気[げんき]になっていく。

related.note: 〜に〜回 counts how often within a span (週に一回); ごとに marks the repeating unit itself.
〜おきに measures the gap between events; ごとに counts each event itself.

entry.title: 最中に
entry.meaning: right in the middle of; in the very midst of
entry.summary: 最中に marks the peak of an ongoing action, often the moment something cuts in — 食事の最中に (right in the middle of dinner), 話している最中に (right as I was talking). It stresses that the action was at full swing when interruption or an event occurred.
pitfalls: 最中に highlights the height of an action in progress, usually broken into by something; it suits continuing actions, not instantaneous ones.
A noun takes の before it: 会議の最中に, not 会議最中に.

examples.ja: 食事の最中に、電話がかかってきた。
examples.en: Right in the middle of dinner, a phone call came in.
examples.f: ｜食事[しょくじ]の｜最中[さいちゅう]に、｜電話[でんわ]がかかってきた。

examples.ja: 話している最中に、急に電気が消えた。
examples.en: Right as I was in the middle of talking, the lights suddenly went out.
examples.f: ｜話[はな]している｜最中[さいちゅう]に、｜急[きゅう]に｜電気[でんき]が｜消[き]えた。

related.note: ているところ marks the stage of an action ('in the middle of doing'); 最中に stresses its very peak, often interrupted.
間に marks a span during which something happens; 最中に zooms in on the height of one ongoing action.
うちに means 'while a state lasts / before it changes'; 最中に is 'right at the peak of an action.'

entry.title: ついでに
entry.meaning: while you're at it; on the same occasion; on the way
entry.summary: ついでに marks doing a second thing while you're already doing the first — you take advantage of one occasion to get another errand done at little extra effort. It attaches to a verb (dictionary or た form) or to a noun with の. The main action comes first; the ついでに action is the bonus.
structure: Verb［dictionary form］／［た form］＋ ついでに
pitfalls: The primary action is stated first; the ついでに part is the extra, secondary thing done 'while you're at it.'
Attach it to a noun with の: 散歩のついでに, not 散歩ついでに.

examples.ja: 買い物に行くついでに、郵便局にも寄ってきます。
examples.en: While I'm out shopping, I'll stop by the post office too.
examples.f: ｜買い物[かいもの]に｜行[い]くついでに、｜郵便[ゆうびん]｜局[きょく]にも｜寄[よ]ってきます。

examples.ja: 散歩のついでに、パンを買って帰った。
examples.en: On my walk, I bought some bread on the way back.
examples.f: ｜散歩[さんぽ]のついでに、パンを｜買[か]って｜帰[かえ]った。

related.note: ながら is doing two actions at the same moment; ついでに is one occasion used to also handle a secondary errand.

entry.title: おかげで
entry.meaning: thanks to; owing to; because of (a good result)
entry.summary: 〜おかげで credits a cause with a good outcome — 'thanks to ~'. 先生のおかげで = thanks to my teacher, 天気が良かったおかげで = thanks to the good weather. The default tone is gratitude, so it normally pairs a cause with a welcome result.
structure: Verb ／ い-adjective ／ な-adjective［plain form］＋おかげで
pitfalls: 〜おかげで normally credits a good result; for a bad result you blame on something, use 〜せいで.
It can be turned ironic ('thanks a lot…') for a bad outcome, but its plain meaning is genuine thanks.

examples.ja: 先生のおかげで、試験に合格できました。
examples.en: Thanks to my teacher, I was able to pass the exam.
examples.f: ｜先生[せんせい]のおかげで、｜試験[しけん]に｜合格[ごうかく]できました。

examples.ja: 天気が良かったおかげで、旅行はとても楽しかったです。
examples.en: Thanks to the good weather, the trip was a lot of fun.
examples.f: ｜天気[てんき]が｜良[よ]かったおかげで、｜旅行[りょこう]はとても｜楽[たの]しかったです。

antonyms.note: 〜せいで pins a bad result on a cause ('because of ~, unfortunately'); 〜おかげで credits a good result.

related.note: 〜ために gives a neutral cause or purpose; 〜おかげで specifically thanks a cause for a good outcome.

entry.title: せいで
entry.meaning: because of; due to (blaming an unwanted result on a cause)
entry.summary: せいで pins a bad outcome on a cause — "because of ~, (something unwanted happened)." 電車が遅れたせいで、遅刻した = I was late because the train was delayed. The result is undesirable, and せいで often assigns fault. Its positive-outcome counterpart is おかげで.
pitfalls: せいで is for unwanted results and often assigns blame; for a welcome result, use おかげで.
At the end of a sentence it becomes 〜のせいだ ("it's the fault of ~").

examples.ja: 昨日夜ふかしをしたせいで、今朝は頭が痛い。
examples.en: Because I stayed up late last night, my head hurts this morning.
examples.f: ｜昨日[きのう]｜夜[よ]ふかしをしたせいで、｜今朝[けさ]は｜頭[あたま]が｜痛[いた]い。

examples.ja: 大雨のせいで、電車が止まってしまった。
examples.en: Because of the heavy rain, the trains stopped.
examples.f: ｜大雨[おおあめ]のせいで、｜電車[でんしゃ]が｜止[と]まってしまった。

antonyms.note: おかげで credits a good result to its cause ("thanks to"); せいで blames a bad one on it.

related.note: ので is a neutral "because" with no blame; せいで adds fault for an unwanted outcome.
〜ために gives a neutral cause (or a purpose); せいで specifically pins down blame for a bad result.

entry.title: ないことはない
entry.meaning: it's not that one can't; it is possible (though with reservation); not impossible
entry.summary: This double negative softly affirms that something is possible after all — 急げば間に合わないことはない = it's not impossible to make it if we hurry. It admits the possibility while holding back full enthusiasm, so it often carries a reluctant or hedged tone. Attach ことはない to a verb's ない form, or to 〜くない for adjectives.
structure: Verb［ない form］＋ ことはない
い-adjective［stem］＋ くないことはない
pitfalls: It's a soft, hedged 'yes, it's possible', weaker than a plain affirmative — often with unspoken reluctance.
Don't confuse it with ことはない meaning 'there's no need to' (謝ることはない = no need to apologize), which has no first ない.

examples.ja: からいものも食べないことはないが、あまり好きではない。
examples.en: It's not that I can't eat spicy food, but I don't really like it.
examples.f: からいものも｜食[た]べないことはないが、あまり｜好[す]きではない。

examples.ja: 急げば、終電に間に合わないことはない。
examples.en: If we hurry, it's not impossible to catch the last train.
examples.f: ｜急[いそ]げば、｜終電[しゅうでん]に｜間に合[まにあ]わないことはない。

related.note: わけではない denies a conclusion ('it doesn't mean that'); ないことはない softly admits a possibility exists.
ことはない (no first ない) means 'there's no need to'; ないことはない is a double negative meaning 'it's not impossible'.

entry.title: てたまらない
entry.meaning: unbearably ~; can't stand how ~; dying to ~
entry.summary: てたまらない expresses a feeling or desire so strong the speaker can hardly bear it — 暑くてたまらない = 'unbearably hot', 会いたくてたまらない = 'dying to see someone'. It attaches to the て-form of adjectives and verbs of emotion or sensation. たまらない literally means 'cannot be endured', so the whole phrase conveys an overwhelming, uncontrollable state.
pitfalls: It describes the speaker's own uncontrollable feeling or sensation, so it pairs with emotion and sensation words, not neutral statements.
For a desire, it attaches to the 〜たい form (見たくてたまらない), not the plain verb.

examples.ja: 久しぶりの故郷が懐かしくてたまらない。
examples.en: I miss my hometown, which I haven't seen in ages, terribly.
examples.f: ｜久[ひさ]しぶりの｜故郷[こきょう]が｜懐[なつ]かしくてたまらない。

examples.ja: 新しいゲームがやりたくてたまらない。
examples.en: I'm dying to play the new game.
examples.f: ｜新[あたら]しいゲームがやりたくてたまらない。

synonyms.note: てならない conveys the same overwhelming feeling but leans formal and favors spontaneous thoughts (思えてならない).
てしょうがない・てしかたがない is the more casual 'can't help feeling'; てたまらない stresses that the feeling is barely bearable.

entry.title: て初めて
entry.meaning: not until ~; only after doing ~ (did I realize/come to)
entry.summary: 〜てはじめて joins the て form to say that only after experiencing X does something Y become true — usually a realization. ひとりで暮らしてはじめて = only after living alone (did I understand...). The 初めて here means 'only at that point', not literally 'for the first time counting occasions'.
pitfalls: 初めて here means 'not until then / only at that point', so it is often followed by realization verbs like 分かる, 気づく.
The X part is a real experience that triggers the realization, not a hypothetical.

examples.ja: ひとりで暮らしてはじめて、親のありがたさが分かった。
examples.en: It was only after living on my own that I understood how much I owe my parents.
examples.f: ひとりで｜暮[く]らしてはじめて、｜親[おや]のありがたさが｜分[わ]かった。

examples.ja: 病気になってはじめて、健康の大切さに気づいた。
examples.en: Not until I got sick did I realize how important health is.
examples.f: ｜病気[びょうき]になってはじめて、｜健康[けんこう]の｜大切[たいせつ]さに｜気[き]づいた。

related.note: からこそ stresses 'precisely because'; てはじめて stresses that the realization came only after the experience.

entry.title: てばかりいる
entry.meaning: to do nothing but ~; to always be ~ing (often critical)
entry.summary: 〜てばかりいる attaches to the て form and says someone does one action over and over and little else — 遊んでばかりいる = does nothing but play around. It usually carries a critical or exasperated tone, painting the behavior as excessive and unbalanced. The いる can conjugate (ばかりいた, ばかりいて).
structure: Verb［て form］＋ ばかりいる
pitfalls: It usually sounds critical — that the person does this to the exclusion of what they should be doing.
Attach ばかり after the て form here: 泣いてばかりいる, not 泣くばかりいる.
Keep it apart from Verb［た form］＋ばかり ('just did'); てばかりいる is a repeated habit, not a one-off that just happened.

examples.ja: 弟は遊んでばかりいて、宿題を全然やらない。
examples.en: My little brother does nothing but play around and never does his homework.
examples.f: ｜弟[おとうと]は｜遊[あそ]んでばかりいて、｜宿題[しゅくだい]を｜全然[ぜんぜん]やらない。

examples.ja: 最近、姉はスマホを見てばかりいる。
examples.en: Lately my older sister does nothing but look at her phone.
examples.f: ｜最近[さいきん]、｜姉[あね]はスマホを｜見[み]てばかりいる。

synonyms.note: ばかり is the base 'only' particle; 〜てばかりいる is its ongoing-habit form with a verb and a critical edge.

related.note: だけ neutrally limits to 'only'; 〜てばかりいる adds the sense of an excessive, unbalanced habit.

entry.title: ばいい
entry.meaning: should ~; it'd be good if ~; you can just ~
entry.summary: 〜ばいい suggests that doing something is a good idea or the way to solve a problem — 分からなければ、先生に聞けばいい = if you don't understand, you can just ask the teacher. It can give advice ('you should just…'), state a solution, or express a wish (雨が止めばいい = I hope the rain stops). The ば-form carries the 'if you do it' sense and いい adds 'that would be good'.
pitfalls: Depending on context, ばいい ranges from friendly advice ('you can just…') to a slightly blunt 'just do it'; tone matters when suggesting.
〜ばよかった (past) expresses regret about what you should have done; 〜ばいい is present advice or a wish.

examples.ja: 道が分からなければ、駅の人に聞けばいいですよ。
examples.en: If you don't know the way, you can just ask someone at the station.
examples.f: ｜道[みち]が｜分[わ]からなければ、｜駅[えき]の｜人[ひと]に｜聞[き]けばいいですよ。

examples.ja: 迷ったら、地図を見ればいいです。
examples.en: If you get lost, you can just look at the map.
examples.f: ｜迷[まよ]ったら、｜地図[ちず]を｜見[み]ればいいです。

related.note: 〜方がいい compares and recommends one option; 〜ばいい points to doing something as the good move or solution.
the 〜たら conditional can replace ば here (聞いたらいい); both give advice about what to do.
〜ばよかった regrets what you should have done; 〜ばいい advises what is good to do now.

entry.title: 場合は
entry.meaning: in the case that ~; in the event of ~
entry.summary: 場合 means 'case' or 'situation', and 〜場合は presents a hypothetical situation and states what to do if it arises. It attaches to plain forms of verbs and adjectives, な-adjective＋な, and noun＋の. Common in rules, manuals, and official notices: 'in the case that A, (do) B'.
pitfalls: 場合 is on the formal side — think manuals, contracts, and notices; in casual speech 〜たら or 〜とき is more common.
A noun connects with の: 地震の場合は, not 地震場合は.

examples.ja: 雨の場合は、試合は中止です。
examples.en: In the event of rain, the match will be cancelled.
examples.f: ｜雨[あめ]の｜場合[ばあい]は、｜試合[しあい]は｜中止[ちゅうし]です。

examples.ja: 分からない場合は、係の人に聞いてください。
examples.en: If you don't understand, please ask a staff member.
examples.f: ｜分[わ]からない｜場合[ばあい]は、｜係[かかり]の｜人[ひと]に｜聞[き]いてください。

related.note: たら is the everyday 'if/when'; 場合は is the formal wording used in rules and notices.
とき marks the time an event actually happens; 場合は sets up a hypothetical situation to prepare for.
なら picks up a topic just raised; 場合は presents a condition on its own terms.

entry.title: とすれば・としたら・とすると
entry.kana: とすれば・としたら・とすると
entry.romaji: to sureba / to shitara / to suruto
entry.meaning: assuming that; supposing; if A (is the case), then B
entry.summary: These three attach to a plain-form clause to set up a supposition and draw a logical consequence — 彼の話が本当だとしたら、大変だ = supposing his story is true, that's a serious matter. You assume A for the sake of argument, then state what would follow. とすれば, としたら, and とすると are largely interchangeable; the second clause is usually a judgement, guess, or conclusion.
structure: Sentence［plain form］＋ とすれば／としたら／とすると
pitfalls: This is a hypothesis for reasoning, so the second clause is typically a judgement or inference, not a request or command.
Don't confuse it with plain たら for 'when': ついたら電話して is temporal, but 本当だとしたら大変だ is 'supposing it's true'.

examples.ja: 今から出発するとすれば、着くのは夜になるだろう。
