examples.en: Assuming we leave now, we probably won't arrive until night.
examples.f: ｜今[いま]から｜出発[しゅっぱつ]するとすれば、｜着[つ]くのは｜夜[よる]になるだろう。

examples.ja: この話が事実だとしたら、大きな問題だ。
examples.en: If this story is true, then it's a serious problem.
examples.f: この｜話[はなし]が｜事実[じじつ]だとしたら、｜大[おお]きな｜問題[もんだい]だ。

synonyms.note: なら also picks up a supposition to comment on; とすれば・としたら leans more toward reasoning out a logical consequence.

related.note: たら often means 'when/after' in time; としたら is purely 'supposing that', for hypothetical reasoning.
と言えば picks up a word to talk about it ('speaking of'); としたら assumes something is so and reasons from it.

entry.title: としても
entry.meaning: even if; even assuming that ~
entry.summary: としても supposes a case and concedes that it does not change the outcome — 'even if / even assuming that ~'. 本当だとしても驚かない = 'even if it's true, I won't be surprised'. It combines a hypothetical (とする) with the concessive も.
pitfalls: としても supposes something hypothetically ('even if we assume'), whereas ても can also concede an actual fact; としても leans clearly on a supposition.
After a noun or な-adjective, insert だ: 本当だとしても, not 本当としても.

examples.ja: 今から急いだとしても、始発には間に合わないだろう。
examples.en: Even if we hurry now, we probably won't make the first train.
examples.f: ｜今[いま]から｜急[いそ]いだとしても、｜始発[しはつ]には｜間に合[まにあ]わないだろう。

examples.ja: たとえ冗談だとしても、そんなことは言うべきではない。
examples.en: Even if it's a joke, you shouldn't say such a thing.
examples.f: たとえ｜冗談[じょうだん]だとしても、そんなことは｜言[い]うべきではない。

synonyms.note: ても concedes 'even if / even though', including actual facts; としても adds the sense of supposing a hypothetical case.

related.note: とすれば・としたら supposes a case and reasons forward from it; としても supposes a case but concedes it changes nothing.
たって is the casual spoken 'even if'; としても is the more composed 'even assuming that ~'.

entry.title: って
entry.meaning: casual quotation: ~ (that)
entry.summary: A casual, conversational marker that reports what someone said or something you heard: "~ they say" or "I heard that ~". It is a spoken shortcut for と (with 言う/聞く) or という. You'll hear it constantly in everyday talk to pass along information.
pitfalls: って is casual — in formal writing or speech, use と or という instead.
It often marks hearsay ("I heard ~") and can trail off without 言う: 明日は雨だって ("they say it'll rain").

examples.ja: 明日は雨だって。
examples.en: They say it'll rain tomorrow.
examples.f: ｜明日[あした]は｜雨[あめ]だって。

examples.ja: あの店は安いって聞きました。
examples.en: I heard that shop is cheap.
examples.f: あの｜店[みせ]は｜安[やす]いって｜聞[き]きました。

synonyms.note: と is the standard, more formal quotation marker; って is its casual spoken form.

related.note: という introduces or names a quoted content; って is the casual contraction of it.
と思う reports what you think; って reports what was said or heard.

entry.title: ということだ
entry.meaning: it means that ~; I hear that ~; in other words
entry.summary: 〜ということだ has two everyday uses: reporting hearsay ('I hear that ~') and drawing or restating a conclusion ('which means that ~'). つまり〜ということだ sums something up; 部長は来ないということだ passes on news. Context tells the two apart.
structure: Sentence［plain form］＋ ということだ
pitfalls: The hearsay use relays information from a source; the conclusion use rephrases or infers, often after つまり.
Don't confuse it with というものだ, which asserts what something truly is.

examples.ja: 部長はあした来られないということだ。
examples.en: I hear the manager can't come tomorrow.
examples.f: ｜部長[ぶちょう]はあした｜来[こ]られないということだ。

examples.ja: 返事がないということは、興味がないということだ。
examples.en: No reply means they're not interested.
examples.f: ｜返事[へんじ]がないということは、｜興味[きょうみ]がないということだ。

synonyms.note: そうだ only reports hearsay; ということだ also draws or restates conclusions.

related.note: というわけだ presents a conclusion that follows naturally from what was said; ということだ can also just relay hearsay.
というものだ asserts the true nature of something; ということだ reports or restates.

entry.title: というのは
entry.meaning: the thing called ~ is; that is to say; the reason is that ~
entry.summary: 〜というのは raises a topic to explain it — either defining it ('~ is (defined as)...') or giving the reason behind it ('the reason is that...'). 「敷金」というのは…お金のことです defines a word; 疲れているというのは、忙しいからです explains a cause, often ending in からだ.
pitfalls: In the definition use it often ends with 〜ことです／意味です.
In the explanatory use it usually ends with 〜からだ ('the reason is that...').

examples.ja: 「敷金」というのは、部屋を借りるときに払うお金のことです。
examples.en: 'Shikikin' refers to money you pay when renting a room.
examples.f: 「｜敷金[しききん]」というのは、｜部屋[へや]を｜借[か]りるときに｜払[はら]うお｜金[かね]のことです。

examples.ja: 最近疲れているというのは、仕事が忙しいからです。
examples.en: The reason I've been tired lately is that work is busy.
examples.f: ｜最近[さいきん]｜疲[つか]れているというのは、｜仕事[しごと]が｜忙[いそが]しいからです。

synonyms.note: というと reacts to a topic or asks for clarification; というのは stops to define or explain it.

related.note: という names or labels a word; というのは takes that named word as the topic to explain.
ということだ restates a conclusion or relays hearsay; というのは sets up a definition or reason.

entry.title: というより
entry.meaning: rather than ~; more like B than A
entry.summary: 〜というより refines how you describe one thing, saying B is a more accurate label than A — 優しいというより気が弱い = not so much kind as timid. It compares two descriptions of the same thing and is often followed by むしろ ('rather').
pitfalls: It weighs two descriptions of one thing, not two separate options — that latter job belongs to plain より.
It's often reinforced by むしろ in the second half.

examples.ja: 彼は優しいというより、ただ気が弱いだけだ。
examples.en: He's not so much kind as just timid.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜優[やさ]しいというより、ただ｜気[き]が｜弱[よわ]いだけだ。

examples.ja: これは趣味というより、もう仕事だね。
examples.en: At this point this is more like work than a hobby.
examples.f: これは｜趣味[しゅみ]というより、もう｜仕事[しごと]だね。

synonyms.note: ではなくて flatly rejects A for B; というより softens it to 'B is the more fitting way to put it'.

related.note: より alone compares two separate things; というより compares two labels for the same thing.

entry.title: くせに
entry.meaning: even though; despite (with blame or contempt)
entry.summary: 〜くせに means 'even though', but always with a critical, reproachful edge — you are blaming or looking down on someone for the contradiction. 知っているくせに教えてくれない = he won't tell me even though he knows. Both clauses usually share the same subject.
pitfalls: It carries blame or contempt, so it is rude toward the person described; for a neutral 'even though', use のに.
It connects to nouns with の and な-adjectives with な: 子供のくせに, 下手なくせに.

examples.ja: 知っているくせに、彼は何も教えてくれなかった。
examples.en: Even though he knew, he told me nothing.
examples.f: ｜知[し]っているくせに、｜彼[かれ]は｜何[なに]も｜教[おし]えてくれなかった。

examples.ja: 自分ではやらないくせに、文句ばかり言う。
examples.en: He does nothing himself, yet he's all complaints.
examples.f: ｜自分[じぶん]ではやらないくせに、｜文句[もんく]ばかり｜言[い]う。

synonyms.note: のに is the neutral 'even though'; くせに adds blame and can't be used approvingly.

entry.title: から〜にかけて
entry.meaning: from ~ through ~ (a continuous span of time or space)
entry.summary: 〜から〜にかけて marks a continuous stretch from one point to another across time or space — 春から夏にかけて = from spring through summer. The boundaries are approximate; it describes a broad range rather than exact endpoints.
structure: Noun ＋ から ＋ Noun ＋ にかけて
pitfalls: The endpoints are vague and the span is one continuous stretch; for a precise 'from X to Y' with clear limits, use から〜まで.
にかけて takes each side as a broad region or period, so exact clock times sound better with まで.

examples.ja: この地方では、夏から秋にかけて雨が多い。
examples.en: In this region there is a lot of rain from summer through autumn.
examples.f: この｜地方[ちほう]では、｜夏[なつ]から｜秋[あき]にかけて｜雨[あめ]が｜多[おお]い。

examples.ja: 今夜から明日の朝にかけて、雪になるでしょう。
examples.en: From tonight through tomorrow morning, it will likely turn to snow.
examples.f: ｜今夜[こんや]から｜明日[あした]の｜朝[あさ]にかけて、｜雪[ゆき]になるでしょう。

related.note: まで marks a clear endpoint 'until'; にかけて spans a vague stretch to an approximate end.

entry.title: っけ
entry.meaning: what was it again? (casual ending to confirm a half-remembered thing)
entry.summary: っけ is a casual sentence-final particle you tack on when you're trying to recall or double-check something you've half-forgotten — 'what was it again?' It usually follows the plain past (〜たっけ) or だ→だっけ. It belongs to relaxed, friendly speech among close people.
pitfalls: It's casual; in polite situations people say 〜でしたっけ / 〜ましたっけ instead.
With nouns and な-adjectives it becomes だっけ: 今日は何曜日だっけ.

examples.ja: あれ、鍵はどこに置いたっけ。
examples.en: Huh, where did I put the keys again?
examples.f: あれ、｜鍵[かぎ]はどこに｜置[お]いたっけ。

examples.ja: 明日の会議は何時からだっけ。
examples.en: What time was tomorrow's meeting again?
examples.f: ｜明日[あした]の｜会議[かいぎ]は｜何[なん]｜時[じ]からだっけ。

entry.title: ふりをする
entry.meaning: to pretend; to act as if; to put on an act of ~
entry.summary: ふりをする means to pretend or put on an act — to behave as if something were true when it isn't. 寝ているふりをする = pretend to be asleep; 知らないふりをする = pretend not to know. Verbs and い-adjectives attach plainly, while nouns and な-adjectives take の／な first.
structure: Verb［plain form］／い-adjective＋ ふりをする
な-adjective＋ な／Noun＋ の ＋ ふりをする
pitfalls: Use the ない form to pretend NOT to do something: 気づかないふりをする = pretend not to notice.
Nouns and な-adjectives take の／な before ふり: 病気のふりをする, 元気なふりをする.

examples.ja: 道で先生に会ったが、気づかないふりをした。
examples.en: I ran into my teacher on the street but pretended not to notice.
examples.f: ｜道[みち]で｜先生[せんせい]に｜会[あ]ったが、｜気[き]づかないふりをした。

examples.ja: 弟は寝ているふりをして、こっそり話を聞いていた。
examples.en: My little brother pretended to be asleep and was secretly listening to us.
examples.f: ｜弟[おとうと]は｜寝[ね]ているふりをして、こっそり｜話[はなし]を｜聞[き]いていた。

related.note: かのように describes an action as if something were the case; ふりをする is deliberately faking a state or behavior.
まるで sets up a 'just like' comparison; ふりをする is putting on a false act on purpose.

entry.title: がち
entry.meaning: tends to; apt to; prone to (usually something unwanted)
entry.summary: 〜がち says something tends to happen often, usually with an unwanted flavor — 忘れがち = apt to forget, 病気がち = prone to illness. It attaches to a verb stem or a noun and describes a recurring tendency, not a single event.
pitfalls: It leans negative (遅れがち, 忘れがち, 曇りがち); for a neutral or positive 'tends to', it sounds off.
It describes a habitual tendency, not what is happening right at this moment.
Attach it to the stem, not the dictionary form: 遅れがち, not 遅れるがち.

examples.ja: 忙しいと、朝ごはんを抜きがちになる。
examples.en: When I'm busy, I tend to skip breakfast.
examples.f: ｜忙[いそが]しいと、｜朝[あさ]ごはんを｜抜[ぬ]きがちになる。

examples.ja: 最近、曇りがちの天気が続いている。
examples.en: Lately there's been a stretch of cloudy weather.
examples.f: ｜最近[さいきん]、｜曇[くも]りがちの｜天気[てんき]が｜続[つづ]いている。

synonyms.note: 〜気味 marks a slight touch of something (degree); がち marks how frequently it happens.
〜っぽい 'tends to / -ish' overlaps but is more colloquial and also covers 'looks like'.

related.note: 〜やすい 'prone to' rates the ease/likelihood of one instance; がち is about frequency of occurrence.

entry.title: 気味
entry.meaning: a touch of; a bit; tending toward (a slight sign of)
entry.summary: 〜気味 attaches to a noun or verb stem to say there is a slight touch or trace of something — 風邪気味 = a touch of a cold, 疲れ気味 = a bit tired. It marks a mild sign or leaning, usually of something not great.
pitfalls: It marks a slight degree ('a bit, a touch'), not a full-blown state; 風邪気味 is coming down with a cold, not having a bad one.
It tends toward negative or unwanted conditions (疲れ気味, 太り気味, 遅れ気味).

examples.ja: 少し疲れ気味なので、今日は早く寝ます。
examples.en: I'm feeling a bit tired, so I'll go to bed early today.
examples.f: ｜少[すこ]し｜疲[つか]れ｜気味[ぎみ]なので、｜今日[きょう]は｜早[はや]く｜寝[ね]ます。

examples.ja: 最近、体重が増え気味で心配だ。
examples.en: Lately my weight has been creeping up, and I'm a little worried.
examples.f: ｜最近[さいきん]、｜体重[たいじゅう]が｜増[ふ]え｜気味[ぎみ]で｜心配[しんぱい]だ。

synonyms.note: がち is 'frequently, apt to' (how often); 気味 is 'a slight touch of' (degree).
っぽい '-ish' overlaps loosely but is broader and more casual.

entry.title: だらけ
entry.meaning: covered in; full of (usually something unwelcome)
entry.summary: だらけ attaches to a noun to say something is covered in or full of that thing — usually something unwelcome, like 泥だらけ (covered in mud) or 間違いだらけ (full of mistakes). It gives a strong impression of an unpleasant excess.
structure: Noun ＋ だらけ ＋ の ＋ Noun
pitfalls: だらけ almost always describes something negative or messy; for a neutral 'full of,' use でいっぱい.
Before a noun it needs の: 傷だらけの車, not 傷だらけ車.

examples.ja: 子供たちは泥だらけになって遊んでいた。
examples.en: The kids were playing, covered head to toe in mud.
examples.f: ｜子供[こども]たちは｜泥[どろ]だらけになって｜遊[あそ]んでいた。

examples.ja: 彼のレポートは間違いだらけだった。
examples.en: His report was full of mistakes.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]のレポートは｜間違[まちが]いだらけだった。

synonyms.note: 〜まみれ is very close but stays physical — smeared or coated with a substance; だらけ also covers non-physical excess like mistakes.

related.note: ばかり ('nothing but') can be neutral; だらけ specifically stresses an unpleasant, messy excess.

entry.title: かける・かけ
entry.meaning: half-done; not yet finished; on the point of ~ing
entry.summary: 〜かける attaches to the ます-stem to mean an action is only half carried out or is just about to happen — 言いかける = start to say, 倒れかける = be on the verge of falling. The noun form 〜かけ describes a left-unfinished thing — 食べかけ = half-eaten, 読みかけ = half-read. Either way, the action is not seen through to the end.
pitfalls: Attach it to the stem: 読みかける, not 読むかける.
〜かけ (noun) labels something left half-done (読みかけの本); 〜かける (verb) also means 'be on the point of ~ing' (泣きかける).

examples.ja: 食べかけのケーキが、テーブルに置いてあります。
examples.en: There's a half-eaten cake sitting on the table.
examples.f: ｜食[た]べかけのケーキが、テーブルに｜置[お]いてあります。

examples.ja: 何か言いかけて、彼は急に黙ってしまいました。
examples.en: He started to say something, then suddenly fell silent.
examples.f: ｜何[なに]か｜言[い]いかけて、｜彼[かれ]は｜急[きゅう]に｜黙[だま]ってしまいました。

antonyms.note: 〜終わる is an action carried all the way to the finish; 〜かけ・かける is one left half-done.

related.note: 〜切る is doing something thoroughly to the very end; 〜かける is stopping partway or only starting.
〜途中で marks being partway through on the way somewhere; 〜かけ marks a thing itself left half-finished.

entry.title: 合う
entry.meaning: to do an action to one another; to do mutually / together
entry.summary: 〜合う attaches to the ます-stem and says that two or more people do the action to or with each other — 話し合う = talk it over together, 助け合う = help one another, 分かり合う = understand each other. The nuance is reciprocal: the action goes both ways. The compound conjugates like an ordinary う-verb (合った, 合って).
pitfalls: Attach it to the stem, not the dictionary form: 話し合う, not 話す合う.
It implies a two-way, mutual action between people; a plain 話す is just 'talk', while 話し合う is 'talk it through with each other'.
Don't confuse this compound suffix with the standalone verb 会う ('to meet someone'), which sounds the same but is written differently.

examples.ja: 家族でよく話し合って、留学することを決めました。
examples.en: We talked it over as a family and decided that I would study abroad.
examples.f: ｜家族[かぞく]でよく｜話し合[はなしあ]って、｜留学[りゅうがく]することを｜決[き]めました。

examples.ja: 困ったときは、友達と助け合うことが大切です。
examples.en: When you're in trouble, it's important to help each other out with your friends.
examples.f: ｜困[こま]ったときは、｜友達[ともだち]と｜助け合[たすけあ]うことが｜大切[たいせつ]です。

entry.title: 〜直す
entry.meaning: to redo; to do (something) over again
entry.summary: 〜直す attaches to the ます-stem to mean doing an action over again, usually to fix or improve the result — 書き直す = rewrite, 考え直す = reconsider, やり直す = start over. The idea is a fresh second attempt, not just repeating for its own sake. The compound conjugates like a う-verb.
pitfalls: Attach it to the stem: やり直す, not やる直す.
On its own 直す means 'to fix or repair'; in this 'do over' meaning it must follow another verb's stem.

examples.ja: レポートを最初から書き直しました。
examples.en: I rewrote the report from the beginning.
examples.f: レポートを｜最初[さいしょ]から｜書き直[かきなお]しました。

examples.ja: もう一度考え直したほうがいいですよ。
examples.en: You'd better think it over again.
examples.f: もう｜一度[いちど]｜考え直[かんがえなお]したほうがいいですよ。

related.note: Both follow a verb stem; 〜始める marks starting the action, 〜直す marks doing it over.

entry.title: 〜づらい
entry.meaning: hard to do (often uncomfortable or a strain for the doer)
entry.summary: 〜づらい attaches to the ます-stem and means an action is hard or uncomfortable to do — often because doing it puts some strain or awkwardness on the speaker. 言いづらい = hard to bring myself to say; 歩きづらい = hard to walk. The compound behaves like an い-adjective (づらかった, づらくない).
pitfalls: 〜づらい often carries a sense that the difficulty is unpleasant or a burden on the doer; 〜にくい is more neutral and also fits purely objective difficulty.
Attach it to the stem: 読みづらい, not 読むづらい.

examples.ja: この字は小さくて読みづらいです。
examples.en: This writing is small and hard to read.
examples.f: この｜字[じ]は｜小[ちい]さくて｜読[よ]みづらいです。

examples.ja: 本当のことは、ちょっと言いづらいです。
examples.en: The truth is a little hard to bring myself to say.
examples.f: ｜本当[ほんとう]のことは、ちょっと｜言[い]いづらいです。

synonyms.note: 〜にくい is the neutral 'hard to'; 〜づらい adds that the difficulty is uncomfortable for the doer.
〜がたい is stronger — 'nearly impossible to' — and more formal or literary.

antonyms.note: 〜やすい means easy or comfortable to do — the opposite of 〜づらい.

entry.title: ところだった
entry.meaning: almost; nearly; was about to (but it didn't actually happen)
entry.summary: Verb［dictionary form］＋ ところだった describes something that very nearly happened but in the end did not — もう少しで転ぶところだった = I almost fell over. It often comes with もう少しで or 危うく ('nearly, narrowly'). The key point is that the event was avoided; you are relieved or startled that it didn't come to pass.
structure: Verb［dictionary form］＋ ところだった
もう少しで／危うく ＋ Verb［dictionary form］＋ ところだった
pitfalls: The action did not actually happen — it was a near miss, not a real event.
Use the dictionary form for 'was about to' (乗り遅れるところだった); the た form + ところ (乗り遅れたところ) means 'had just done it', which is the opposite outcome.

examples.ja: もう少しで電車に乗り遅れるところだった。
examples.en: I very nearly missed the train.
examples.f: もう｜少[すこ]しで｜電車[でんしゃ]に｜乗り遅[のりおく]れるところだった。

examples.ja: 危うく大事な約束を忘れるところだった。
examples.en: I almost forgot an important appointment.
examples.f: ｜危[あや]うく｜大事[だいじ]な｜約束[やくそく]を｜忘[わす]れるところだった。

related.note: 〜かける is an action started but left half-done; ところだった is one that nearly started but never actually happened.

entry.title: からといって
entry.meaning: just because ~ (it doesn't mean); simply because
entry.summary: [plain form] + からといって introduces a reason that one might expect to justify a certain conclusion, and then rejects that conclusion: 'just because X, it does not follow that Y'. It is almost always paired with a negative or limiting ending such as わけではない or とは限らない.
structure: Sentence［plain form］＋ からといって
pitfalls: It is typically followed by a negative/limiting statement (〜とは限らない、〜わけではない); it exists to reject an over-hasty conclusion.
The reason it raises is real; what it denies is only the assumed conclusion drawn from it.

examples.ja: 都会に住んでいるからといって、みんなが生活に満足しているわけではない。
examples.en: Just because someone lives in the city doesn't mean everyone is satisfied with their life.
examples.f: ｜都会[とかい]に｜住[す]んでいるからといって、みんなが｜生活[せいかつ]に｜満足[まんぞく]しているわけではない。

examples.ja: 安いからといって、質が悪いとは限らない。
examples.en: Just because it's cheap doesn't necessarily mean the quality is poor.
examples.f: ｜安[やす]いからといって、｜質[しつ]が｜悪[わる]いとは｜限[かぎ]らない。

related.note: というわけではない is the denial half ('it's not that ~'), which からといって often leads into.
必ずしも ('not necessarily') frequently appears in the concluding clause paired with からといって.

entry.title: なんか・なんて
entry.meaning: things like ~; such as ~ (often dismissive or emphatic)
entry.summary: なんか and なんて are casual, emotional versions of など. After a noun they mean 'things like ~ / such as ~', usually with a dismissive or belittling tone — スポーツなんか興味がない ('no interest in stuff like sports'). なんて can also follow a whole clause to show surprise or disbelief — 負けるなんて ('to think you'd lose!'). The feeling behind them is what sets them apart from plain など.
pitfalls: なんか・なんて often sound dismissive or belittling, so avoid them for things you mean to treat with respect.
They are the casual, feeling-laden cousins of など, which is the neutral 'and so on / such as'.

examples.ja: スポーツなんか全然興味がない。
examples.en: I have no interest at all in things like sports.
examples.f: スポーツなんか｜全然[ぜんぜん]｜興味[きょうみ]がない。

examples.ja: 君が負けるなんて、信じられない。
examples.en: You, losing? I can't believe it.
examples.f: ｜君[きみ]が｜負[ま]けるなんて、｜信[しん]じられない。

synonyms.note: など is the neutral 'such as / and so on'; なんか・なんて add a casual, often dismissive feeling.

entry.title: に際して
entry.meaning: on the occasion of; at the time of
entry.summary: に際して marks a special or significant occasion at which something is done — 入学に際して ('on the occasion of enrolling'). It is formal and reserved for notable events such as ceremonies, departures, or beginnings, not everyday moments.
pitfalls: Reserved for weighty, often one-time occasions; for ordinary, repeated times use 〜時 instead.
Very formal (speeches, notices, documents); overusing it in casual talk sounds stiff.

examples.ja: 契約に際して、こちらの書類にご記入ください。
examples.en: At the time of signing the contract, please fill in these documents.
examples.f: ｜契約[けいやく]に｜際[さい]して、こちらの｜書類[しょるい]にご｜記入[きにゅう]ください。

examples.ja: 卒業に際して、お世話になった先生に感謝の言葉を述べた。
examples.en: On the occasion of graduating, I expressed words of gratitude to the teacher who had helped me.
examples.f: ｜卒業[そつぎょう]に｜際[さい]して、お｜世話[せわ]になった｜先生[せんせい]に｜感謝[かんしゃ]の｜言葉[ことば]を｜述[の]べた。

synonyms.note: にあたって is a near-synonym for a special occasion; に際して leans slightly more formal and written.

related.note: に先立ち marks acting in advance of an event; に際して marks acting at the moment of the event itself.

entry.title: に伴って・に伴い
entry.kana: にともなって・にともない
entry.meaning: along with; as; accompanying (a change)
entry.summary: に伴って (and its stiffer form に伴い) links two changes: as the first situation develops or changes, a second one follows along with it as a natural accompaniment or consequence — 人口の増加に伴って = along with the rise in population. It attaches to a noun, or to a dictionary-form verb + の. The register is formal, common in news and reports.
pitfalls: Both sides normally describe a change or development, one accompanying the other; it is not used to join two static, unrelated facts.
に伴い is the more formal, written form of に伴って; the meaning is the same.

examples.ja: 経済の発展に伴って、人々の暮らしも大きく変わってきた。
examples.en: Along with economic development, people's lives have changed greatly as well.
examples.f: ｜経済[けいざい]の｜発展[はってん]に｜伴[ともな]って、｜人々[ひとびと]の｜暮[く]らしも｜大[おお]きく｜変[か]わってきた。

examples.ja: 台風の接近に伴い、多くの電車が運転を見合わせている。
examples.en: With the approach of the typhoon, many trains are suspending their service.
examples.f: ｜台風[たいふう]の｜接近[せっきん]に｜伴[ともな]い、｜多[おお]くの｜電車[でんしゃ]が｜運転[うんてん]を｜見合[みあ]わせている。

synonyms.note: につれて also links two gradual, proportional changes; に伴って also covers one-off consequences that accompany an event.
にしたがって likewise expresses one change tracking another; the two overlap closely in this 'as ~ changes' sense.

related.note: と共に can mean 'as ~ changes' too; に伴って foregrounds one change accompanying or causing another.

entry.title: に応じて
entry.meaning: depending on; in accordance with; to match ~
entry.summary: 〜に応じて means something varies flexibly in response to a changing condition — the result adjusts to fit it. 収入に応じて = 'according to income'. It attaches to nouns, and 〜に応じた modifies a following noun (要望に応じたプラン). The nuance is adaptation: as the condition changes, the outcome changes with it.
pitfalls: It implies flexible adjustment to a variable condition, with the outcome shifting to match it.
Use 〜に応じた (not 〜に応じて) when modifying a noun: 状況に応じた対応.

examples.ja: 収入に応じて、税金の額が変わります。
examples.en: The amount of tax changes according to your income.
examples.f: ｜収入[しゅうにゅう]に｜応[おう]じて、｜税金[ぜいきん]の｜額[がく]が｜変[か]わります。

examples.ja: お客様のご要望に応じて、プランを自由に選べます。
examples.en: You can freely choose a plan to match the customer's requests.
examples.f: お｜客様[きゃくさま]のご｜要望[ようぼう]に｜応[おう]じて、プランを｜自由[じゆう]に｜選[えら]べます。

synonyms.note: に従って means 'in accordance with / as ~ proceeds'; に応じて stresses flexibly adapting the result to a variable.
次第で means the outcome hinges on ~ ('depending on'); に応じて stresses proportional adjustment to the condition.

related.note: によって covers 'depending on / by means of / due to' broadly; に応じて specifically means adapting flexibly to fit.

entry.title: に反して
entry.meaning: contrary to; against; in contradiction to ~
entry.summary: に反して attaches to a noun and says the result runs counter to it — often 予想 (prediction), 期待 (expectation), or 意志 (will). 予想に反して = contrary to expectations. It marks a clash between what was anticipated or intended and what actually happened. Before a noun, switch to the form に反する (期待に反する結果).
pitfalls: It pairs with nouns like 予想, 期待, ルール, 意志; it is not attached directly to a plain verb clause.
Before a noun, use に反する: 予想に反する結果, not 予想に反して結果.

examples.ja: 予想に反して、試合は簡単に終わった。
examples.en: Contrary to expectations, the match ended easily.
examples.f: ｜予想[よそう]に｜反[はん]して、｜試合[しあい]は｜簡単[かんたん]に｜終[お]わった。

examples.ja: 両親の希望に反して、彼は大学をやめた。
examples.en: Against his parents' wishes, he quit university.
examples.f: ｜両親[りょうしん]の｜希望[きぼう]に｜反[はん]して、｜彼[かれ]は｜大学[だいがく]をやめた。

related.note: に対して contrasts two things or aims an action at a target; に反して stresses going against an expectation or rule.

entry.title: に基づいて
entry.meaning: based on; on the basis of; in accordance with ~
entry.summary: に基づいて marks the foundation that an action or judgment is built on — データに基づいて = based on the data, 事実に基づいて = based on the facts. What follows is done in line with that basis. Before a noun, use に基づく or に基づいた (事実に基づいた話). It has a somewhat formal, factual tone.
structure: Noun ＋ に基づく／に基づいた ＋ Noun
pitfalls: The basis takes に: 経験に基づいて, not 経験を基づいて.
It fits solid grounds like data, facts, rules, or experience; for 'according to (a source of information)', によると is the natural choice.

examples.ja: アンケートの結果に基づいて、新しい商品を作った。
examples.en: Based on the survey results, we made a new product.
examples.f: アンケートの｜結果[けっか]に｜基[もと]づいて、｜新[あたら]しい｜商品[しょうひん]を｜作[つく]った。

examples.ja: この映画は本当にあった事件に基づいています。
examples.en: This movie is based on a real incident.
examples.f: この｜映画[えいが]は｜本当[ほんとう]にあった｜事件[じけん]に｜基[もと]づいています。

related.note: をもとに means 'using X as material or reference'; に基づいて stresses conforming to X as a firm basis.
によると reports what a source says; に基づいて marks the grounds an action rests on.
にしたがって means following along with a rule or a change; に基づいて grounds a decision on a basis.

entry.title: にわたって
entry.meaning: throughout; over; spanning (a period or range)
entry.summary: にわたって marks that something extends across the whole of a span — a period, an area, or a range of items. 三日間にわたって = over (the full) three days; 全国にわたって = across the entire country. The noun before it names the scope. Before a noun, the form becomes にわたる (長期にわたる交渉). The register is formal and written.
pitfalls: The preceding noun states the extent covered (time, distance, area, or number), so it needs breadth, not a single point in time.
Before a noun, use にわたる (長期にわたる交渉), not にわたって.

examples.ja: 会議は数時間にわたって続き、参加者はみな疲れ切っていた。
examples.en: The meeting went on for hours on end, and all the participants were worn out.
examples.f: ｜会議[かいぎ]は｜数[すう]｜時間[じかん]にわたって｜続[つづ]き、｜参加[さんか]｜者[しゃ]はみな｜疲[つか]れ｜切[き]っていた。

examples.ja: この作家の作品は、幅広い世代にわたって読まれている。
examples.en: This author's works are read across a wide range of generations.
examples.f: この｜作家[さっか]の｜作品[さくひん]は、｜幅広[はばひろ]い｜世代[せだい]にわたって｜読[よ]まれている。

synonyms.note: を通じて・を通して also means 'throughout / across'; にわたって stresses the full breadth of the span, を通じて the continuity through it.
にかけて 'over / through' runs from one point to another; にわたって covers the entire extent of a range.

entry.title: に沿って
entry.meaning: along; in accordance with
entry.summary: に沿って has two linked senses: physically 'along' something long (川に沿って歩く = 'walk along the river') and figuratively 'in line with' a plan, rule, or wish (計画に沿って進める = 'proceed in accordance with the plan'). The core image is following the length or intent of something without departing from it.
structure: Noun ＋ に沿って／に沿った
pitfalls: It covers both a physical line (道路に沿って) and an abstract guideline (方針に沿って); context tells them apart.
The attributive form before a noun is に沿った: ご要望に沿った提案 ('a proposal in line with your wishes').

examples.ja: この道に沿ってまっすぐ行くと、右手に駅が見えます。
examples.en: If you go straight along this road, you'll see the station on your right.
examples.f: この｜道[みち]に｜沿[そ]ってまっすぐ｜行[い]くと、｜右手[みぎて]に｜駅[えき]が｜見[み]えます。

examples.ja: お客様のご希望に沿って、旅行の計画を立てました。
examples.en: In accordance with the customer's wishes, we drew up the travel plan.
examples.f: お｜客様[きゃくさま]のご｜希望[きぼう]に｜沿[そ]って、｜旅行[りょこう]の｜計画[けいかく]を｜立[た]てました。

synonyms.note: にしたがって means acting in obedience to a rule or instruction; に沿って means keeping in line with a plan, path, or wish.
に基づいて means grounding an action on a basis or source; に沿って means staying aligned with a guideline or intent.

related.note: に応えて means actively fulfilling a demand aimed at you; に沿って means proceeding in line with a plan or wish.

entry.title: に加えて
entry.meaning: in addition to; on top of
entry.summary: Noun＋に加えて stacks one thing on top of another — 家賃に加えて光熱費も ('on top of rent, utilities too'). It is a somewhat formal way to add an extra element of the same kind onto an existing base.
structure: Verb／い-adjective／な-adjective［plain form］＋ のに加えて
pitfalls: It attaches to a noun; to add a whole clause, nominalize with の — 忙しいのに加えて ('on top of being busy').
It quietly stacks a like item onto a base; unlike だけでなく it doesn't carry the 'not only ~ but even (surprisingly)' punch.

examples.ja: この地域は交通が便利なことに加えて、家賃も安い。
examples.en: This area has convenient transport, and on top of that the rent is cheap.
examples.f: この｜地域[ちいき]は｜交通[こうつう]が｜便利[べんり]なことに｜加[くわ]えて、｜家賃[やちん]も｜安[やす]い。

examples.ja: 強い風に加えて気温も下がり、外はとても寒くなった。
examples.en: In addition to the strong wind, the temperature dropped, and it got very cold outside.
examples.f: ｜強[つよ]い｜風[かぜ]に｜加[くわ]えて｜気温[きおん]も｜下[さ]がり、｜外[そと]はとても｜寒[さむ]くなった。

synonyms.note: 上に also piles one thing onto another and works after clauses too; に加えて is a touch more formal and noun-based.
だけでなく leans on a 'not only ~ but also' contrast; に加えて neutrally adds one item to another.

related.note: ばかりか adds a further, often stronger point ('not only ~ but even'); に加えて simply totals up two elements.

entry.title: をめぐって
entry.meaning: concerning; over (a matter of dispute)
entry.summary: をめぐって / をめぐる marks the central issue that people argue, debate, compete, or hold conflicting views about — 'over, concerning, surrounding'. It typically introduces a matter of contention involving several parties. Use をめぐる when modifying a following noun (をめぐる議論).
pitfalls: It implies multiple parties in disagreement or discussion around the topic, unlike the neutral 'about' of について.
Before a noun, switch to the form をめぐる: をめぐる論争, not をめぐって論争.

examples.ja: その土地の所有権をめぐって、二つの家族が長く争ってきた。
examples.en: Two families have long been in dispute over the ownership of that land.
examples.f: その｜土地[とち]の｜所有[しょゆう]｜権[けん]をめぐって、｜二[ふた]つの｜家族[かぞく]が｜長[なが]く｜争[あらそ]ってきた。

examples.ja: 新しい法案をめぐる議論が、国会で続いている。
examples.en: Debate over the new bill continues in the Diet.
examples.f: ｜新[あたら]しい｜法案[ほうあん]をめぐる｜議論[ぎろん]が、｜国会[こっかい]で｜続[つづ]いている。

synonyms.note: について is a neutral 'about / concerning' with no conflict implied; をめぐって suggests contention among parties.

related.note: において marks a domain or setting ('in, regarding'); をめぐって marks the specific issue people are at odds over.

entry.title: をきっかけに・がきっかけで
entry.kana: をきっかけに・がきっかけで
entry.romaji: o kikkake ni / ga kikkake de
entry.meaning: with ... as the trigger; taking ... as the start
entry.summary: をきっかけに(して) / がきっかけで marks an event as the trigger or occasion that set off a change, a new habit, or a development — 'taking X as the trigger, ever since X'. It is neutral about whether the result is good or bad, and belongs to everyday as well as written Japanese.
structure: Noun ＋ をきっかけに（して）
pitfalls: がきっかけで foregrounds X as the cause, while をきっかけに frames X as something taken up as a starting point.
It marks the trigger of a change; the following clause should describe the new development that resulted.

examples.ja: 入院をきっかけに、彼は食生活を見直すようになった。
examples.en: His hospital stay was the trigger for him to start rethinking his diet.
examples.f: ｜入院[にゅういん]をきっかけに、｜彼[かれ]は｜食生活[しょくせいかつ]を｜見直[みなお]すようになった。

examples.ja: ある本との出会いがきっかけで、彼女は作家を目指し始めた。
examples.en: An encounter with a certain book was the trigger, and she began aiming to become a writer.
examples.f: ある｜本[ほん]との｜出会[であ]いがきっかけで、｜彼女[かのじょ]は｜作家[さっか]を｜目指[めざ]し｜始[はじ]めた。

synonyms.note: を契機に is the more formal, written near-synonym; をきっかけに suits everyday triggers and small changes too.

entry.title: を除いて
entry.meaning: except for; excluding; apart from
entry.summary: を除いて / を除き sets one item aside from an otherwise general statement — 'except for, excluding, apart from'. What follows is presented as true for everything but the excepted thing: 日曜を除いて毎日 = 'every day except Sunday'.
pitfalls: を除き is the more formal, written form of を除いて.
It carves out a specific exception from a general claim; compare 以外, which is a more neutral, everyday 'other than'.

examples.ja: 日曜を除いて、この図書館は毎日利用できます。
examples.en: This library can be used every day except Sunday.
examples.f: ｜日曜[にちよう]を｜除[のぞ]いて、この｜図書館[としょかん]は｜毎日[まいにち]｜利用[りよう]できます。

examples.ja: 一部の地域を除き、明日は全国的に晴れるでしょう。
examples.en: Except for some areas, it will be sunny nationwide tomorrow.
examples.f: ｜一部[いちぶ]の｜地域[ちいき]を｜除[のぞ]き、｜明日[あした]は｜全国[ぜんこく]｜的[てき]に｜晴[は]れるでしょう。

synonyms.note: 以外 ('other than') is the everyday, neutral counterpart; を除いて more explicitly frames an item as an exception being removed.

entry.title: かねない
entry.meaning: might well (do something bad); could end up ~; is capable of
entry.summary: Verb stem + かねない says that an undesirable outcome is quite possible — 'might well happen / could well end up doing'. It always points to a bad or worrying result. It is the negated form of かねる, and the pair together are a favorite source of confusion.
pitfalls: It is only for undesirable possibilities: 事故を起こしかねない, never a welcome result.
Attach it to the ます-stem: やりかねない, not やるかねない.

examples.ja: そんな無理な計画では、失敗しかねない。
examples.en: With such an unreasonable plan, it could well end in failure.
examples.f: そんな｜無理[むり]な｜計画[けいかく]では、｜失敗[しっぱい]しかねない。

examples.ja: 寝不足が続くと、体を壊しかねません。
examples.en: If you keep going without enough sleep, you could well ruin your health.
examples.f: ｜寝不足[ねぶそく]が｜続[つづ]くと、｜体[からだ]を｜壊[こわ]しかねません。

synonyms.note: 恐れがある also warns of a bad possibility but is more formal and follows a dictionary-form verb or noun; かねない attaches to the stem.
かもしれない is a neutral 'might' for any outcome; かねない specifically implies the possibility is a bad one.

related.note: かねる (affirmative) means 'cannot / find it hard to do'; かねない is its negation but has drifted to mean 'might well (do something bad)'.

entry.title: かねる
entry.meaning: to be unable to; to find it hard to (do) — often a polite refusal
entry.summary: Verb stem + かねる means the speaker cannot, or finds it difficult to, do something. It very often works as a polite refusal — お答えしかねます softens a 'no'. It is not physical impossibility but an inability or reluctance given the circumstances, and it belongs to formal, business-like speech.
pitfalls: Attach it to the ます-stem: 分かりかねる, not 分かるかねる.
It is a formal way to decline, meaning 'I am not able to'; it does not literally mean 'I hate to'.

examples.ja: 申し訳ありませんが、その件についてはお答えしかねます。
examples.en: I'm very sorry, but I am unable to answer regarding that matter.
examples.f: ｜申し訳[もうしわけ]ありませんが、その｜件[けん]についてはお｜答[こた]えしかねます。

examples.ja: お客様のご要望には、こちらでは対応しかねます。
examples.en: We are unable to accommodate your request here.
examples.f: お｜客様[きゃくさま]のご｜要望[ようぼう]には、こちらでは｜対応[たいおう]しかねます。

synonyms.note: がたい also means 'hard to do' (理解しがたい), often about judgment or emotion; かねる leans toward being unable to, and to polite refusals.

related.note: かねない is the negation of かねる but has shifted to mean 'might well (do something bad)' rather than 'be unable to'.
にくい describes something being physically hard to do (書きにくい); かねる is more about inability or reluctance in a situation.

entry.title: ずにはいられない
entry.meaning: can't help but do; can't keep oneself from doing
entry.summary: ずにはいられない says you can't stop yourself from doing something — the urge or feeling is too strong to hold back. 笑わずにはいられない = can't help laughing. It's the formal, written partner of ないではいられない, and する becomes せずにはいられない.
structure: Verb［ない-form stem］＋ ずにはいられない
する → せずにはいられない
pitfalls: する becomes せずにはいられない, not しずにはいられない.
It describes a feeling or urge you can't suppress — usually your own; it's not for an outside obligation like "must, because the rules say so."

examples.ja: あの映画の最後は、泣かずにはいられなかった。
examples.en: At the end of that movie, I couldn't help crying.
examples.f: あの｜映画[えいが]の｜最後[さいご]は、｜泣[な]かずにはいられなかった。

examples.ja: 困っている人を見ると、助けずにはいられない。
examples.en: When I see someone in trouble, I can't help but help them.
examples.f: ｜困[こま]っている｜人[ひと]を｜見[み]ると、｜助[たす]けずにはいられない。

synonyms.note: ないではいられない means exactly the same; ずにはいられない is its more formal, written form.

related.note: 〜ざるを得ない is being forced to act by circumstances; ずにはいられない is an inner urge you can't hold back.
〜てたまらない is an unbearably strong feeling; ずにはいられない is an action you can't stop yourself from taking because of one.

entry.title: ざるを得ない
entry.meaning: have no choice but to ~; cannot help ~ing
entry.summary: 〜ざるを得ない attaches to a verb's ない-form base to say the speaker is forced by circumstances into the action, often reluctantly — 認めざるを得ない = have no choice but to admit it. Formal in tone, with する → せざるを得ない.
structure: Verb［ない form, drop ない］＋ ざるを得ない
する → せざるを得ない
pitfalls: Formed on the ない-base minus ない: 行かない → 行かざるを得ない.
Irregular: する → せざるを得ない, not しざるを得ない.
It conveys reluctant compulsion by outside circumstances, not a free personal choice.

examples.ja: 台風で、旅行を中止せざるを得なかった。
examples.en: Because of the typhoon, we had no choice but to cancel the trip.
examples.f: ｜台風[たいふう]で、｜旅行[りょこう]を｜中止[ちゅうし]せざるを｜得[え]なかった。

examples.ja: これだけ証拠があれば、事実を認めざるを得ない。
examples.en: With this much evidence, I have no choice but to admit the facts.
examples.f: これだけ｜証拠[しょうこ]があれば、｜事実[じじつ]を｜認[みと]めざるを｜得[え]ない。

synonyms.note: よりほかない also means 'nothing to do but'; ざるを得ない stresses reluctant compulsion by circumstance.
ないわけにはいかない is 'can't not do', driven by duty or social obligation; ざるを得ない is driven by unavoidable circumstances.
〜しかない is a plainer, more colloquial 'have no choice but'; ざるを得ない is more formal.

related.note: 〜ざる is the classical negative base on which this fixed pattern is built.

entry.title: てはいられない
entry.meaning: can't afford to stay ~; can't just keep ~ing
entry.summary: てはいられない is the negative potential of ている plus は — 'cannot remain in this state'. It says the speaker cannot afford to keep doing something or stay as they are because circumstances demand action — のんびりしてはいられない = 'I can't afford to take it easy'. It conveys urgency or emotional pressure to stop and act.
pitfalls: It means one cannot stay in the current action or state because something more pressing calls for action.
The driving force is often urgency or emotion — you feel you must not just sit still.

examples.ja: 締め切りが近いのだから、のんびりしてはいられない。
examples.en: The deadline is near, so I can't afford to take it easy.
examples.f: ｜締め切[しめき]りが｜近[ちか]いのだから、のんびりしてはいられない。

examples.ja: 友達が困っているのを、黙って見てはいられなかった。
examples.en: I couldn't just stand by and watch my friend struggle.
examples.f: ｜友達[ともだち]が｜困[こま]っているのを、｜黙[だま]って｜見[み]てはいられなかった。

synonyms.note: てばかりはいられない adds ばかり ('only'), stressing you can't do just that one thing forever; てはいられない is the plain 'can't stay as I am'.

entry.title: ものの
entry.meaning: although ~; even though ~; ~ but
entry.summary: 〜ものの concedes a fact and then presents something that runs counter to what it would lead you to expect — 'although X, (nevertheless) Y'. X is acknowledged as true, yet Y falls short of or contradicts the natural expectation. It is formal and written.
structure: な-adjective ＋ な／である ＋ ものの
Noun ＋ である ＋ ものの
pitfalls: The first clause is admitted as true; the second undercuts the expectation drawn from it — 'bought it, but haven't used it'.
It is written and formal; in speech けれど(も) covers the same 'although' more casually.

examples.ja: 新しいパソコンを買ったものの、忙しくてまだ一度も使っていない。
examples.en: Although I bought a new computer, I've been so busy I haven't used it even once.
examples.f: ｜新[あたら]しいパソコンを｜買[か]ったものの、｜忙[いそが]しくてまだ｜一[いち]｜度[ど]も｜使[つか]っていない。

examples.ja: 頭では理解しているものの、実際にやってみると難しい。
examples.en: Although I understand it in my head, when I actually try it, it's difficult.
examples.f: ｜頭[あたま]では｜理解[りかい]しているものの、｜実際[じっさい]にやってみると｜難[むずか]しい。

synonyms.note: けれども is an everyday 'but/although'; ものの is its more formal, written counterpart.
ながらも also concedes 'even while'; ものの concedes a completed fact, then reverses the expectation.

related.note: くせに concedes with blame or reproach; ものの is neutral concession.

entry.title: ものなら
entry.meaning: if (one could) ~; if it were possible to ~ (but it's hard)
entry.summary: 〜ものなら follows a potential verb to set up a difficult or unlikely 'if you could…' — できるものなら ('if it were at all possible'). It implies the thing is hard to achieve, and the main clause says what one would then do, often a wish. Note the separate, harsher 〜（よ）うものなら pattern.
structure: Verb［volitional］＋ ものなら ［if you dare］
pitfalls: With a potential verb it means 'if you could (but it's hard)': 戻れるものなら戻りたい ('I'd go back if only I could').
Don't confuse it with 〜（よ）うものなら (volitional + ものなら), which warns of dire consequences 'if one were to…'.

examples.ja: 帰れるものなら、今すぐ故郷に帰りたい。
examples.en: If only I could, I'd go back to my hometown right now.
examples.f: ｜帰[かえ]れるものなら、｜今[いま]すぐ｜故郷[こきょう]に｜帰[かえ]りたい。

examples.ja: できるものなら、あの日に戻ってやり直したい。
examples.en: If it were at all possible, I'd go back to that day and start over.
examples.f: できるものなら、あの｜日[ひ]に｜戻[もど]ってやり｜直[なお]したい。

synonyms.note: なら is a plain conditional; ものなら adds that the condition is hard or unlikely to meet.

related.note: 〜ようものなら (volitional) warns of dire results 'if one were to'; ものなら (potential) wishes 'if only one could'.

entry.title: ものがある
entry.meaning: there is something ~ about it; really is ~; you can genuinely feel ~
entry.summary: 〜ものがある says that something strongly possesses a certain quality, which the speaker senses — 心を打つものがある ('there is something moving about it'). It voices a heartfelt impression that X genuinely has some quality worth noting, warmer and more evaluative than a plain 〜だ.
structure: な-adjective ＋ な ＋ ものがある
pitfalls: It expresses the speaker's felt impression that X truly has some quality; it is warmer and more evaluative than a plain statement.
The subject is usually an experience, work, or performance that evokes the feeling, not a concrete object one 'has'.

examples.ja: 彼の長年の努力には、心を打つものがある。
examples.en: There is something truly moving about his many years of effort.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]の｜長年[ながねん]の｜努力[どりょく]には、｜心[こころ]を｜打[う]つものがある。

examples.ja: この作品の完成度の高さには、驚くべきものがある。
examples.en: The sheer polish of this work is genuinely astonishing.
examples.f: この｜作品[さくひん]の｜完成[かんせい]｜度[ど]の｜高[たか]さには、｜驚[おどろ]くべきものがある。

related.note: ものだ states a general truth or heartfelt exclamation; ものがある points to a specific quality the speaker strongly senses.

entry.title: ことか
entry.meaning: how …!; what …! (deep emotion)
entry.summary: ことか turns a statement into a heartfelt exclamation, usually paired with a question word like どんなに, どれほど, or なんと. It voices strong emotion — how happy, how worried, how long — rather than asking a real question. It has a slightly literary, emotional ring.
structure: どんなに／どれほど／なんと ＋ ［plain form］＋ ことか
pitfalls: It normally needs a degree word (どんなに, どれほど, なんと) to carry the exclamation; ことか alone does not do the job.
Despite the か, it is not a question — it is an emphatic outpouring of feeling.

examples.ja: 合格の知らせを聞いて、どんなにうれしかったことか。
examples.en: When I heard I had passed, oh, how happy I was!
examples.f: ｜合格[ごうかく]の｜知[し]らせを｜聞[き]いて、どんなにうれしかったことか。

examples.ja: この日をどれほど待っていたことか。
examples.en: How long I have waited for this day!
examples.f: この｜日[ひ]をどれほど｜待[ま]っていたことか。

related.note: ことに front-loads the emotion word to color a fact ('to my surprise, …'); ことか makes the whole line an exclamation of degree.
ものだ can voice deep feeling or fond recollection; ことか is specifically an exclamation of 'how much.'

entry.title: ことだから
entry.meaning: since it's ~ (given what we know of them); knowing ~
entry.summary: 〜ことだから builds a prediction on the known character of a person or group. Because we know what they are like, we can guess how they will act — 几帳面な彼のことだから遅れないだろう = knowing how punctual he is, he surely won't be late. It attaches to a noun (usually a person) + の.
structure: Noun［person／group］＋ の ＋ ことだから
pitfalls: The noun is normally a specific person or group you both know; the guess leans on their established character.
It sets up a prediction about that person's behavior, so it usually leads into だろう・にちがいない, not a plain statement of fact.

examples.ja: しっかり者の彼女のことだから、準備は完璧だろう。
examples.en: Knowing how dependable she is, her preparations are surely perfect.
examples.f: しっかり｜者[しゃ]の｜彼女[かのじょ]のことだから、｜準備[じゅんび]は｜完璧[かんぺき]だろう。

examples.ja: 約束を守る田中さんのことだから、きっと来てくれるはずだ。
examples.en: Since it's Tanaka, who always keeps his word, I'm sure he'll come.
examples.f: ｜約束[やくそく]を｜守[まも]る｜田中[たなか]さんのことだから、きっと｜来[き]てくれるはずだ。

related.note: だけに draws a heightened result from a known fact ('all the more because'); ことだから predicts behavior from someone's character.
こともあって states a contributing reason ('partly because'); ことだから predicts an action from what someone is like.

entry.title: ことなく
entry.meaning: without ~ing; never once ~ing
entry.summary: 〜ことなく attaches to a dictionary-form verb to mean 'without doing that action' — 休むことなく働いた = worked without resting. It is the more formal, written counterpart of 〜ないで／〜ずに, and often stresses that something carried on the whole time without that action ever interrupting it.
pitfalls: Attach it to the dictionary form (止まることなく), not the ない form.
It belongs to formal or written Japanese; in speech 〜ないで or 〜ずに is more natural.

examples.ja: 彼は最後まで諦めることなく、走り続けた。
examples.en: He kept running to the very end without ever giving up.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜最後[さいご]まで｜諦[あきら]めることなく、｜走[はし]り｜続[つづ]けた。

examples.ja: この工場は三十年間、一度も止まることなく稼働している。
examples.en: This factory has run for thirty years without stopping even once.
examples.f: この｜工場[こうじょう]は｜三[さん]｜十[じゅう]｜年間[ねんかん]、｜一[いち]｜度[ど]も｜止[と]まることなく｜稼働[かどう]している。

synonyms.note: ずに also means 'without doing'; ことなく is more formal and often more emphatic about continuity.
なしに attaches to a noun ('without ~'); ことなく attaches to a verb ('without doing ~').

entry.title: ことから
entry.meaning: from the fact that; judging from; owing to the fact that
entry.summary: ことから presents a fact as the grounds you reason from — 'from the fact that A, we can tell / it came about that B.' It often explains how a conclusion is reached, or how a name or reputation arose. The B clause is a judgment, result, or naming that follows from A.
pitfalls: ことから frames A as evidence you infer B from; plain から simply gives a cause, without that 'judging from' nuance.
な-adjectives and nouns take な／である before ことから (静かなことから, 有名であることから).

examples.ja: 窓が割れていたことから、どろぼうが入ったことが分かった。
examples.en: From the fact that the window was broken, we knew a burglar had gotten in.
examples.f: ｜窓[まど]が｜割[わ]れていたことから、どろぼうが｜入[はい]ったことが｜分[わ]かった。

examples.ja: 空が急に暗くなったことから、もうすぐ雨になると思った。
examples.en: Judging from how suddenly the sky darkened, I figured it would rain soon.
examples.f: ｜空[そら]が｜急[きゅう]に｜暗[くら]くなったことから、もうすぐ｜雨[あめ]になると｜思[おも]った。

related.note: から states a straightforward reason; ことから presents a fact as evidence you draw a conclusion from.
ので gives an objective cause for a result; ことから emphasizes reasoning outward from a known fact.
ことだから reasons from someone's known character; ことから reasons from an observed fact or circumstance.

entry.title: ことは〜が
entry.meaning: it's true that ~, but; ~, yes, but ~ (partial concession)
entry.summary: By repeating the same predicate around ことは and following with が, you concede a point partway before qualifying it — 話せることは話せるが (I can speak it, sure, but…). It admits the first half is true, then adds a reservation.
structure: ［plain form］＋ ことは ＋ ［same word, plain form］＋ が／けれど ＋ Sentence
pitfalls: Repeat the same predicate on both sides of ことは (高いことは高いが), not two different words.
It grants the point only partly; the real message lands in the が clause that follows.

examples.ja: 日本語が話せることは話せるが、まだ上手ではない。
examples.en: It's true I can speak Japanese, but I'm still not good at it.
examples.f: ｜日本語[にほんご]が｜話[はな]せることは｜話[はな]せるが、まだ｜上手[じょうず]ではない。

examples.ja: このかばんは、高いことは高いが、丈夫で長く使える。
examples.en: This bag is expensive, yes, but it's sturdy and lasts a long time.
examples.f: このかばんは、｜高[たか]いことは｜高[たか]いが、｜丈夫[じょうぶ]で｜長[なが]く｜使[つか]える。

related.note: けど simply joins a 'but' clause; ことは〜が specifically concedes the point half-heartedly before qualifying it.
ものの concedes an established fact then adds a contrary result; ことは〜が repeats the predicate to grant it only partly.
とはいえ is a formal 'that said'; ことは〜が is a colloquial 'true, but' built by repeating the word.

entry.title: あげく
entry.meaning: in the end; after all (following a long, often troublesome process)
entry.summary: 〜あげく marks that after much time, effort, or trouble, a result finally comes — and that result is usually undesirable or regrettable. さんざん迷ったあげく = after hesitating a great deal, in the end. It follows a た-form verb or a noun + の, and often appears as あげくに or あげくの果てに. Use it to stress that a drawn-out process led to a (frequently bad) outcome.
pitfalls: The following result is usually negative or regrettable, not a neutral or happy one.
Attach it to the た-form: 迷ったあげく, not 迷うあげく.

examples.ja: 長時間言い争ったあげく、結局結論は出なかった。
examples.en: After arguing for a long time, in the end no conclusion was reached.
examples.f: ｜長時間[ちょうじかん]｜言い争[いいあらそ]ったあげく、｜結局[けっきょく]｜結論[けつろん]は｜出[で]なかった。

examples.ja: さんざん悩んだあげくの決断だったが、後悔はしていない。
examples.en: It was a decision made after agonizing endlessly, but I have no regrets.
examples.f: さんざん｜悩[なや]んだあげくの｜決断[けつだん]だったが、｜後悔[こうかい]はしていない。

synonyms.note: た末に also marks 'after much ~, finally', but is more neutral and can lead to a positive result; あげく leans negative.

related.note: 結果 states a neutral 'as a result of ~'; あげく adds that the process was long and trying and the outcome regrettable.

entry.title: 上に
entry.meaning: on top of that; besides; not only ~ but also
entry.summary: 〜上に adds a second point in the same direction as the first — 'and on top of that'. 駅から近い上に = close to the station, and on top of that…. Both points lean the same way (both good, or both bad), so it stacks reasons rather than contrasting them.
pitfalls: 〜上に piles on a point in the same direction (good + good, or bad + bad); it does not contrast the way 一方で does.
Watch the attachment by word type: 近い上に (い-adj), 静かな上に (な-adj), 病気の上に (noun).

examples.ja: この部屋は駅から近い上に、家賃も安いです。
examples.en: This room is close to the station, and on top of that the rent is cheap.
examples.f: この｜部屋[へや]は｜駅[えき]から｜近[ちか]い｜上[うえ]に、｜家賃[やちん]も｜安[やす]いです。

examples.ja: 彼は約束の時間に遅れた上に、謝りもしませんでした。
examples.en: He was late for our appointment, and on top of that he didn't even apologize.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜約束[やくそく]の｜時間[じかん]に｜遅[おく]れた｜上[うえ]に、｜謝[あやま]りもしませんでした。

synonyms.note: 〜だけでなく ('not only ~ but also') adds a second item too; 〜上に leans more on 'and worse/better still, on top of that'.
〜のみならず is the stiff, written 'not only ~ but also'; 〜上に is everyday and stresses stacking a further point.
〜ばかりか adds a surprising further point ('not only ~ but even ~'); 〜上に simply piles on more of the same tendency.

related.note: 〜し loosely lists reasons or points; 〜上に more tightly stacks a second point on top of the first.

entry.title: 上で
entry.meaning: after doing ~ and then; upon ~; in the course of ~
entry.summary: With the past form or a noun + の, 〜上で means 'after deliberately doing X, then do Y' — 相談した上で = after discussing it, then… . With the dictionary form it means 'in the course of / for the purpose of' (生きる上で = in living / in life). The 'after' use marks a considered step taken before the next action.
pitfalls: With the past form (確認した上で) it means 'after taking step X, then do Y', and is more formal and deliberate than 〜てから.
With the dictionary form (働く上で) it shifts to 'in the course of / for the purpose of', not 'after'.

examples.ja: 家族とよく相談した上で、お返事します。
examples.en: I'll give you my answer after discussing it thoroughly with my family.
examples.f: ｜家族[かぞく]とよく｜相談[そうだん]した｜上[うえ]で、お｜返事[へんじ]します。

examples.ja: 契約書の内容をよく確認した上で、サインしてください。
examples.en: Please sign only after carefully checking the contents of the contract.
examples.f: ｜契約[けいやく]｜書[しょ]の｜内容[ないよう]をよく｜確認[かくにん]した｜上[うえ]で、サインしてください。

related.note: 〜てから is the everyday 'after doing'; 〜た上で is more formal and stresses X as a deliberate step taken before Y.
〜後で just orders two events in time; 〜た上で implies you do X on purpose as a basis for doing Y.

entry.title: 以上は
entry.meaning: now that; since; given that
entry.summary: 〜以上は presents an established fact as firm grounds, so that a fitting resolve, duty, or natural conclusion follows — 'now that ~, since ~'. 引き受けた以上は = now that I've taken it on, 約束した以上は = since I promised. The second clause typically expresses determination, obligation, or an inevitable consequence rather than a neutral remark.
pitfalls: 以上は gives a reason ('since / now that'); don't confuse it with 以上に ('more than').
The following clause carries resolve, obligation, or a natural conclusion — not a plain neutral statement.

examples.ja: 一度引き受けた以上は、最後まで責任を持ってやります。
examples.en: Now that I've taken it on, I'll see it through to the end with full responsibility.
examples.f: ｜一度[いちど]｜引き受[ひきう]けた｜以上[いじょう]は、｜最後[さいご]まで｜責任[せきにん]を｜持[も]ってやります。

examples.ja: 社会人である以上は、時間を守るのは当然のことだ。
examples.en: Since one is a working adult, keeping to schedule is only natural.
examples.f: ｜社会[しゃかい]｜人[じん]である｜以上[いじょう]は、｜時間[じかん]を｜守[まも]るのは｜当然[とうぜん]のことだ。

synonyms.note: からには is very close in meaning and more common in speech; 以上は is somewhat more formal.
上は also means 'now that', but is more literary and follows a verb of decision or action already taken.

entry.title: からには
entry.meaning: now that; since; given that (so one should ~)
entry.summary: [plain form] + からには means 'now that / since X is the case', and because it is so, the speaker draws a firm consequence: the main clause states a resolve, an obligation, or a natural expectation (should, must, of course). It commits the speaker more strongly than a plain から.
structure: Noun／な-adjective ＋ である ＋ からには
pitfalls: The main clause usually expresses determination or obligation (〜べきだ、〜つもりだ、〜なければならない), not a neutral fact.
It presents X as a settled premise; use it when a decision or situation is already fixed, not for a mere hypothesis.

examples.ja: 引き受けたからには、最後まで責任を持ってやり遂げます。
examples.en: Now that I've taken it on, I will see it through to the end and take full responsibility.
examples.f: ｜引き受[ひきう]けたからには、｜最後[さいご]まで｜責任[せきにん]を｜持[も]ってやり｜遂[と]げます。

examples.ja: 試合に出るからには、優勝を目指したい。
examples.en: Since I'm going to take part in the match, I want to aim for the championship.
examples.f: ｜試合[しあい]に｜出[で]るからには、｜優勝[ゆうしょう]を｜目指[めざ]したい。

synonyms.note: 以上は means much the same 'now that / since', and is nearly interchangeable; からには sounds a touch more conversational.
上は also means 'now that', but is more formal and written; からには is the everyday choice.

related.note: Plain から just gives a reason; からには adds that, given the premise, a matching resolve or obligation follows.

entry.title: からこそ
entry.meaning: precisely because; it is exactly because ~ that ~
entry.summary: 〜からこそ emphasizes that this reason, and no other, is the real cause — 家族がいるからこそがんばれる = it's precisely because I have a family that I can keep going. こそ highlights the から clause as the one decisive reason, often for something positive.
pitfalls: It stresses one reason as the true, decisive one; plain から just states a reason without that emphasis.
The main clause often takes のだ／んです to complete the 'that's exactly why…' feel.

examples.ja: 家族がいるからこそ、毎日がんばれる。
examples.en: It's precisely because I have a family that I can give it my all every day.
examples.f: ｜家族[かぞく]がいるからこそ、｜毎日[まいにち]がんばれる。

examples.ja: 難しいからこそ、挑戦する価値がある。
examples.en: Precisely because it's hard, it's worth taking on.
examples.f: ｜難[むずか]しいからこそ、｜挑戦[ちょうせん]する｜価値[かち]がある。

related.note: から just gives a reason; からこそ marks it as the one decisive reason.
こそ is the emphasis particle; からこそ applies that emphasis to a reason clause.

entry.title: からして
entry.meaning: even (starting with); judging from
entry.summary: からして has two related uses. After a noun it means 'even ~ / starting with ~': it picks one representative example to imply that the rest is the same — 態度からして = 'even his attitude, to begin with'. It can also mean 'judging from', presenting grounds for an evaluation.
pitfalls: In the 'even ~' use, the noun is a first, representative example implying the whole, and the following clause is usually an evaluation.
The 'even/starting with' sense often carries a critical or emphatic tone about the example chosen.

examples.ja: あの店は、店員の態度からして感じが悪い。
examples.en: At that shop, even the staff's attitude, for a start, is unpleasant.
examples.f: あの｜店[みせ]は、｜店員[てんいん]の｜態度[たいど]からして｜感[かん]じが｜悪[わる]い。

examples.ja: 名前からして、この料理は外国のものだと分かる。
examples.en: Just from the name, you can tell this dish is a foreign one.
examples.f: ｜名前[なまえ]からして、この｜料理[りょうり]は｜外国[がいこく]のものだと｜分[わ]かる。

synonyms.note: からすると / からすれば covers the 'judging from' sense; からして adds the distinct 'even (to begin with)' use that からすると lacks.

related.note: さえ also highlights an extreme example ('even ~'); からして presents its example as a starting point that implies the rest.

entry.title: からすると・からすれば
entry.kana: からすると・からすれば
entry.meaning: judging from; from the standpoint of; considering
entry.summary: Noun + からすると / からすれば presents the basis or standpoint of a judgment — 'going by X' or 'from X's point of view'. It may take a piece of evidence (この様子からすると) or a person's perspective (親からすれば), and the main clause states the conclusion drawn from it.
structure: Noun ＋ からすると／からすれば
pitfalls: It marks the grounds or viewpoint of an inference; the main clause is the conclusion, so it usually ends in a judgment (〜だろう、〜に違いない).
With a person, it gives that person's perspective, not necessarily the speaker's own opinion.

examples.ja: あの慌てぶりからすると、何か問題が起きたに違いない。
examples.en: Judging from how flustered he is, something must have gone wrong.
examples.f: あの｜慌[あわ]てぶりからすると、｜何[なに]か｜問題[もんだい]が｜起[お]きたに｜違[ちが]いない。

examples.ja: 親からすれば、子どもはいくつになっても心配なものだ。
examples.en: From a parent's point of view, you worry about your children no matter how old they get.
examples.f: ｜親[おや]からすれば、｜子[こ]どもはいくつになっても｜心配[しんぱい]なものだ。

synonyms.note: から見ると frames the same idea as a viewpoint one 'looks from'; からすると is essentially interchangeable in the 'judging from' sense.
からして also means 'judging from', but additionally has an 'even (to begin with)' use that からすると does not.

related.note: によると cites a source of information ('according to'); からすると draws the speaker's own inference from evidence or a standpoint.

entry.title: 際に
entry.meaning: when; on the occasion of; at the time of
entry.summary: 際に is a formal 'when' for notable occasions or special situations — applying for something, visiting on business, a ceremony. You meet it often in written notices and polite speech; in everyday conversation とき does the same job more plainly.
pitfalls: 際に is formal and suits special or official occasions; for ordinary everyday 'when,' use とき.
A noun takes の before it: 卒業の際に, not 卒業際に.

examples.ja: お申し込みの際に、身分証明書が必要です。
examples.en: When you apply, you will need a form of identification.
examples.f: お｜申し込[もうしこ]みの｜際[さい]に、｜身分[みぶん]｜証明[しょうめい]｜書[しょ]が｜必要[ひつよう]です。

examples.ja: 東京へ出張した際に、旧友と会った。
examples.en: When I was in Tokyo on a business trip, I met up with an old friend.
examples.f: ｜東京[とうきょう]へ｜出張[しゅっちょう]した｜際[さい]に、｜旧友[きゅうゆう]と｜会[あ]った。

related.note: とき is the neutral, everyday 'when'; 際に is its formal counterpart for notable occasions.
最中に means 'right in the middle of an ongoing action'; 際に marks the occasion or moment when you do something.

entry.title: 次第
entry.meaning: as soon as ~; depending on ~
entry.summary: 次第 has two jobs. After a verb stem it means "as soon as ~; the moment ~ is done" (連絡がつき次第 = as soon as I get in touch), and the following clause looks to the future — a plan or request. After a noun it means "depends on ~" (天気次第 = depends on the weather). It's a formal expression common in business and announcements.
pitfalls: With the "as soon as" use, what follows is a plan or request that hasn't happened yet — don't put a past-tense result after it.
It's formal; for casual "as soon as" in everyday speech, 〜たらすぐに is more natural.

examples.ja: 準備ができ次第、出発します。
examples.en: We'll set off as soon as the preparations are ready.
examples.f: ｜準備[じゅんび]ができ｜次第[しだい]、｜出発[しゅっぱつ]します。

examples.ja: 参加するかどうかは、あなた次第です。
examples.en: Whether or not to take part is up to you.
examples.f: ｜参加[さんか]するかどうかは、あなた｜次第[しだい]です。

related.note: 〜次第で extends the noun use to "depending on ~, the outcome varies."
次第に uses the same kanji but means "gradually" — a different point entirely.
〜たとたん is a spontaneous, often surprising past event; 次第 looks ahead to a planned action.

entry.title: た末に・の末に
entry.romaji: ta sue ni / no sue ni
entry.meaning: after (much) ~; finally, at the end of
entry.summary: 末に marks a long or difficult process that finally leads to a result — 'after much ~, in the end...'. It stresses that the outcome came only after considerable effort, hesitation, or hardship. The result may be good or bad, but the focus is the drawn-out road to it.
pitfalls: Use the た-form for verbs (悩んだ末に) and の for nouns (議論の末に).
It stresses a result reached after a prolonged process; for a simple sequence 'after doing', use 〜てから instead.

examples.ja: さんざん迷った末に、留学することを決めた。
examples.en: After endless hesitation, I finally decided to study abroad.
examples.f: さんざん｜迷[まよ]った｜末[すえ]に、｜留学[りゅうがく]することを｜決[き]めた。

examples.ja: 長い議論の末に、計画は中止と決まった。
examples.en: After lengthy discussion, it was decided in the end that the plan would be scrapped.
examples.f: ｜長[なが]い｜議論[ぎろん]の｜末[すえ]に、｜計画[けいかく]は｜中止[ちゅうし]と｜決[き]まった。

synonyms.note: あげく also means 'in the end after ~', but almost always leads to a bad or unwanted outcome; 末に is neutral.

related.note: 結果 focuses on the outcome '(as) a result of'; 末に stresses the long process that led there.

entry.title: 〜たところで
entry.meaning: even if (one does/did) ~, it would be no use
entry.summary: 〜たところで sets up a hypothetical and dismisses it as futile: even if you do X, the result won't help. The main clause is negative or pointless — 急いだところで間に合わない = even if I hurry, I won't make it. Though it uses the た-form, it refers to a hypothetical or future action, and often follows いくら or 今さら.
pitfalls: The main clause is negative or futile: 'even if ~, it won't help' — not a neutral 'even if'.
It takes the た-form but points to a hypothetical/future action, not a past one.

examples.ja: 今から走ったところで、終電には間に合わないだろう。
examples.en: Even if I run now, I still won't make the last train.
examples.f: ｜今[いま]から｜走[はし]ったところで、｜終電[しゅうでん]には｜間に合[まにあ]わないだろう。

examples.ja: いくら悔やんだところで、過ぎたことはもう戻らない。
examples.en: No matter how much you regret it, what's done can't be undone.
examples.f: いくら｜悔[く]やんだところで、｜過[す]ぎたことはもう｜戻[もど]らない。

synonyms.note: たって is a casual 'even if'; たところで adds the specific nuance that the effort would be pointless.
ても is a neutral 'even if'; たところで strongly implies the outcome would be futile.

entry.title: たところ
entry.meaning: have just finished doing (this very moment)
entry.summary: Verb［た form］＋ ところ marks an action that finished a moment ago — you are right at the point just after it. It pins the event to the immediate present on a timeline, so it fits sentences like 'I just this second arrived.'
structure: Verb［た form］＋ ところ（だ／です）
pitfalls: 〜たところ is the moment just after finishing; 〜ているところ is the middle of doing, and 〜るところ is about to start.
Compared with 〜たばかり, 〜たところ points to the exact moment, while 〜たばかり just feels 'not long ago.'

examples.ja: 今、駅に着いたところです。
examples.en: I've just arrived at the station right now.
examples.f: ｜今[いま]、｜駅[えき]に｜着[つ]いたところです。

examples.ja: ご飯を食べたところだから、おなかがいっぱいだ。
examples.en: I just finished eating, so I'm full.
examples.f: ご｜飯[はん]を｜食[た]べたところだから、おなかがいっぱいだ。

synonyms.note: 〜たばかり also means 'just did,' but stresses little time has passed rather than the exact moment.

related.note: 〜ているところ is in the middle of doing; 〜たところ is the moment just after finishing.
〜るところ is about to do; 〜たところ has just done.

entry.title: ばかりか
entry.meaning: not only ~ but even ~
entry.summary: 〜ばかりか means 'not only ~ but even ~' — it states one thing and then adds a second, usually more extreme or surprising, that goes beyond it. 手伝ってくれないばかりか、邪魔までした = not only did he not help, he even got in the way. The added part often takes も or さえ. It attaches to nouns and plain-form clauses.
pitfalls: The second element usually escalates beyond the first (often with も／さえ); it is not for adding a merely equal, neutral point.
The added fact is frequently unexpected or worse, so ばかりか often carries an emotional or evaluative colouring.

examples.ja: 彼は約束を破ったばかりか、謝ろうともしなかった。
examples.en: Not only did he break his promise, he didn't even try to apologize.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜約束[やくそく]を｜破[やぶ]ったばかりか、｜謝[あやま]ろうともしなかった。

examples.ja: その店は値段が安いばかりか、味も素晴らしいと評判だ。
examples.en: That restaurant has a reputation for being not only cheap but delicious on top of it.
examples.f: その｜店[みせ]は｜値段[ねだん]が｜安[やす]いばかりか、｜味[あじ]も｜素晴[すば]らしいと｜評判[ひょうばん]だ。

synonyms.note: だけでなく 'not only ~ but also' is neutral; ばかりか adds a stronger, often surprising second point.
のみならず is the formal 'not only ~ but also'; ばかりか highlights an escalating, often unexpected addition.
どころか 'far from ~, on the contrary'; ばかりか adds to the first fact, while どころか overturns it.

related.note: さえ 'even'; ばかりか frequently pairs with も／さえ in the added clause to mark the extra element.

entry.title: ばかりに
entry.meaning: simply because; all because of; on account of (leading to an unwelcome result)
entry.summary: ばかりに points to a single cause and blames an unfortunate outcome on it — 'all because of just this, that bad thing happened.' It carries a note of regret or frustration, so the result is almost always negative. Typically the clause before ばかりに is a plain-form verb, often in the past (忘れたばかりに = all because I forgot).
structure: な-adjective＋ な／Noun＋ である ＋ ばかりに
pitfalls: The result is almost always something bad or regrettable; ばかりに doesn't fit happy outcomes.
It pins the blame on one single cause, unlike a neutral から／ので — the nuance is 'only because of this one thing, unfortunately...'.

examples.ja: 少し油断したばかりに、試合に負けてしまった。
examples.en: All because I let my guard down for a moment, I ended up losing the match.
examples.f: ｜少[すこ]し｜油断[ゆだん]したばかりに、｜試合[しあい]に｜負[ま]けてしまった。

examples.ja: パスポートを忘れたばかりに、旅行に行けなかった。
examples.en: Simply because I forgot my passport, I couldn't go on the trip.
examples.f: パスポートを｜忘[わす]れたばかりに、｜旅行[りょこう]に｜行[い]けなかった。

synonyms.note: せいで also blames a cause for a bad result; ばかりに stresses that it was just this one thing that caused it.

related.note: だけに means 'precisely because' and works for good or bad results; ばかりに points to a single cause and expects a bad one.

entry.title: ばかりだ
entry.meaning: keeps only getting ~ (a one-way change, usually for the worse)
entry.summary: A dictionary-form change verb plus ばかりだ says a situation keeps moving in a single direction, with nothing to stop it — 病気は悪くなるばかりだ = the illness just keeps getting worse. It usually carries a negative, worsening tone: things go on changing one way only. The verb is a change verb in dictionary form.
pitfalls: This ばかりだ takes a dictionary-form change verb and means 'keeps heading one way (often worse)'; it differs from 〜たばかり ('just did') and from plain 〜ばかり ('only').
It leans negative — a one-way slide; 〜一方だ is close but ばかりだ stresses that nothing improves.

examples.ja: 物の値段は、上がるばかりだ。
examples.en: Prices just keep on rising.
examples.f: ｜物[もの]の｜値段[ねだん]は、｜上[あ]がるばかりだ。

examples.ja: 練習しないと、下手になるばかりですよ。
examples.en: If you don't practice, you'll only get worse.
examples.f: ｜練習[れんしゅう]しないと、｜下手[へた]になるばかりですよ。

related.note: 〜一方だ also marks a one-way change; 〜ばかりだ adds the sense that nothing stops or improves it.
〜たばかり means 'just did (moments ago)'; 〜ばかりだ with the dictionary form means a situation keeps changing one way.
〜ばかりで lists 'only this, nothing else'; 〜ばかりだ marks a steady one-way change.

entry.title: はともかく
entry.meaning: setting ~ aside; regardless of ~; never mind ~, the point is
entry.summary: 〜はともかく sets a topic aside as not the point right now, shifting the focus to what follows — 'never mind X, the real issue is Y'. Often 〜はともかく(として). X is downplayed as secondary here, not dismissed as unimportant in general.
structure: Noun ＋ はともかく（として）
Sentence ＋ か ＋ はともかく（として）
pitfalls: It parks X as 'not what matters now' and moves to a more important Y; it doesn't claim X is worthless overall, only that we're leaving it aside here.
After a question-like clause it takes か: 行くかどうかはともかく ('setting aside whether to go').

examples.ja: 味はともかく、この店は値段が安くて助かる。
examples.en: Taste aside, this shop is cheap, which is a real help.
examples.f: ｜味[あじ]はともかく、この｜店[みせ]は｜値段[ねだん]が｜安[やす]くて｜助[たす]かる。

examples.ja: 結果はともかく、最後まで全力を尽くしたことに意味がある。
examples.en: Regardless of the outcome, there is meaning in having given it my all to the end.
examples.f: ｜結果[けっか]はともかく、｜最後[さいご]まで｜全力[ぜんりょく]を｜尽[つ]くしたことに｜意味[いみ]がある。

related.note: を問わず means 'regardless of any value of X'; はともかく sets one specific X aside to focus on Y.

entry.title: 〜はさておき
entry.meaning: setting ~ aside; leaving ~ aside for now
entry.summary: 〜はさておき sets one topic aside in order to move on to a more pressing or important one — 'leaving ~ aside, let's get to ~'. 冗談はさておき = joking aside, 建前はさておき = setting the official line aside. It attaches to a noun and is a common way to pivot from a lesser matter to the real point at hand.
pitfalls: It attaches directly to a noun (冗談はさておき), signalling a deliberate pivot to the main issue.
The item set aside is simply postponed as less urgent, not judged; it does not carry the critical 'neglecting' tone of 〜はそっちのけで.

examples.ja: 冗談はさておき、そろそろ本題に入りましょう。
examples.en: Joking aside, let's get down to the main topic.
examples.f: ｜冗談[じょうだん]はさておき、そろそろ｜本題[ほんだい]に｜入[はい]りましょう。

examples.ja: 味はさておき、この店は雰囲気だけは抜群にいい。
examples.en: Taste aside, this restaurant's atmosphere alone is outstanding.
examples.f: ｜味[あじ]はさておき、この｜店[みせ]は｜雰囲気[ふんいき]だけは｜抜群[ばつぐん]にいい。

synonyms.note: はともかく also brackets a matter off; はさておき leans more on 'setting it aside to move on to the main point'.

related.note: はそっちのけで is neglecting a duty to do something else and sounds critical; はさておき is a neutral shift of topic.

entry.title: 反面
entry.meaning: on the other hand; while; but at the same time
entry.summary: 〜反面 attaches to a clause to point out a contrasting side of the very same thing — one quality alongside its opposite. 便利な反面 = 'convenient, but on the other side…'. The two facets belong to a single subject.
pitfalls: It contrasts two sides of one and the same subject; use 一方で to contrast two different subjects or situations.
With な-adjectives use な (便利な反面) and with nouns use である (医者である反面).

examples.ja: この仕事は収入が高い反面、責任もとても重い。
examples.en: This job pays well, but on the other side the responsibility is very heavy too.
examples.f: この｜仕事[しごと]は｜収入[しゅうにゅう]が｜高[たか]い｜反面[はんめん]、｜責任[せきにん]もとても｜重[おも]い。

examples.ja: 都会の生活は便利な反面、家賃がとても高い。
examples.en: City life is convenient, but on the flip side the rent is very high.
examples.f: ｜都会[とかい]の｜生活[せいかつ]は｜便利[べんり]な｜反面[はんめん]、｜家賃[やちん]がとても｜高[たか]い。

related.note: 一方で contrasts two separate things; 反面 contrasts two sides of the same one.
代わりに frames a trade-off ('in exchange'); 反面 just notes an opposite quality coexisting.

entry.title: ながらも
entry.meaning: although; even though; despite ~
entry.summary: ながらも is a concessive connector: it links two clauses that clash, meaning 'although / despite'. It attaches to a verb ます-stem, an い-adjective, a な-adjective, or a noun — 忙しいと言いながらも ('although he says he's busy'), 狭いながらも ('cramped though it is'). The も makes the contrast explicit, so what follows goes against what the first part leads you to expect.
pitfalls: This is the concessive ながら ('although'), not the ながら of two simultaneous actions ('while doing'); the added も signals the contrast.
The two clauses must clash — the second goes against what you would expect from the first.

examples.ja: 彼は忙しいと言いながらも、いつも手伝ってくれる。
examples.en: Even though he says he's busy, he always helps me out.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜忙[いそが]しいと｜言[い]いながらも、いつも｜手伝[てつだ]ってくれる。

examples.ja: 狭いながらも、自分の部屋を持てて嬉しい。
examples.en: Cramped though it is, I'm happy to have my own room.
examples.f: ｜狭[せま]いながらも、｜自分[じぶん]の｜部屋[へや]を｜持[も]てて｜嬉[うれ]しい。

synonyms.note: Plain concessive ながら carries the same 'although'; ながらも just states the contrast more firmly.
ものの also means 'although' but is more written; ながらも attaches tightly to a stem or adjective.

related.note: のに often adds complaint or dissatisfaction; ながらも is a neutral concessive.

entry.title: つつある
entry.meaning: to be in the process of ~; to be gradually ~ing
entry.summary: つつある attaches to the ます-stem to say a change is steadily under way and moving toward a certain state — 減りつつある = 'is gradually decreasing', 回復しつつある = 'is on the way to recovering'. It emphasizes a continuous progression in one direction and, like つつ, has a formal, written flavor. It pairs most naturally with verbs of change.
pitfalls: Attach it to the ます-stem: 変わりつつある, not 変わるつつある.
Unlike a plain ている, つつある stresses a gradual, ongoing shift toward a new state, so it suits change verbs (増える, 減る, 治る) rather than momentary actions.
It is formal and largely written; in conversation ている is more usual.

examples.ja: この町の人口は、年々減りつつある。
examples.en: The population of this town is steadily declining year by year.
examples.f: この｜町[まち]の｜人口[じんこう]は、｜年々[ねんねん]｜減[へ]りつつある。

examples.ja: 医療技術の進歩で、その病気は治りつつある。
examples.en: With advances in medical technology, that illness is gradually being cured.
examples.f: ｜医療[いりょう]｜技術[ぎじゅつ]の｜進歩[しんぽ]で、その｜病気[びょうき]は｜治[なお]りつつある。

related.note: Plain つつ means 'while doing ~' (two simultaneous actions); つつある means a single change is ongoing.

entry.title: っぱなし
entry.meaning: leaving something in a state (often through neglect); leaving it on/open/as-is
entry.summary: っぱなし attaches to the ます-stem and means leaving the result of an action in place — the light left on (つけっぱなし), the door left open (開けっぱなし). It usually carries a hint of carelessness: you did something and neglected to undo it. It can also describe an action that just keeps going without a break.
pitfalls: Attach it to the stem: つけっぱなし, not つけるっぱなし.
It usually implies something was left the way it shouldn't be (negligence), unlike the neutral まま.

examples.ja: 電気をつけっぱなしにして出かけてしまった。
examples.en: I went out and left the lights on.
examples.f: ｜電気[でんき]をつけっぱなしにして｜出[で]かけてしまった。

examples.ja: 窓を開けっぱなしにしていたら、部屋が寒くなった。
examples.en: I'd left the window open, and the room got cold.
examples.f: ｜窓[まど]を｜開[あ]けっぱなしにしていたら、｜部屋[へや]が｜寒[さむ]くなった。

related.note: まま neutrally states a state left unchanged; っぱなし adds the nuance that leaving it that way was careless.

entry.title: 〜抜く
entry.meaning: to do all the way through; to see through to the end (despite hardship)
entry.summary: 〜抜く attaches to the ます-stem and says an action was carried all the way to the end, usually against difficulty — 走り抜く = run all the way through, 考え抜く = think something through completely, やり抜く = see it through to the finish. The nuance is persistence and endurance, not mere completion. It conjugates as an う-verb (抜いた, 抜いて).
pitfalls: Attach it to the stem: やり抜く, not やる抜く.
〜抜く stresses enduring through hardship to the finish, while 〜切る stresses using something up or reaching a clean end — 戦い抜く (fight all the way through) vs 使い切る (use it all up).

examples.ja: どんなに苦しくても、最後まで走り抜くつもりだ。
examples.en: No matter how hard it gets, I intend to run all the way to the finish.
examples.f: どんなに｜苦[くる]しくても、｜最後[さいご]まで｜走り抜[はしりぬ]くつもりだ。

examples.ja: 悩み抜いた末に、彼女は会社を辞める決心をした。
examples.en: After agonizing over it thoroughly, she made up her mind to quit the company.
examples.f: ｜悩み抜[なやみぬ]いた｜末[すえ]に、｜彼女[かのじょ]は｜会社[かいしゃ]を｜辞[や]める｜決心[けっしん]をした。

synonyms.note: 〜切る also means 'do thoroughly / completely'; 抜く emphasizes persevering through hardship, 切る emphasizes finishing off entirely.
〜通す means 'keep doing all the way through'; 抜く adds the sense of pushing through difficulty to the end.

related.note: 〜終わる neutrally marks finishing an action; 抜く adds the effort and endurance of reaching the end.

entry.title: がたい
entry.meaning: hard to bring oneself to; difficult (almost impossible) to do
entry.summary: 〜がたい attaches to the ます-stem and marks an action as hard, sometimes nearly impossible, to do — 信じがたい = hard to believe, 忘れがたい = unforgettable. It is formal and rather literary, and pairs with a limited set of verbs of thinking, feeling, and perception. The whole compound behaves like an い-adjective.
pitfalls: It joins only a narrow set of verbs (信じる, 想像する, 理解する, 忘れる, 認める); it does not combine freely with any verb the way にくい does.
More formal and written than 〜にくい; in casual speech people usually say にくい or づらい instead.
Attach it to the stem: 信じがたい, not 信じるがたい.

examples.ja: 彼が嘘をついたなんて、信じがたい話だ。
examples.en: The idea that he told a lie is hard to believe.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]が｜嘘[うそ]をついたなんて、｜信[しん]じがたい｜話[はなし]だ。

examples.ja: あの日の景色は、今でも忘れがたい。
examples.en: The scenery of that day is unforgettable even now.
examples.f: あの｜日[ひ]の｜景色[けしき]は、｜今[いま]でも｜忘[わす]れがたい。

synonyms.note: 〜にくい is the everyday 'hard to do'; がたい is formal and limited to a few verbs of thought and perception.
〜づらい is 'hard/uncomfortable to do', often physical or social; がたい is a more abstract 'hard to bring oneself to'.

antonyms.note: 〜やすい 'easy to do' is the plain opposite of this difficulty family.

entry.title: ようがない
entry.meaning: there's no way to ~; it's impossible to ~ (no means available)
entry.summary: The ます-stem plus ようがない says there is no method or means to do something, so it simply can't be done — 連絡しようがない = there's no way to get in touch. It stresses a missing means rather than a lack of ability. Also written 〜ようもない.
structure: Verb［stem］＋ ようがない／ようもない
pitfalls: Attach it to the stem: 直しようがない, not 直すようがない.
It means 'no means to do it'; 'no way that [it's true]' (logical) is わけがない.

examples.ja: 住所がわからないので、手紙を送りようがない。
examples.en: I don't know the address, so there's no way to send the letter.
examples.f: ｜住所[じゅうしょ]がわからないので、｜手紙[てがみ]を｜送[おく]りようがない。

examples.ja: こんなに壊れていては、もう直しようがない。
examples.en: It's broken this badly — there's just no way to fix it now.
examples.f: こんなに｜壊[こわ]れていては、もう｜直[なお]しようがない。

related.note: わけがない denies that something could be true (logic); ようがない denies there's any means to do it.
ことができる is 'able to do'; ようがない is the flat 'no way to do it at all'.

entry.title: てならない
entry.meaning: can't help feeling ~; ~ terribly
entry.summary: てならない follows the て-form to say a feeling or impression wells up beyond the speaker's control — 気になってならない = 'I can't help worrying', 思えてならない = 'I can't help feeling that ...'. It often attaches to verbs of spontaneous thought and emotion. Similar to てたまらない, it leans somewhat formal and is especially common with 気がする, 思える, and the like.
pitfalls: It works best with spontaneous feelings and impressions (思えてならない, 気になってならない), not deliberate actions.
It is a touch more formal and written than てたまらない, which sounds more everyday.

examples.ja: 試験の結果が気になってならない。
examples.en: I can't help worrying about the exam results.
